#3257. Navigator (NVGS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record vessel-sale profits offset softer July and August utilization.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Navigator Holdings Ltd. (NVGS +0.74%) reported record reported net income for the third quarter of 2026, primarily supported by significant gains from the sale of non-core vessels in the Unigas pool. Management stated that the underlying shipping business remained profitable despite expected seasonal moderation in utilization and freight rates during the early part of the quarter. The company completed the divestment of eight smaller vessels and secured long-term financing for its entire six-vessel newbuilding program, which is scheduled for deliveries over the next two years. Leadership highlighted a significant reduction in net leverage and a strengthened liquidity position, which supports an increased fixed dividend and an expanded share repurchase program.

Randy Giveans: Welcome to The third quarter 2026 financial results. On today's call, we have Mads Peter Zacho, Chief Executive Officer, Gary Chapman, Chief Financial Officer, Øyvind Lindeman, Chief Commercial Officer, and myself, Randy Giveans, Chief Investor Relations Officer. I must advise you that this conference call is being recorded today. As we conduct today's presentation, we will be making various forward-looking statements, and these statements include, but are not limited to, the future expectations, plans, and prospects from both a financial and operational perspective, and are based on our assumptions, forecasts, and expectations as of today's date, November 4th, 2026, and as such, are subject to material risk and uncertainties.

Actual results may differ significantly from our forward-looking information and financial results. Additional information about these factors and assumptions are included in our annual and quarterly reports filed with the SEC. With that, I now pass the floor to our CEO, Mads Peter Zacho. Please go ahead.

Mads Peter Zacho: Thank you. Good morning and good afternoon, and thank you so much for joining this Navigator earnings call for Q3 2026. Before I turn to the quarter, let me briefly touch on the Middle East. Conditions in the Strait of Hormuz have not materially improved, and from our perspective, and since we have not had any ships trading in the strait over the past eight months, the effect continues to be primarily commercial and positive. The disruption is supporting U.S. natural gas liquids and petrochemical exports, while longer voyages continue to add ton-miles. Please turn to slide number four. Q3 was another strong quarter for Navigator Gas.

We delivered record reported net income and EPS, supported by gains from our vessel sales. At the same time, our underlying business remained solid through what we had expected would be a seasonally softer quarter. TCE averaged just over $30,000 per day. Utilization was softer during July and August, but importantly, recovered to around 94% in September. That recovery has continued unabated into the start of the fourth quarter. For me, the key message this quarter is not really so much where we started Q3, it is where we finished it and the position that we are in today. Our markets are firm. Our balance sheet is stronger, with net leverage now down to 1.7x adjusted EBITDA.

We have completed the Unigas transaction, generating approximately $183 million of proceeds and around $70 million of profit across Q3 and Q4. Again, evidence to how we consistently sell high-quality yet older non-core assets well above book value, and thereby generating solid sales gains. All six of our new buildings are now fully financed at some of the lowest margins ever achieved by Navigator. Our planned U.K. redomiciliation remains on track, with shareholder approval to be sought on November 16th, 2026, and completion targeted by year-end 2026. More importantly, the fundamentals around our core markets continue to strengthen. U.S. export capacity for natural gas liquids, such as propane and ethane, continues to grow.

The handysize order book remains very limited at around 7%, while 17% of the existing fleet is already more than 25 years of age. That is the supply and demand picture that we really like. Looking into Q4, we are seeing higher utilization and higher TCE rates. We also expect volumes at our ethylene export terminal to recover from the seasonally softer third quarter. We end the final quarter of the year with good momentum, very strong balance sheet, and considerable flexibility to continue investing in the business while returning substantial capital to the shareholders. Over to you, Gary. Please tell us a little bit about the financial details.

Gary Chapman: Thanks, Mads, and hello, everyone. Following on from our last call in August, the third quarter unfolded broadly as we anticipated. After our exceptional second quarter, chartering activity moderated in the early part of the third quarter as customers reduced inventories and delayed purchases. But importantly, that did not pause the underlying picture. Utilization recovered to approximately 94% in September. At the same time, we completed sales under the Unigas transaction, reduced our leverage, further funded our newbuild program, and continued to return capital to shareholders. So the financial story this quarter is not simply our reported profit, but also the strengthening of our platform beneath it.

Turning to slide six, average TCE was $30,314 per day, down from last quarter's all-time high of close to $34,000, and only about 2% below the $30,966 of the third quarter a year ago. This was a moderation we guided to back in August. Utilization was 87.9% for the quarter, compared with 90.8% last quarter and 89.3% in the third quarter of 2025. It was very much a quarter of two halves, around 85% in July and August, recovering to approximately 94% in September, with utilization remaining firm through October. Total operating revenues were $155 million, slightly above the $153 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Voyage expenses were higher, principally reflecting higher bunker costs on spot voyages, which are largely passed through in revenue to our customers. Vessel operating expenses in the quarter were $42.8 million, down 13% on last year, reflecting our reduced fleet size, and also down on a per vessel per day basis at $8,928 from $9,275 a year ago, reflecting the timing of costs and project-related expenses. However, our forecast for vessel operating expenses for the full-year remains at $9,250 per day per vessel. Reported EBITDA reached a record $120.8 million, and net income attributable to stockholders was $78.3 million, or $1.28 per share. The principal driver was the approximately $48 million of profit on vessel sales completed during the quarter.

To distinguish the underlying operating result from those disposal gains, adjusted EBITDA was $67.8 million. Adjusted net income attributable to stockholders was $25.4 million, and adjusted EPS was $0.42. Compared to the same period last year, although this third quarter, we experienced fewer earnings days, marginally lower TCE, and a slightly lower contribution from the ethylene export terminal, partly offset by lower operating costs, reported earnings reached a record while underlying earnings remained solid. The sales gains demonstrate clear value realization from our fleet, but the adjusted figures provide a cleaner view of recurring quarterly performance, and on both measures, the business remained profitable and cash generative. Moving to slide seven, we had another busy quarter of disciplined capital allocation.

First, we delivered the second quarter shareholder return we had committed to. We repurchased 661,482 shares for approximately $14.2 million and paid the $0.07 cash dividend. Together, that was a return of capital of $18.5 million, or 35% of second quarter net income attributable to stockholders. During the third quarter, we also repaid $28.9 million of scheduled amortization against our debt, repaid a further $201.5 million of debt, including $156.7 million of revolving facilities that remain available for us to redraw, and paid $21.4 million to the shipyards for our newbuild programs. Set against this, in the third quarter, we received $129.9 million net proceeds from asset sales between July and September.

We drew $72.5 million from a combination of debt facilities towards our newbuild vessels, and we received $12.7 million as net cash distributions from our equity investments, together with some insurance recoveries. Overall, at September 30th, cash and cash equivalents totaled $221 million, and restricted cash was $48 million. Including the $156.7 million of undrawn vessel facilities, total liquidity was approximately $425.8 million, of which approximately $378 million was available, i.e., excluding our restricted cash. By October 31st, total liquidity had risen to approximately $482 million, or approximately $434 million as available, excluding the restricted cash. Equity, excluding non-controlling interest, was $1.3 billion, up from $1.23 billion at the start of the year.

The key message here is that the Unigas vessel sales did more than generate an accounting gain. It converted non-core assets into cash, removed associated debt, and simplified the fleet, while preserving substantial liquidity for our newbuild program and other disciplined uses of capital. Slide eight shows how we have used the proceeds from our fleet sales to strengthen our balance sheet, with debt reduced, our newbuilds fully financed on attractive terms, and returns going to shareholders. For the third quarter, our board yesterday declared a dividend of $0.08 per share, the higher fixed element we announced in August being a 14% increase, payable on December 3rd to shareholders of record on November 17th.

We currently anticipate repurchasing $22.6 million of shares by December 31st, subject to the terms of our capital return policy and applicable approvals. Together, that is a return of capital of $27.4 million, or 35% of net income attributable to stockholders. As a reminder, our policy applies to reported net income attributable to stockholders, and that includes profits on sales of vessels. Our newbuild financing, as mentioned, during the quarter, we drew $72.5 million of secured pre-delivery finance as shipyard milestones were reached on three of our Panda ethane ethylene vessels.

In parallel, long-term financing is now in place for all six newbuild vessels, including our two ammonia vessels, which were secured at a margin of 135 basis points over SOFR from delivery. In August 2026, we also repaid $26.7 million and refinanced the remaining $47.9 million of our $74.6 million facility with a new facility that matures in 2031, thus pushing out the maturity. We have now paid $153 million to the shipyards for our six vessels under construction, with a further $10 million of capitalized interest, which together make up the $163 million of vessels under construction you will see on our balance sheet.

Our share in the Morgan's Point terminal remains unencumbered, as were nine of our vessels at September 30th. Two of those were Unigas vessels delivered to buyers in October, leaving us with seven unencumbered vessels today. At September 30th, net debt to last 12 months adjusted EBITDA was 1.7x, falling from over two times at the end of June 2026. Net debt was just short of $500 million, compared with approximately $653 million at June 30th, a reduction of about $153 million. Net debt now represents approximately 25% of the on-water fleet market value, or 21%, including a valuation of our Morgan's Point terminal investment. This characterizes the overall balance sheet we have discussed on previous calls.

We want to invest in attractive growth, maintain an efficient but conservative balance sheet, and return capital. We believe this quarter shows that these priorities can reinforce one another when asset sales, our newbuild program, financing, and operating cash flows are managed together. Slide nine brings back the two strengths I highlighted last time: dependable operating cash flow and a low all-in cash breakeven. Our latest estimated all-in cash breakeven for 2026 is $21,720 per vessel per day. Against the third quarter TCE of $30,314 per day, we continue to see meaningful headroom of approximately $8,600 per day, or about 40% of cash breakeven, even after seeing some normalization from our second quarter record operating results.

The breakeven estimate includes more than $175 million of forecast operating expenses, approximately $111 million of debt amortization, and approximately $42 million of net interest expense. Full-year 2026 guidance is $175 million-$177 million for vessel operating expenses, $39 million-$42 million for cash G&A, $123 million-$124 million for depreciation, and $42 million-$43 million for net interest expense. For the fourth quarter, guidance can be found also on the slide. As we said last quarter, the sale of the smaller Unigas vessels changes the denominator over which some of our costs are spread.

The more relevant point, however, is that the remaining fleet continues to produce a solid margin over the all-in cash break-even, while our guidance begins to reflect the fleet transition away from the smaller vessels, more of which will be seen as we enter 2027. Slide 10 is our consistency story. Reported EBITDA of $120.8 million was a record, but the number I would draw your attention to is adjusted EBITDA of $67.8 million, because it extends a consistent run, 15 consecutive quarters since the start of 2023, with at least $60 million of adjusted EBITDA, averaging $72 million over that period. That consistency is the more durable story behind quarter-to-quarter movements in utilization and terminal throughput.

Our earnings remain sensitive to freight rates. On a full-year basis, we estimate that each additional $1,000 per day of TCE could add approximately $17 million of annual adjusted EBITDA, equivalent to approximately $0.28 in annual EPS, all else being equal. This is a sensitivity, not guidance, but it illustrates the operating leverage within our platform. Looking ahead, the moderation in the early part of the quarter was consistent with the pattern we described in August, but utilization recovered to approximately 94% in September and remained firm through October. We therefore currently expect fleet utilization, TCE, and terminal earnings to improve sequentially in the fourth quarter, subject, of course, to the forward-looking statements Randy read at the start.

The drydock schedule, projected costs, and off-hire days are included in the appendix on slide 27 as usual, to help with modeling for those that are interested. To bring it all together, reported earnings were a record, helped by vessel gains, but underlying performance was solid and as guided. Net debt is down $153 million to $500 million. Leverage is 1.7x last 12 months adjusted EBITDA. Total liquidity was $482 million at October 31st, and we are returning $27.4 million under our 35% policy, including an $0.08 cash dividend, with all six of our newbuilds now financed. All of that gives us the confidence and flexibilities to pursue opportunities as they arise.

With that, I will hand over to Øyvind for the commercial update. Øyvind, please go ahead.

Øyvind Lindeman: Thank you, Gary, and good morning, everyone. If there is one thing to take away from my section today, it is this: ships are sailing further to deliver the same cargoes. When voyages get longer, you need more ships, which tightens the market. Keep that in mind as we go through the next few slides. Let us start with the choke points on slide 12. On the left is the Strait of Hormuz. Gas carrier traffic is still running at only a fraction of normal levels. You can see a pickup in recent months, but much of that are ships sailing through in laden condition, transferring cargo ship-to-ship near Oman and returns.

That is a very inefficient logistics, and it is not an indication of normal trade coming back. In the middle is the Panama Canal. There are fewer slots, higher costs, and longer waits at both the old and the new locks. We don't expect this to get any better over the next few months. As you can see on the right-hand side, many ships trading from the U.S. to Asia are going the long way around via the Cape of Good Hope. Every one of those detours ties up more ships. Now to slide 13 and U.S. ethylene exports. When Hormuz closed on February 28th, buyers rushed to secure supply.

The only place to look for substitute supply was the U.S., and you can see that on the right-hand slide. U.S. exports peaked in March, April, and May. Then in June and July, buying paused. Talk of possible U.S.-Iran peace negotiations made customers wait and see. When the disruption didn't go away, buyers came back. For us, that played out in three ways: where the cargoes go, how busy our ships are, and what we earn. Let me take them one at a time. First, where the cargoes go. Early on, Chinese buyers had plenty of inventory, so Europe took most of the U.S. ethylene exports. That has changed.

On the left, look at the gap between the gray line, which is the U.S. ethylene price, and the dark blue line, which is the Asian price. That's now the widest spread, so the cargoes are heading to Asia. On the right graph, you can see Asia's share go from zero in the second quarter to around three-quarters by September. Why does that matter for shipping? A round trip from Morgan's Point to Asia takes more than twice as long as one to Europe, and even longer if we need to head via Cape of Good Hope. It's the same cargo with more than twice the ship time. Second, how busy our ships are, on slide 14.

Longer voyages mean fewer ships are free for the next cargo. If you follow the green dashed line on the left, our utilization jumped almost 8 points in September to 94%. For the quarter as a whole, we ran at 87.9% above the five-year average. This isn't just an ethane and ethylene story. LPG demand was picking up too, so both markets were pulling in the same direction. Thirdly, what we earn. When ships get busier, rates follow. We saw it right after Hormuz closed, and we're seeing it again now. Ethylene spot rates have nearly doubled from the quiet months of June and July.

To be fair, ethylene export volumes from the quarter were a bit below what we hoped, but rates firmed into quarter end, nearing the levels we saw just after the closure, and we expect volumes to pick up over the coming months. Now, turning to fleet supply on slide 15. The short version is that Handysize picture looks healthy, and it hasn't changed much since last quarter. The order book is around 7% of the fleet, the lowest of any of the gas carrier segments, with deliveries spread over the next three years. That's a good place to be.

On top of that, around 17% of the Handysize fleet is over 25 years old, so depending on how many of those ships get scrapped, the fleet could actually shrink over the next few years. On the demand side, there's plenty coming. Industry sources such as Argus Media forecast around 37 million tons of additional LPG export capacity globally coming by 2030, more ethane export capacity from the U.S., and several million tons of new ammonia production. All of that needs ships, and not just the big ones. It needs midsize and handysize ships as well. That's why the orders for larger ships don't worry us too much.

To back it up, if you missed it, I'll reiterate what Enterprise Products Partners communicated at their recent earnings call. They raised their 2025 to 2030 Permian NGL production growth forecast from previously 23% to 34% on the back of increasing gas-to-oil ratios for each barrel produced. Permian keeps on giving to the NGL industry. Finally, rates on slide 16. Over the past few months, the market has gone from fair to strong. This chart shows 12-month time charter rates. What stands out is how strong LPG is across VLGCs, midsize, and handysize. In fact, semi-refrigerated handysize LPG rates have nearly caught up with ethylene-capable vessels.

Ethylene charters are a small market with only a few deals to compare against, so I wouldn't read too much into that. But the bigger point is this. Because we can trade in both petrochemicals and LPGs, our earnings are more resilient than if we were just in one. To wrap up, September's strong utilization has carried on through October, and rates are firming across LPG, ethane, and ethylene. I'll mirror what Mads and Gary mentioned before me. We started the fourth quarter on a good footing. With that, I'll hand it over to Randy.

Randy Giveans: Thank you, Øyvind. Following up on some of the earlier comments, there have been several recent developments that we want to provide some additional details on. Starting on slide 18. During the third quarter, we paid $0.07 quarterly cash dividend totaling $4.3 million, and we repurchased over 660,000 common shares of NVGS in the open market, and that totaled $14 million for an average price of less than $21.50 per share. As previously announced, our capital return policy now includes a higher fixed quarterly dividend of $0.08 per share within our overall payout target of 35% of net income. Accordingly, we're returning a total of $27.4 million to shareholders during this fourth quarter.

Of this amount, approximately $4.9 million will be paid as dividends, with the remaining $22.6 million to be allocated to share repurchases between now and the end of the year. At the current share price, we plan on repurchasing 1 million shares over the next two months. Given that NVGS shares continue to trade at a significant discount to our net asset value of more than $32 per share, we believe these share buybacks remain one of the most attractive uses of capital and a highly accretive way to create shareholder value.

With a strong balance sheet, robust earnings, and our upcoming newbuilding deliveries, we hope to continue to steadily improve our capital return policy in the coming quarters and years. Looking at our ethylene export terminal on slide 19. As previously guided, terminal throughput declined to 264,000 tons during the third quarter as European demand softened, international arbitrage narrowed, and customers worked through inventories that had been built earlier in the year.

Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, where we are today, and as seen on the bottom left chart, throughput is on the rise due to higher naphtha prices, global inventory restocking, and a stronger pull from Asia, which has also boosted the tonnage demand for cargoes from Morgan's Point to the Far East. Commercial activity remains very strong. In addition to the four new offtake contracts that have been signed since January, the widening arbitrage and increasing international ethylene demand has led numerous customers to engage in conversations for new take-or-pay contracts beginning in 2027. At the same time, we expect the remaining capacity available during the fourth quarter to be marketed at firm spot rates.

As shown in the chart on the bottom right, the U.S. is expected to maintain a substantial cost advantage for many years, supported by structurally low domestic ethylene prices. Turning to our fleet on slide 20, we continue to execute on our fleet renewal program through the sale of older non-core assets while preparing to take delivery of the first of six highly efficient newbuildings. Beginning with the vessel sales, we recently completed the sale of eight vessels operating in the Unigas pool and shares in the pool company itself for around $183 million.

These transactions generated a total book gain of $70 million, with $48 million recognized during the third quarter and the remaining $22 million expected in the fourth quarter. Following these sales, our fleet now consists of 46 vessels with an average age of 12.8 years and an average capacity of 22,900 cubic meters. On the growth side, our newbuilding program consists of four mid-sized dual-fuel liquefied ethane/ethylene carriers and two mid-sized ammonia-fueled liquefied ammonia carriers. The total shipyard cost is $586 million, of which $153 million has already been paid. Importantly, we have secured $461 million of debt financing on very attractive terms.

As a result, around 21% of the total shipyard cost on a weighted average basis needs to be funded by our equity, with the rest being covered by debt. We expect to get some cash back as the newbuildings are delivered. The first of these six newbuildings will be delivered next month and will immediately commence its time charter, and we will take delivery of our remaining newbuildings throughout the next two years. These vessels will further strengthen our competitive position, enhance our customer service offering, and support long-term value creation for shareholders.

Finishing on slide 21, I would like to personally invite all of you again to join us in Houston for our 2026 Analyst Investor Day, which takes place in just two weeks. Tuesday afternoon, November 17th, we will host our tours at the Morgan's Point Ethylene Export Terminal and climb aboard one of our vessels, subject to availability, as they are in very high demand. Later that evening, the management team and members of our board will also host a dinner for our analysts and investors. And the next day, Wednesday, November 18th, we will host company and industry presentations covering market trends, a financial update, as well as our medium-term strategy.

We will then have lunch, followed by an appreciation event for analysts, shareholders, customers, and partners. The outlook for the weather is only surpassed by the outlook for our business. The best is yet to come. With that, I will now turn the call back over to Mads for closing remarks.

Mads Peter Zacho: Thanks a lot, Randy. Let me finish with three takeaways from today. First of all, Q3 demonstrated the resilience of our business. The quarter started more slowly, as we expected, but utilization recovered strongly in September and remained firm through October. Rates are improving, tonnage volumes are increasing, and we expect both TCE and utilization to be higher in the fourth quarter. Second, we continue to execute on the transformation of our fleet and our company. The Unigas exit is now complete. At the same time, all six newbuildings are fully financed, with the first vessel due for delivery next month.

So we are replacing smaller and older vessels with larger, more efficient ships, and we are doing so while we are maintaining considerable financial flexibility. Third and last, our balance sheet and capital return remain clear strengths. Net leverage is down to 1.7x adjusted EBITDA. Available liquidity has increased to $434 million by the end of October. And for Q3, we are returning 35% of net income to shareholders through the increased cash dividend and share buybacks. If we are looking ahead, the fundamentals remain attractive. U.S. exports continue to grow, longer voyages are adding ton-miles, the Handysize order book remains limited, and our flexible fleet allows us to benefit from strong demand across LPG, ethane, ethylene.

So we enter the final quarter of the year with improving markets, a stronger balance sheet, and a clear path for continued fleet renewal and growth. We are in a strong position right now, and we intend to use that position with discipline. Thanks a lot for listening. Back to you, Randy.

Randy Giveans: Thank you, Mads. Operator, we will now open the lines for some Q&A. To raise your hand, you can press star nine, and then you will have to unmute yourself by pressing star six. Or if joining us on Zoom, just use the raise hand function. First question, your line should be open.

Chris Robertson: Hi. Thank you, Randy. This is Chris Robertson at Deutsche Bank. Thanks for taking my questions. If so, what's the average length of those contracts? Maybe what's the current floor in terms of net profitability that the contracts currently provide?

Randy Giveans: Hey, Chris. We haven't disclosed all of those numbers. The majority of the offtake or the capacity is sold going forward. Some of those are shorter-term contracts, some of those are multi-year contracts. So we really have a portfolio approach. We're still marketing the remainder of the capacity. Chris Robertson: Got it. Thanks, Randy. Mads Peter Zacho: We do have a portfolio of business development opportunities, and that does include terminal or infrastructure assets. So, we do. Chris Robertson: Thank you, Mads. I will turn it over. Thank you, guys.

Randy Giveans: Thank you, Chris. Next caller, your line should be open.

Speaker 5: About kind of $430 million of available liquidity kind of post the Unigas sales, and just wanted to get your latest thoughts on kind of the priority list for using some of this capacity and maybe how you are balancing maybe some potential consolidation opportunities in your vessel classes versus accretive buybacks.

Mads Peter Zacho: Yeah, it is a good and pressing question. I think if you just step back for a little bit, given the geopolitical surroundings right now, and I think our ability to forecast, if we just look back over the last couple of years, I mean, forecasting some of the events that have come in and impacted our business, our visibility is not super great now. And that in itself speaks for maybe running the balance sheet a little bit stronger right now than we probably would have in, let us say, three, four, five years back. That being said, we do not, for our day-to-day operations, need the level of cash that we have on the balance sheet right now.

And I think arguably, you could also say that the leverage ratios that we are running right now are maybe a little bit lower than they could be. That means that we do have capital available, and I think a mixed approach where we prioritize growth and capital return at the same time. When it comes to growing the business, we did order six vessels one, two years ago. During 2026, we haven't bought a lot of assets, so maybe we're a little bit behind on that front, and we continue to look for consolidation opportunities. It's not so easy.

At a time when the rates are strong, the sellers of secondhand tonnage, they have high price expectations, and we're not necessarily interested in going out overpaying for those assets. So, we may have to be a little bit patient here, but it's definitely high on our agenda. I think we're quite pleased with the new buildings that we ordered one and two years ago. We think we got them at good prices, and we think the outlook for deploying them profitably, it's still the case. So, we also don't want to rule out, you could say, doing more new buildings in the short to mid-term. That being said, we'll be very disciplined about it.

We'll be very predictable, and it'll be organic evolution, so to speak, in growing our business. On the other hand, capital return, I think we have the capacity to continue or even exceed what we've done in the past, where we have returned via the capital return policy significant amounts of capital, but on the other hand, also taking the opportunity from time to time to do ad hoc share buybacks. We've done about once a year over the past three years, and that's definitely in the cards that when we see weakness in our share price, that's a good opportunity to deploy some of that cash. So, expect more of the same.

We will be growing our business in a very disciplined manner, but on the other hand, continue, if not increasing, the capital return.

Speaker 5: Okay, got it. That's very helpful. Maybe just second question, wanted to touch on some of the charter rates you're seeing. It sounds like, you know, step down in third quarter, but sounds like there's several tailwinds into fourth quarter. Just want to get your latest thoughts on kind of outlook for charter rates in the fourth quarter relative maybe to what you saw with record levels in the second quarter, and any kind of initial kind of outlook that you can provide into 2027.

Øyvind Lindeman: Utilization is up in mid-90%, which is great, which we commented on. When you saw on that rate slide, both handysize ethylene and handysize LPG rates were up. That is the difference between second quarter and going into fourth quarter. What that means is that ethylene, ethane is up to where it is very strong, almost at the same levels that we saw in second quarter. But in addition to, those LPG rates are also pulling in the right direction. So we have two of our main ship segments, LPG and petrochemical, moving in the same sort of tightening market, which is great to see and be part of.

Speaker 5: Okay, perfect. Thanks for the time today.

Randy Giveans: Thanks, Chad. Next caller, your line should be open.

Speaker 6: Thanks, Randy, and Mads, Øyvind, and Gary. A good update. My question actually was just on the last one that Spiro was asking, just in terms of, and Øyvind, you sort of answered it, but just wanted to get a maybe slight deeper response. Q2 is obviously a record in terms of revenue, but the earnings, you had a slight dip in Q3 as you telegraphed, but now it looks like the fourth quarter's really started off on very firm footing. Randy, you mentioned, I think it was in your closing remarks, that the best is yet to come. Do you think that's as quick as Q4 being the record in terms of relative, I say, to Q2?

Do you think it can actually exceed your performance then?

Mads Peter Zacho: I think we tend to be a little bit cautious on predicting, you could say, the exact financial performance of the year. I think it's more the underlying drivers that we like to comment on, and I think here, the utilization and the rates input that Øyvind has given you, where utilization, yeah, mid-90%, the beginning of the quarter, which is strong, and we see that unabated going into November. That's one data point. The other data point is that now it's broader, the recovery in the rates. It's not only on the ethylene rates, it's also on the semi-refs. That should give you some guidance as to how we see that play out.

But going as far as you could say, predicting whether we'll be above Q2 operating or not, I think we'll just refrain from that.

Speaker 6: That's fair. I appreciate your comments, Mads. Maybe just a follow-up on that. Your first ethylene MGC that's delivering, I think in December?

Speaker 6: You put that on a charter. Just want to get a sense, is that a long-term contract, or is this more of a one or two voyages upon delivery? Any sense you can give us in terms of what that contract profile looks like?

Øyvind Lindeman: I think we have disclosed it in the fleet list. There is a one-year charter that commences upon delivery of the ship at very healthy rates. The other, the two last newbuildings, so the LPG ammonia ships that we have there on five-year charters, and the three remaining ethane ethylene vessels that are being delivered next year, June, September, December, are all being affirmed and worked at the moment. We are hoping that will land into place soon and we can announce.

Speaker 6: Thanks, Øyvind. Just maybe a follow-up on those final three. Is it thinking also something similar to one year, or is there a bit of a go-both?

Øyvind Lindeman: We like to have a little mix. Some are longer, some are shorter, so we will see.

Speaker 6: Very good. All right. Thank you, guys. I will pass it back.

Randy Giveans: Thanks so much. Next caller, your line should be open.

Jostein Aschjem: Hello, guys. This is Jostein Aschjem from DNB calling. You mentioned the high price expectation among potential candidates for consolidation, and Randy also mentioned the $32 NAV. How do you sort of balance between the growth prospects versus the high prices on older tonnage? Is there potential to do some divestments going forward as well? What is sort of your targets in terms of fleet size going forward as well? Thank you.

Mads Peter Zacho: Yeah. No, it's a good question, and we have been quite active in selling older non-core tonnage over the past year, and we will continue. I mean, once our ships are getting past the 20-year mark, we tend to offer them for sale. We have one today, Navigator Pluto, it is more than 25 years of age. So that may be sold over the next half year or so. So we will continue to focus on rejuvenating our fleet by selling some of the older non-core or less flexible assets.

So expect that to be happening also, not quite to the speed that you saw with the eight Unigas vessels being sold just over the last quarter or so, but a few here and there. That begs the question, so what does that mean in terms of your fleet size? Now, you shouldn't count them one for one, because if we are selling, let us say, a 12,000 cubic meter Unigas vessel, it is a very different ship in terms of earnings capacity compared to a 48,000 cubic meter mid-size ethylene carrier.

So the capacity in the new building book that we have, it is actually going up both when you calculate the value or when you calculate the capacity of the ships. That being said, we will be looking to gradually, over time, grow our fleet. You mentioned the discount that we are trading at to our NAV. We are keenly aware that doing share buybacks when our share price is way below the NAV will remain to be our key priority. We will balance those priorities about deploying capital as capital return, because that is a good way to spend the money, but also maintaining, you could say, a healthy business overall that has some long-term duration.

Those are the two concerns that we are balancing, and I think we have ample opportunity with the cash flow that we are generating and with the strong balance sheet that we have, that we can actually do both things at the same time.

Jostein Aschjem: Yeah, thank you very much for the extensive answer. Maybe moving a bit back to the market as well. You mentioned in the report that you see some tailwinds from very strong markets across the larger vessels as well for the VLGCs, VLECs, and also MGCs. How do you see the impact from MGCs, maybe my most predominantly for your vessel fleets impacting the rates into Q4 versus Q3?

Øyvind Lindeman: I think it's very helpful. Both the very large gas carriers and the medium gas carrier segments are doing very well. That supports our ambitions and our rates for the handysize LPG ships. They're all in tandem pointing upwards. We're all doing well on the rate side.

Jostein Aschjem: Very good. Thank you very much.

Randy Giveans: Thanks for joining, Jostein. Next caller, I see your hand here, Climent.

Climent Molins: Hi, guys. Thank you for taking my questions. Most has already been covered, but I wanted to follow up on Omar's questions on time charters. With spot rates at very elevated levels and term contracts also creeping up, sorry about that, is there any appetite to further increase your term cover? Or even, what kind of quotes are you currently seeing for one-year contracts for ethylene-capable handies or the usual semi-refs?

Øyvind Lindeman: I refer back to that chart, which is actually a 12-month time charter assessment done by Clarksons ship brokers. Both ethylene and LPG semi-ref is about $1.04 million, $1.05 million per month. That is the rate level that is being quoted. Now we see some of the shorter ones are higher, some of the longer ones are a little bit below, but it is a good guidance across the fleet. I think if you are running some modeling, just use those numbers.

Climent Molins: Makes sense. Thank you. That is everything. I will turn it over.

Randy Giveans: Thanks so much. I believe that is the end of our Q&A. Mads, turn over to you for closing remarks.

Mads Peter Zacho: Just want to say thank you all for listening in. I thank you a lot for all the good questions that were asked. If you need any further elaboration, please do come back to us. We will be happy to discuss our business and answer your questions. Hopefully, give us a call. Give Randy a call.

There’s always something worth watching on Prime Video, but with so many shows competing for a place on the trending list, figuring out what deserves a spot on your watchlist can be tricky. The streamer’s top 10 shows list is actually a handy place to start, but not everything trending is necessarily worth binge-watching. So, I’ve picked out three shows from this week’s rankings that I think are worth your time.

That includes a little something for everyone, whether you’re after a gritty action-thriller now streaming its second season, a crime comedy pairing an unlikely duo with plenty of chemistry, or a lighthearted romantic drama full of unexpected connections. They offer three very different viewing experiences, but each has something that makes it worth adding to your watchlist. Here’s what I’d be checking out this week.

This list is based on the Prime Video U.S. top 10 shows as of Wednesday, November 4, 2026.

Prime Video’s “The Terminal List” is back, and it’s clearly still a hit with viewers, currently sitting at No. 1 on the platform’s charts. Based on Jack Carr’s bestselling military thriller novels, the action-packed series also leans into its psychological drama and the emotional weight that comes with these experiences. After a four-year wait since its 2022 debut, all eight episodes of season 2 are now available to stream, giving fans plenty to get stuck into. If you enjoy shows like “Reacher” and “Tom Clancy’s Jack Ryan,” this should be your next pick.

James Reece (Chris Pratt) is a Navy SEAL commander whose entire platoon is ambushed during a covert mission. After returning home with conflicting memories of what happened, Reece begins investigating the operation and discovers that the people responsible may be closer to home than he ever imagined. As he follows a trail of evidence, he finds himself caught up in a far-reaching government conspiracy. Season 2 picks up after Reece completes his revenge mission, following him as he’s drawn into a new operation involving the CIA, a former ally and a resurgent Al-Qaeda network.

Fancy something a little lighter after all the action and drama? “Wild Cards” is a fun crime series that should be right up your alley if you enjoyed shows like “Psych,” “White Collar” or “Castle.” It has witty banter and an entertaining central partnership with plenty of episodic mysteries, making it an easy show to dip in and out of. All 10 episodes of season 3 are now available on Prime Video, so you can catch up at your own pace without needing to buy individual episodes or sign up for an extra subscription. It’s a great choice when you want something entertaining.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

“Wild Cards” follows the unlikely partnership between demoted detective Cole Ellis (Giacomo Gianniotti) and clever con artist Max Mitchell (Vanessa Morgan). After Max is arrested and helps Ellis solve a local case, the pair are offered a chance to turn things around. The catch is that they have to work together, with Ellis relying on traditional police work and Max using her talent for disguises, elaborate schemes and talking her way into almost any situation. As they investigate a new case each week, the two gradually learn how to work as a team, despite their very different approaches to solving crimes.

“Love in Disguise” is a fun South Korean series that puts a fresh spin on the romantic comedy formula by adding a little mystery and suspense. Based on the popular Kakao web novel, the show brings together the playful chaos of a gender-swap rom-com with the twists of a corporate thriller. It’s a slightly different take on the K-drama formula, giving viewers plenty of romantic complications alongside a more suspenseful storyline. If you enjoy Korean dramas that offer romance, comedy and a few unexpected twists, this one is worth checking out.

Kang Jae-hee (Seol In-ah) is a former special forces officer turned detective who goes undercover to investigate Yoon Yi-jun (Yim Si-wan), the wealthy heir to a powerful business empire and the prime suspect in his secretary’s murder. To get close to him and uncover evidence, Jae-hee disguises herself as a man and takes a job as his personal secretary. However, keeping her real identity under wraps isn’t easy, especially as Yi-jun becomes increasingly suspicious of his new employee. As the investigation progresses, their complicated working relationship takes some unexpected turns.

#3253. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

#3252. Adobe puts its marketing AI agent inside ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot

Adobe’s CX Enterprise Coworker now plugs into the AI tools marketers already use. New MCP connectors also link it to Amazon Ads, Demandbase, Meta campaigns and Snowflake.

Adobe’s AI agent for marketing teams now works inside ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Databricks Genie, the company said on Wednesday. Adobe expects Amazon Quick, IBM and Snowflake to follow soon.

The agent, CX Enterprise Coworker, plans and runs customer experience work across Adobe’s marketing software. In ChatGPT, it comes as a plugin. Adobe made the agent generally available in June.

Adobe says the agent tracks campaign results and trends. It also forecasts audiences, improves customer journeys and helps with planning and project management. It runs with human oversight. It is built on two open standards for AI agents: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A).

Anjul Bhambhri leads engineering for the product at Adobe.

“Today, marketers often use AI tools in isolation, without the organizational context and domain intelligence needed to personalize every stage of the customer lifecycle,” Bhambhri said.

Adobe also launched connectors that link the agent to other companies’ systems through ready-made MCP servers. Partners include Amazon Ads, Demandbase, Microsoft Work IQ, RainFocus and Snowflake. There is also a connector for Meta ad campaigns. Marketers can then pull data and take actions across several systems with a single request, Adobe said.

Consulting firms including Accenture, Deloitte Digital, EY, IBM and PwC are building industry-specific versions of the agent. Agencies such as dentsu, Havas, Omnicom, Publicis and WPP also add their own tools to it.

Rob Howard runs Copilot’s platform and extensibility work at Microsoft.

“This gives marketing teams the speed and flexibility to orchestrate more personalized experiences at scale,” Howard said.

Adobe says more than 20,000 brands use its software for content, customer engagement and brand visibility. In August, it put its creative tools inside ChatGPT. It has also signed agentic AI deals with Jet2 for holidays and Heathrow’s new website.

The iPhone Duo adapted iOS 27 for a new form factor but, in the process, got some criticism for the decision to lock the taskbar to the right-hand side. In fact, if you're a leftie and want to use the Duo with a single hand, you've got to use the non-dominant one.

That situation just got a little better with the arrival of the iOS 27.3 developer beta this week. The update brings Reachability to the iPhone Duo, allowing users to move the content within reach, just as you can on a candybar iPhone.

Only instead of shifting the content from the top down, the Duo will now let users swipe left from the left or right from the right edge of the screen to bring it within striking distance of your preferred thumb.

For left-handed users, it's a step in the right direction, and it will work on both the 5.4-inch outer display and the 7.6-inch nano-textured inner display.

Reachability will be turned on by default once the software update is installed, but if you want to find it yourself, head to Settings > Accessibility > Reachability.

Alongside bringing Reachability to the Duo, 27.3 will also give Siri AI a much bigger playground to explore across iOS, macOS, iPadOS and visionOS. The upgraded assistant will now work inside Music, Messages, Photos, Calendar and Reminders, letting users, for example, ask it to build a specific playlist in Apple Music or create Calendar events.

Going further, Apple is also opening Siri AI's capabilities up to third-party developers via App Intents. Essentially, this could make good on the promise years ago that Apple Intelligence would be able to work across a user's apps to build a personal context.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Back in 2024, then-CEO Tim Cook laid out what set Apple's AI plans apart: “Our unique approach combines generative AI with a user’s personal context to deliver truly helpful intelligence."

It seems like reality is about to finally caught up to the vision.

"Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more," Apple posted on its developer site.

"So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order. For complex requests, we’re also introducing skills to let you teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience."

The public release for iOS 27.3 is planned for later this year, at which point we could really see Siri AI start to spread its wings.

#3250. Apple now explicitly bans employees from using confidential information in prediction markets

Apple has updated its insider trading policy to explicitly prohibit employees from using confidential information to bet on prediction markets. Here are the details.

Following yesterday’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings report, Apple today published its fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, which is a mandatory annual filing with the SEC that provides a detailed look at the company’s finances, business, and risks.

Among the documents included in the filing is an updated version of Apple’s insider trading policy.

Until last year, Apple’s insider trading policy, filed with the SEC as Exhibit 19.1, included the following prohibitions:

However, the updated policy includes a new prohibition:

No Trading in Prediction Markets Based on Confidential Information. Do not participate in “prediction markets” or similar platforms to wager, bet, trade, buy or sell contracts based on the outcome of future events, or otherwise enter into event contracts, when such activity involves the use of Apple Confidential Information (as defined in Apple’s Business Conduct Policy) about Apple or any other company (including Apple suppliers, manufacturers, vendors or customers, such as cellular network carriers or other business partners) obtained in connection with your work at Apple. You must also not tip Apple Confidential Information to others who may participate in such markets. Apple Confidential Information includes, but is not limited to, material nonpublic information. This prohibition applies whether or not the activity constitutes insider trading or securities trading under applicable laws.

While much of this may seem obvious, how insider trading rules apply to prediction markets has been something of a gray area, to put it mildly. And while major prediciton markets explicitly ban the practice in their terms of service, enforcement remains a challenge.

In Apple’s case, the new language explicitly extends restrictions beyond traditional securities trading, making it clear that employees cannot use confidential information to place bets on prediction markets, even when those transactions don’t qualify as insider trading under applicable laws.

You can read Apple’s full 2026 Form 10-K on its Investor Relations page.

#3249. Here's What a $1,000 Investment in AMD Could Be Worth by 2030

AMD's latest quarterly results indicate that the stock is primed for a big jump by 2030.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +1.01%) has been one of the top-performing stocks in 2026, clocking impressive gains of over 120% as of this writing, and the good news is that it can deliver further gains to investors thanks to an acceleration in growth.

AMD released its third-quarter results on Nov. 3, and the stock soared the following day. Let's see why that was the case and check how much upside this fast-growing semiconductor stock could deliver by the end of the decade.

AMD's Q3 revenue increased 45% year over year to $13.4 billion. The company's non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.09 increased by 74% from the year-ago period. AMD's data center business was the primary driver of its impressive growth, with the segment's revenue nearly doubling year over year to a record $8.5 billion.

It is worth noting that AMD's revenue and earnings easily exceeded Wall Street's expectations. The company noted healthy demand for its Epyc server processors and Instinct data center graphics cards. The good news for AMD investors is that the company expects data center revenue to accelerate in the current quarter. What's more, its full-year data center revenue is on track to double from 2025 levels.

Looking ahead, AMD expects the data center segment to account for 80% of its top line in 2027. That implies a major improvement over the previous quarter, when the data center segment produced 64% of AMD's top line. Moreover, the increasing reliance on the data center business is a good sign for AMD, given the ongoing weakness in the personal computer market.

AMD reported an 8% year-over-year decline in its client and gaming segment revenue last quarter to $3.7 billion. Notably, its PC-focused client processor revenue increased 7% from the year-ago period despite a 21% decline in PC industry shipments last quarter. The gaming segment continues to struggle due to the aging gaming console generation. However, the potential arrival of a new generation of gaming consoles next year could lift this segment and complement the healthy growth AMD has been witnessing in data centers.

Importantly, AMD expects significant acceleration in growth despite challenging conditions in the gaming and PC markets. The company expects revenue to increase by 66% year over year in the current quarter, a substantial step up from the 45% growth seen in the previous one.

If you have $1,000 in investable cash right now after paying your bills, clearing expensive loans, and saving enough for tough times, buying AMD stock could be a smart move before it soars higher. That's because the company has tremendous earnings growth potential, as evident from the following chart.

Assuming its bottom line increases by even 20% in 2029 and 2030, its earnings per share could reach $33.41 by the end of the decade (using 2028's estimated earnings per share of $23.20 as the base). If AMD trades at 30 times earnings at that time, in line with the tech-laden Nasdaq-100 index's earnings multiple, its stock price could reach $1,002. That's 93% higher than AMD's current stock price.

So, AMD can turn a $1,000 investment into more than $1,900 in just over four years, making it an ideal investment for anyone looking to add a growth stock to their portfolio.

#3248. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

#3247. macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look

Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

What a journey for Markdown, @gruber The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

#3246. Why are premium domains so expensive?

A normal .com costs about $11 a year to register. The best names can sell for millions. Here is why.

Premium domains are expensive because each name exists only once, and short, memorable ones are long gone. Registries and owners price them on demand. They help brands get remembered, but they do not boost Google rankings, and some renew at premium prices.

Registering a normal .com address is cheap. Since 1 November, registrars pay Verisign, which runs .com, $10.97 a year per name, after a 7% rise, Domain Name Wire reported. Yet Voice.com sold for $30M in 2019.

The gap comes down to scarcity. Every domain name exists only once, and the short, clear words people remember were registered decades ago. No amount of money creates a second one.

Some premium names have never been registered. Registries, the companies that run each extension, flag short or keyword-rich names in advance and charge more for them. Some keep charging a premium every year.

Most famous premium names, though, are resold by people or companies that already own them. The owner sets the price, which is usually negotiable. After the sale, these names normally renew at the standard rate.

A short, familiar name is easier to say, type and remember, so more people find a business without searching for it. It can also make a young company look established. Swedish startup Lovable recently took over lovable.com from an Italian lingerie brand.

What a premium name does not buy is a better Google ranking. “Keywords in a TLD do not give any advantage or disadvantage in search,” Google says.

Demand can lift a whole extension: the AI boom pushed .ai, Anguilla’s country code, past 1M registrations. It earned the island $80M from January to July, nearly half its government revenue, the Jamaica Gleaner reported. Slovenia’s .si saw 20,000 sign-ups in a day after Trump renamed AI “Super Intelligence”.

The sticker price can mislead. A domain sold for $1 in its first year may renew at $20, and some registry premiums stay expensive every year. Before buying, check the first-year price, the renewal fee and what you would pay to transfer it.

#3245. I played the Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2, and it’s even better than my childhood memories

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.
