The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a joy to revisit from start to finish thanks to its gorgeous 4K visuals, full orchestral score, and slick modern controls. It may not be a brand-new adventure, but it’s the definitive remake fans have always wanted and easily the best way to experience the legendary game that started it all.

Smart quality-of-life upgrades throughout

Intuitive, modern controls with gyro support

Orchestral soundtrack feels grand and cinematic

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Platforms: Nintendo Switch 2Price: $69.99 / $59.99 (digital), £58.99 / £49.99 (digital), $109.95 AUD / $94.95 AUD (digital)Release Date: November 4, 2026Genre: Action-adventure

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is exactly what I wanted from one of the most anticipated remakes yet. Instead of a reimagining, it’s a one-to-one remake that does exactly what it needs to — overhauling the N64 classic’s visuals and gameplay — but despite being based on a 28-year-old game, it still manages to feel fresh.

Even though the updated art style initially drew criticism, it really grew on me over the course of my 20+ hour playthrough. From the details in the fabric of Link’s clothes to the way the water moved around him while diving for rupees, the game’s overhauled graphics continued to impress me. In fact, I had to remind myself to cut through the grass and shrubbery in Hyrule Field to look for items instead of just staring at it in awe. Then to top it all off, the new orchestral score makes the game feel incredibly cinematic.

Although Nintendo didn’t reimagine Ocarina of Time, it did take common complaints to heart. Being able to jump on command is big enough on its own, but the game makes exploring dungeons easier too with a fully controllable camera and having key gear mapped to your D-pad instead of hidden away behind menus. Gyro aiming also makes solving puzzles with your bow or grabbing Gold Skulltulas with your hookshot feel that much more rewarding.

Is it worth experiencing the boy without a fairy transform into the Hero of Time once again on the Nintendo Switch 2 though? Find out in my full review.

When it comes to classics like Ocarina of Time, it’s hard not to remember how you experienced them with rose-tinted glasses. Just go back and play the original on Nintendo Switch Online to see what I mean. With the new remake on the Nintendo Switch 2 though, it looks and feels the way my childhood imagination always convinced me it did.

The Great Deku Tree looks absolutely massive — and equally imposing — when you’re standing in front of it as Young Link in the game’s intro. The same is true when you leave Kokiri Forest for the first time and step out into the rolling expanse of Hyrule Field, greeted by the owl Kaepora Gaebora. The world of Ocarina of Time is nowhere near as big as that of Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom, but the remake’s visuals certainly fooled me into thinking it was, despite replaying the game multiple times over the years.

The locations and dungeons you visit throughout the game are quite impressive too, especially given how much work Nintendo put into the small details. From dust hanging in the air as the sun pours into the Temple of Time to seeing individual strands of hay in the scarecrow Pierre, my eyes couldn’t stop going over the little things as I played through Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2 in docked mode on my TV.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The visuals alone make this remake easy to recommend, but it’s the modern controls that truly made me feel like the Hero of Time.

Navigating a 3D world with a single analog stick was a real pain, which is why Nintendo implemented modern camera controls in the Ocarina of Time remake. They work just as you’d expect them to, with your controller’s right analog stick giving you 360 degrees of freedom to look around and explore Hyrule as you see fit.

Personally, I found these new camera controls to be tremendously useful when solving puzzles in dungeons and especially as I hunted for Gold Skulltulas. Switching to Z-targeting when taking on large groups of enemies was a quick reminder of just how far we’ve come with this remake.

The biggest upgrade when it comes to controlling Link though is the addition of a dedicated jump button. Timing my jumps and making it safely onto narrow platforms was a whole lot easier this time around. Likewise, I found the new gyro aiming to feel just as natural when using my bow and arrow or even when casting my line while fishing.

Ocarina of Time’s menus have been given the same attention to detail and visual overhaul as the rest of the game. The main menu is much more polished, but instead of having to jump back into it over and over again to change your equipment, you can do so using a new Breath of the Wild-style pop-up overlay. With a tap of either bumper, you can browse through and equip whatever you need for a particular puzzle or enemy on the fly, which really helps speed up both combat and traversal.

While you use this menu to switch from your slingshot to your boomerang, donning a new mask or, more importantly, switching boots is even easier. Just like in Ocarina of Time’s 3DS remake, your boots are now mapped to down on the D-pad. Nintendo did streamline some aspects of the game’s dungeons, but this small tweak alone makes the dreaded Water Temple a whole lot easier to traverse.

As for Link’s fairy companion Navi, she’s still right by your side throughout your journey. However, there are far fewer interruptions, and when she does speak, you actually want to listen. A big part of this comes down to the fact that Navi is now fully voice-acted and doesn’t constantly nag you with “Hey!”, “Listen!”, or “Watch out!”.

Whether it’s Zelda’s Lullaby or the Sun’s Song, music plays a pivotal role in Ocarina of Time from start to finish. From your namesake instrument down to the various themes that greet you when you enter Goron City or the Lost Woods, this remake was quite literally music to my ears.

For starters, the entire soundtrack was re-recorded with a full live orchestra. Ocarina of Time has never sounded this good. Alongside punchier battle sound effects, every track sounded superb in surround sound through my TV setup, and held up just as well using virtual surround in handheld mode.

Nintendo also took the Switch 2’s built-in microphone into account. If you know Epona’s Song or another tune by heart, you don't even have to input the notes using A, B, X, Y, and the bumpers — you can simply hum the melody and the game will do the rest. There’s also an optional electronic ocarina accessory from Hori that pairs with the game if you want to physically play the notes yourself, though I didn’t have a chance to test it out firsthand.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may not be a brand-new adventure in the Zelda universe, but it’s by far the best way to replay this timeless classic. Its stunning 4K visuals keep your eyes glued to the screen, while the completely redone orchestral soundtrack will linger in your head long after you put down the controller. Meanwhile, the addition of modern controls alongside small but significant quality-of-life upgrades make what used to feel tedious feel completely natural.

If you played and loved the original, this remake is an absolute must. If Breath of the Wild was your first taste of the series, Ocarina of Time lets you experience the foundational game that made modern 3D Zelda possible, complete with all the polish you’d expect from Nintendo. There has never been a better time to strap on your sword and shield, step out of Kokiri Forest, and see what you’ve been missing.

#3243. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3241. The Ultimate Dividend Growth Stock to Buy With $2,000 Right Now

Home Depot stock has delivered dividend growth since 1987.

It's common knowledge that dividend stocks tend to attract more conservative investors. While these stocks rarely experience rapid growth, they tend to be well-suited for wealth preservation and income generation.

Fortunately, many of these stocks also increase their payouts periodically, bolstering their value as long-term holdings. If one is looking to start building a position by investing $2,000 in such a stock, Home Depot (HD +6.53%) is likely an excellent option, and here's why.

Income investors will like that Home Depot has hiked its dividend for 17 straight years. The retail stock suspended increases in the late 2000s amid the housing crisis. Still, annual payout hikes had also been the norm since Home Depot's first dividend payment in 1987.

At approximately $330 per share, about $1,980 will buy an investor six shares of Home Depot.

Currently, Home Depot shareholders earn $9.32 per share annually in dividends, totaling $55.92 in yearly dividend income for six shares. This amounts to a dividend yield of 2.8%, far above the S&P 500's (^GSPC +1.58%) average of 1.1%.

Investors can likely expect the payout hikes to continue. Over the trailing 12 months, Home Depot generated just over $15.1 billion in free cash flow, well above the $9.3 billion the payout cost the company over the same period. That leaves ample room for rising payouts and investments in the company.

As mentioned, today's Home Depot stock is best-suited for investors focused on rising dividend income and wealth preservation. With a footprint of more than 2,360 stores, the company now adds few new locations annually. The U.S. and Canadian markets offer little opportunity for new development, and past efforts at international expansion failed, effectively limiting growth.

Nonetheless, Home Depot has responded to that challenge by leaning into strategies such as targeting professional contractors in addition to its traditional do-it-yourself customer base. Omnichannel retail, private label brands, and value-added services and rentals have also boosted revenues.

Amid that approach, it reported $89 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, a 5% yearly increase. Net income rose by under 1% to almost $8.1 billion over the same period due to higher operating costs.

However, some of that spending is investment in digital capabilities and expanded supply chain facilities. That could bring efficiencies that boost profits longer term, which should foster continued dividend growth and, eventually, a higher stock price that could make it worth holding for a decade.

A $2,000 investment in Home Depot stock could be the start of a growing income stream.

Admittedly, the company is unlikely to deliver rapid revenue and profit growth. Still, the need to maintain and update properties is ongoing, and Home Depot is well-positioned to meet it for individuals and businesses alike. That makes it likely that revenue and earnings will continue to increase.

Moreover, it has delivered dividend growth in almost every year since 1987, and its payout is well above the S&P 500 average. Given that its free cash flow is well above the cost of the dividend, Home Depot will probably maintain its track record of rising payouts for a long time to come.

#3240. Aformic raises $6.95M to move its factory robots into AI data centres

The South Carolina startup's self-driving forklifts and carts already move parts for Toyota, 3M and Oshkosh Defense.

Aformic, which makes self-driving forklifts and carts for factories, raised a $6.95M seed round led by Veteran Ventures Capital. It says it has more than $34M in orders and plans new robots for building and maintaining AI data centres.

Industrial robotics startup Aformic has raised a $6.95M seed round led by Veteran Ventures Capital, the company said on Wednesday. ff Venture Capital, Mana Ventures, Red Beard Ventures and Alamo Angels also took part.

Based in Duncan, South Carolina, Aformic makes self-driving forklifts and carts that move parts and materials around factories and warehouses. They navigate without tape or markers on the floor, and its Qursor software plans their routes and assigns tasks.

The company was spun out of AIUT, a Polish industrial automation group, and still has an engineering and production centre in Gliwice, Poland.

Aformic says it has won more than $34M in orders and has hundreds of robots in use. Its customers include Toyota, Hitachi, 3M, Hyundai Mobis and Oshkosh Defense. Over the past year, it says, its robots drove more than 186,000 miles inside customers’ plants.

“AFORMIC was built to automate the industries that matter,” said chief executive Michal Fiuk, a US Army veteran.

The money will fund more engineers and sales staff, work on Qursor, and new robots for other jobs, including helping to build and maintain AI data centres. Data centre builders say a shortage of skilled workers is now one of their biggest bottlenecks.

Investors are backing factory robots in a big way. Earlier this week, Tutor Intelligence raised $75M from a16z for robots that customers rent by the hour, and Toyota spin-out Walden Robotics launched with $300M in July.

After retiring from IBM as a senior software engineer in 2017, Ralph Earle has published two poetry collections.

I step into the warm moist airamong the columns of the pines,their net of twigs and rootscomplex as any lines of code.

The trees purify and anchor.Their branches balance my restlessness.

Their calling is to be present,mine to develop apps. Our tasksverge toward a common logic:living filaments of root, of interface.

Ralph Earle joined the IBM Software Lab in Raleigh, N.C., in 1990 as a technical editor and retired as a senior software engineer in 2017. #3237. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3236. Novo Nordisk Stock Jumped After Earnings — But Its CEO Won't Give 2027 Guidance. Here's What Investors Should Know

The Wegovy maker raised its outlook again and the stock jumped. But its CEO refused to forecast next year, and handed investors six clues instead.

Novo Nordisk (NVO +4.95%) gave investors a lot of what they wanted on Wednesday. Third-quarter sales rose 4% at constant exchange rates to about $11.9 billion, ahead of Wall Street estimates closer to $11 billion. Sales of obesity drugs jumped 22%. And the company raised its full-year outlook again, now calling for sales growth of anywhere from a 2% decline to a 2% gain. In August, it was expecting a decline of up to 6%.

The stock rose about 5% to more than $42 on Wednesday, but the question investors keep asking, according to one analyst, is about next year, and that's the one Novo wouldn't answer.

When an analyst at BNP Paribas asked whether Novo could return to sales growth in 2027, Doustdar was direct. "We're not going to guide," he said, "but let me go out of my way and provide even more building blocks for next year so maybe you can do your own math."

There's an obvious reason for the caution. Chief Financial Officer Karsten Munk Knudsen is leaving after 27 years, and his replacement, Luigi La Corte, is coming over from skin-care company Galderma. Knudsen stays through the end of the year, and Novo plans to give its 2027 forecast with its full-year results in February.

So instead of a number, Doustdar offered three pluses and three minuses. Here's how they stack up.

The first plus is the Wegovy pill. Novo says it has passed 8 million U.S. prescriptions since launch, which it calls the strongest U.S. drug launch by volume in more than a decade outside of vaccines. The firm notes that the franchise has a more than 50% share in the U.S. branded obesity market, and Novo plans to have it in more than 20 international markets by the middle of next year, up from seven today.

The second is a Medicare program that started covering weight-loss drugs for seniors in the middle of this year. Since it only counted for half of 2026, it will count for a full year in 2027.

The third is new products. Novo plans to launch CagriSema, its next-generation obesity drug, in the U.S., and a new hemophilia treatment on both sides of the Atlantic, pending approvals.

The minuses are just as concrete. Novo is losing patent protection for semaglutide, the active ingredient in Wegovy and Ozempic, in some international markets, and Doustdar said the hit was larger in the third quarter than in the second. China is already a drag, and it "is not going to go away just because Christmas turns into, again, a new year," he said. Novo loses exclusivity there next year, too.

The last one is subtler. Novo got a boost this year from favorable pricing adjustments, and Doustdar said investors shouldn't expect that to repeat to the same degree. Then he added, candidly: "I don't know that."

Here's the detail that probably matters most. When an analyst at Jefferies asked whether Novo's U.S. weight-loss business would have grown at all without the Medicare program, the company's head of U.S. operations, Jamey Millar, didn't dodge. Without it, he said, the whole weight-loss drug category looked "relatively flat" from May to October. He added that the pill's 20% growth from the second quarter was "largely but not exclusively" driven by the program.

That's a real dependence on a government program. And Millar said employers are still pulling back on covering these drugs because of the cost. "Whether it's Pepsi, Starbucks, other large employers, when they see the cost trend, they move against" it, he said.

Prices are falling, too. Novo is cutting its U.S. list prices on Jan. 1, and Millar said Ozempic prices are eroding about 10% to 15% a year. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly (LLY +0.61%) is competing hard with its own pill.

Put Doustdar's list together, and you get a company that's roughly balanced for next year. The good news is real, but the headwinds are just as specific. Novo's own long-term goal, set in September, is mid-single-digit sales growth through 2030, which is steady but not spectacular for a company that used to be one of the fastest growers among healthcare stocks. Shares are down about 9.5% over the past year, and more than 70% from 2024 highs.

For long-term investors, that's not necessarily a reason to stay away. Novo is still the volume leader in weight-loss drugs: It generated more than 28 billion Danish kroner (over $4 billion) of free cash flow in the third quarter alone, and the pill is selling. But the refusal to guide is a useful signal, as it could mean that even management isn't sure 2027 will be a growth year.

If you're thinking about buying, the February forecast is the moment to watch. A positive number would suggest the pill and the launches can outrun the patent losses. Until then, Novo looks like one of the more interesting turnaround stories among pharmaceutical stocks, albeit perhaps not a finished one.

#3235. Galantas CEO Mario Stifano on AI, data centres and the copper supply gap

Galantas CEO Mario Stifano explains why AI data centres depend on copper, power and new mines. Gold’s role in chips will grow, he says, but stay specialised.

Mario Stifano is chief executive of Galantas Gold, a gold and copper company listed on the TSX Venture Exchange in Toronto and on AIM in London. He has more than 25 years of experience across exploration, development and producing mining companies. Galantas is developing the Andacollo gold project in Chile, a former producing mine, and the Indiana gold-copper project.

We asked him how the AI and data-centre build-out is changing demand for gold, copper and new mines.

Gold has traditionally been viewed as a store of value, but it also plays an important role in advanced electronics and computing. As AI and digital infrastructure continue to expand, how do you see gold’s role in the technology sector evolving?

Most people picture gold in a vault or in jewellery. Fewer think about the gold inside the devices they use every day. Engineers have relied on it for decades because it conducts electricity well, doesn’t corrode, and can be made into extremely thin wires and coatings. When a connection has to work every time, those properties matter.

I expect that role to continue as computing becomes more demanding. But I wouldn’t assume every increase in AI investment means the same increase in gold demand. Manufacturers are always looking for ways to use less of an expensive material.

You can see that tug-of-war in the numbers. The World Gold Council reported about 323 tonnes of technology demand in 2025, essentially flat on 2024. AI applications supported demand, but thinner wires, leaner designs and weaker consumer electronics offset that growth. So gold can become more important in specific high-end components without a dramatic jump in total tonnage.

The rapid expansion of AI data centers is driving demand for copper and other essential materials. How is this infrastructure boom reshaping demand for metals, and where does gold fit into the broader picture?

Start with the electricity. A data centre needs reliable power every hour it operates. That means looking past the servers to the substations, cables, transformers and generating capacity behind them.

The IEA’s latest analysis found that data-centre electricity use grew 17% in 2025. It expects that use to roughly double by 2030, with AI-focused facilities growing faster still. That gives you a sense of the physical build-out that companies are planning.

Copper runs through that whole electrical system. And AI is adding demand at the same time as utilities, transport and industry are investing in electrification. The mining industry has to plan for all of it together.

Gold plays a different role. It’s used selectively in electronics, where reliability justifies the cost, while copper’s exposure is spread across the physical infrastructure. For gold, technology matters, but it is still one part of a market driven mainly by investment, central banks and jewellery.

As tech companies invest billions in AI infrastructure, could growing demand for copper and other critical materials create supply chain bottlenecks that ultimately slow down technological progress?

Yes. The technology industry and the mining industry work on very different timelines. A commitment to spend billions on AI infrastructure doesn’t mean the materials will be there when construction teams need them.

S&P Global found that mines starting production between 2020 and 2024 took almost 18 years on average from discovery. Before construction even begins, a company has to drill the deposit, prove its economics, complete engineering, obtain approvals and secure financing.

For copper, the pressure goes well beyond AI. Data centres compete for supply with electricity networks, electric vehicles and other industries. The IEA’s 2026 outlook estimates that, under today’s policies, existing and announced projects could leave primary copper supply about 25% short of requirements in 2035.

Closing that gap takes more than new discoveries. It means financing projects that can actually deliver, expanding and restarting suitable operations, and recovering more from ore already being processed. Otherwise, technology companies face higher costs, longer equipment lead times and delayed projects.

That’s why I put so much weight on work that has already been done. Our Andacollo gold project in Chile is a former producing mine. We still have refurbishment, technical and financing work ahead of us, but we’re not starting from a blank page.

AI is increasingly being used to analyze geological data and identify mineral deposits. How could these technologies transform gold exploration, particularly when it comes to discovering resources that traditional methods may have overlooked?

One opportunity that really interests me is getting more out of work that has already been done.

An established mining district can hold decades of drilling, surveys and geological records. Different companies collected that information at different times, often looking for different things. There’s real value in bringing it together and asking questions that were hard to investigate before.

Canada is backing exactly this idea, with a federal and territorial pilot in the Northwest Territories that uses AI to scan and analyse drill core already sitting in government storage.

The majors are doing it too. Agnico Eagle works with GeologicAI, combining AI with drill-core scanning to make its resource models more complete and reliable.

At Galantas, our team in Chile spends a lot of time reading drill core and surface geology, and we share some of that work through our Field Notes video series. Technology can help, but experienced geologists still have to understand the core.

And you still have to drill. A model can suggest where to look; it can’t prove you have an economic deposit. For me the test is simple: does it help the team make a better decision about the next drill hole? Exploration capital is limited, so better targeting makes a real difference to how far that capital goes.

Gold is valued in high-reliability electronic components for its conductivity and resistance to corrosion. Could advances in AI hardware, semiconductors, and high-performance computing create new opportunities for gold, or will its role remain relatively specialized?

Specialised doesn’t mean unimportant. A component can contain very little gold and still depend on it to perform reliably.

There are new applications worth watching. One is co-packaged optics, which places optical connections right next to the processor so AI systems can move data faster and use less power. Some of the optical components and high-frequency electrodes in those designs use gold.

The World Gold Council sees it as a potentially small but meaningful new source of demand if it’s widely adopted in AI data centres. It’s still early.

I’d leave the engineering judgments to the chip makers. From a mining perspective, I want to know three things. Is the technology being adopted commercially? How much material does it need? And can something cheaper do the same job?

There will always be pressure to use less gold because of its price. But where it offers a clear reliability advantage, it earns its place. That points to a specialised role with room to grow, not a story where AI suddenly transforms the whole gold market.

Building the next generation of AI data centers requires massive investments in electricity grids and power distribution systems, where copper plays a critical role. Are technology companies underestimating their dependence on physical resources, and what happens if supply cannot keep pace?

I wouldn’t assume the technology companies don’t understand the dependency. The better question is whether everyone in the chain is working to a realistic timetable.

A server can be ordered. A grid connection may need new lines, approvals and equipment that can’t be delivered right away. The IEA has estimated that, unless these constraints are addressed, around 20% of planned data-centre projects worldwide could be at risk of delay. That’s mainly a grid problem rather than a copper shortage, but it shows how physical the AI build-out really is.

The supply chain also runs deeper than most people realise. In its 2026 outlook, the IEA warned that the near-term copper supply picture has worsened considerably, partly because of tight supplies of sulphuric acid. Many copper operations need that reagent to process their ore, and Chile, where we operate, is one of the major producers that use the process. Most people in tech have never thought about sulphuric acid, but it can affect how much copper reaches the market.

If supply can’t keep pace, companies will delay projects, pay more or build somewhere else. Long-term purchasing commitments and earlier conversations with suppliers help those suppliers expand with confidence. In mining, we know a good asset is only part of the equation; you also need power, infrastructure and financing. Digital infrastructure is no different.

How are machine learning, automation, and predictive analytics changing the economics of gold exploration and production, and could these technologies help smaller companies compete more effectively with established industry players?

The biggest opportunity is getting more value from the money we already spend. Drilling is expensive. Equipment downtime is expensive. Losing recoverable gold during processing is expensive. Those are specific problems technology can help address.

In exploration, better analysis of historical drilling and geological information can help a team decide where to drill next. It doesn’t guarantee a discovery, but better targeting can help a company make more effective use of its exploration budget.

In production, consider recovery: the percentage of metal in the ore that the plant successfully extracts. In a simplified example, if the material processed contains 100,000 ounces of gold, improving recovery from 90% to 92% means recovering another 2,000 ounces from the same feed. You still have to account for the cost of achieving that improvement, but you haven’t had to mine additional tonnes to access those ounces.

There are practical examples of this approach. BHP and Microsoft have described using real-time plant data and AI recommendations at Escondida to help operators adjust processing conditions with the aim of improving copper recovery.

Predictive maintenance tackles another cost. Identifying a developing equipment problem can allow a repair during a planned shutdown instead of an unexpected failure that interrupts production.

For smaller companies, access to specialist software and service providers can put better analytical tools within reach. But the tools still need reliable data and experienced people. Large operators retain advantages in both.

I would start with a problem we can measure, test the technology and compare the benefit with its full cost. A smaller company doesn’t need to match a major miner’s technology budget. It needs to spend its own budget effectively.

As the technology industry looks for more sustainable supply chains, could advances in electronic waste recycling, AI-driven material recovery, and more efficient production reduce the need for newly mined gold and copper?

Yes, to a degree. Recovering more metal from products we’ve already made makes sense. The question is how much can be collected and recovered economically, and when it becomes available.

The UN’s Global E-waste Monitor found that only 22.3% of the e-waste generated in 2022 was documented as formally collected and recycled. That’s measured by weight, not the recovery rate for any one metal, but it shows how much room there is to improve.

AI-assisted sorting and better processing can help. They still need collection networks, suitable facilities and a business model that covers the cost.

Timing matters too. Recycling depends on products reaching the end of their lives, and copper installed in a grid today may stay in service for decades.

So I see recycling and mining as complementary. More recycling improves supply security and reduces how many new mines we need. It doesn’t remove the need to invest in mining.

Looking toward 2030, which developments do you believe will have the greatest impact on the future of gold and critical metals: AI-powered exploration, rising demand from data centers, or the challenge of bringing new mineral supplies online?

For the period to 2030, I’d put delivering supply first. I also think it’s the one the market gives the least weight.

A discovery made today might be very important, but it’s unlikely to produce metal before 2030. That makes the projects already being permitted, financed and built far more relevant this decade. So is what existing operations can add through expansions, better recovery and sensible restarts.

AI will help with those decisions. I expect much of its near-term value to come from understanding known assets better and helping operations run more consistently.

But the asset still has to work. It needs the right geology and metallurgy, a realistic development plan, financing and the ability to operate responsibly. Better software doesn’t change that.

I’d also separate gold from copper. Data centres are part of copper’s wider infrastructure story. For gold, technology plays a role, but monetary conditions, investment demand and central-bank buying will matter more.

The question I keep coming back to is simple: which projects can actually deliver, at what cost, and when?

Included in today’s macOS 27.3 beta 1 is a great-looking screensaver featuring an animated version of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display wallpaper. Watch it below.

As it does for most new Macs, Apple designed a striking-looking wallpaper to mark the launch of the new MacBook Pro.

Continuing its tradition of incorporating product names into its wallpapers, the new design features a series of flowing, metallic-looking lines that spell out the word “PRO.”

Unsurprisingly, the design also proved divisive, with some users saying it reminds them of a glitchy, broken screen. Granted, the timing is particularly unfortunate, given the recent reports of display issues affecting the iPhone Duo.

#3233. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3232. How to get access to Sonos AI features, as company aims to avoid another app disaster

When Sonos tried a major app update two years ago, things did not go well. Much-loved features disappeared, older speakers experienced connection problems, and accessibility features were broken. That debacle saw the company’s CEO fired.

The company is taking a much more cautious approach as it moves into the AI era with a Sonos 27voice update, enabling natural-language voice control via Hey Sonos requests …

The whole mess started when Sonos launched the company’s first headphones, the Ace, intended to compete with AirPods Max. The app needed to be updated to support these, and the company decided to use it as an opportunity for a ground-up rebuild, launching a completely new app just ahead of the launch.

Customers responded angrily to the loss of key functionality, compatibility issues with older speakers, and accessibility problems. Sonos initially downplayed the complaints, but CEO Patrick Spence subsequently emailed customers to apologize, and provide a timeline for fixes, subsequently making seven promises. However, customers weren’t impressed, and called for Spence to be fired – later getting their wish.

This time around, Sonos started out with a modest update in the form of the Sonos 27 app, leaving the more substantial changes to a subsequent Sonos 27voice version. This will replace the more limited voice control available today, much like the update from old Siri to Siri AI.

Rather than pushing it out to all customers, Sonos is adopting a very cautious approach. First, you’ll have to request early access to the beta and be approved. Second, the company is testing the feature with a relatively small group of users. Third, it’s seeking detailed feedback from beta testers before a planned launch next year.

The new features work in much the same way as Siri on HomePods.

You can use Sonos 27voice at any time by saying the wake word, “Hey Sonos.” While Sonos is listening, the white status light on your Sonos product will glow brighter and the volume will lower if any audio is playing. A confirmation tone will play after Sonos understands your request.

The company says you can then use natural language for both music-related commands and information searches. The company gives the following music examples:

As well as a couple of general knowledge examples:

Sonos says that early access to the beta is only available to customers based in the US, that numbers will be limited, and enrollment is not guaranteed. However, if you want to request access, here’s how to do so:

If accepted, access begins from Friday and you’ll find setup instructions here.

#3231. I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing

Benjamin Skuse set out to test whether AI-generated research could pass for the real thing.

Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.

According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.

Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.

“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”

Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.Round 1: Creating the ForgeryTo give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.Luigi AvantaggiatoI assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI Jorge Cuadel CalleI took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.ROUND 2: FARS1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.Burden on AcademicsMahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers  Round 1: The Fake PaperCreated with free versions of ChatGPT and GeminiGhost citationsMany references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.Questionable scientific claimsAn expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.Too many acronymsThe expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.Round 2: The AI-Research PaperCreated by the autonomous research system FARSToo many preprintsThe references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.Nonsense in a figureOne technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”AI artifactsAnother figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him.
