I’ve been testing the iPhone 18 Pro Max ever since it launched in September, putting it through some marquee matchups against rivals like the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Pixel 11 Pro XL. Honestly, it’s the best camera phone around, thanks largely to its strong main camera performance, low-light capabilities, mechanical variable aperture, and new Pro Controls. I didn’t think another phone could come close to matching it, but I was wrong.

It’s been years since I last tested an Oppo device, mostly because stateside availability has always kept them just out of reach for the average consumer. But after putting the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max through its paces for the past month, it’s become my favorite camera phone.

You’d think its triple 200MP camera suite would be what truly puts it ahead of the pack, but it turns out to be the game-changing attachable Hasselblad lens that really seals the deal for me. Far from a gimmicky clip-on accessory, this optic unlocks the optical reach, depth, and fidelity that genuinely make it close to replacing my mirrorless camera. Here’s why.

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is an impressive camera phones, packing a versatile 200MP triple camera setup, massive 8,000 mAh silicon-carbon battery, 6.78-inch AMOLED display, MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro processor, 80W SuperVOOC wired charging, and 50W wireless charging.

One of my colleagues already drilled down into an Oppo Find X10 Pro Max vs. iPhone 18 Pro Max photo face-off, so I’m not going to rehash why the Oppo came out on top. Instead, I’m going to show and tell you what makes the Find X10 Pro Max stand out from the many other camera phones I’ve tested this year.

First and foremost, it starts with the hardware — a triple 200MP camera system. I’ll be the first to tell you that you should never judge a camera simply by the number of megapixels it claims. You have to evaluate the rest of the equation, especially sensor sizes and apertures.

The 200MP main shooter features a large 1/1.3-inch sensor, a wide f/1.5 aperture, and OIS. Equally notable is the 200MP periscope telephoto with 3x optical zoom, boasting a sizable 1/1.56-inch sensor and f/2.1 aperture.

That telephoto sensor is critical: through sensor cropping and Oppo’s processing algorithms, it pulls off a staggering 120x digital zoom. That easily eclipses the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s 40x ceiling, giving me triple the zoom reach of Apple's flagship. In fact, the only other phone I’ve tested this year that matches that level of reach is the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

For me, the true test is how well a phone behaves under low light — and the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is an absolute beast. Take a look at that first shot above I captured at sunset by the beach, which handles the stark contrast in lighting exceptionally well.

With the sun dipping over the horizon, the golden glow never overpowers the scene, maintaining a rich contrast across the foreground elements. But what’s even more impressive is the sheer number of stars it resolves in the process, cleanly rendering the Pleiades star cluster right alongside the twilight sky.

The Find X10 Pro Max pulls in astonishing amounts of light without relying on overly aggressive computational brightening that turns dark night skies into a noisy mess. You can see it across the rest of the sample shots above. For the best results, I recommend switching over to its "Master" mode, which lets you fine-tune the manual exposure settings to your exact liking.

Flagships aren’t just defined by their main cameras; they also live or die by versatile telephoto systems that pull you closer to distant subjects while preserving fine detail. On its own, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max’s native periscope camera is an absolute powerhouse. Whether I’m trying to read small text on a distant street sign or resolve faint details across a landscape, it doesn't disappoint.

I can clearly tell that computational processing kicks in at longer focal lengths, but virtually all modern flagships leverage AI upscaling to draw out fine textures. Just look at the first set of shots I captured by the waterfront, where I start with the ultrawide camera and step through all the primary focal lengths all the way to 120x.

The distant building across the inlet is practically indistinguishable in the ultrawide frame, but it sharpens into view with each successive crop — culminating in a 120x capture that brings into focus the individual bricks along the exterior wall, blades of grass in the foreground, and distinct roof shingles.

You can see its resolving power in some of the other sets of images, like pulling out intricate architectural carvings across the facade of the New York Public Library and keeping street signs fully legible from across the road.

My personal favorite is the shot of the bearded dragon I captured through its glass enclosure. What’s impressive is the staggering amount of detail, which makes it look like I had the lens parked right in front of its face based on the tight framing and definition — but in reality, I was standing about a foot away.

Lastly, I want to talk about what truly sets the Find X10 Pro Max apart: the Hasselblad telephoto converter kit. I’ve tested plenty of add-on lenses for both iPhones and Android devices over the years, and while some perform better than others, they almost always compromise on raw optical quality. What changes the game here is that this converter kit was engineered specifically to match the optics of the Find X10 Pro Max’s telephoto sensor — and the difference in output is immediately noticeable.

It's quickly become my go-to tool for nature and wildlife photography, letting me pull tight frames on distant subjects without disturbing them. The best part isn’t just the staggering amount of detail it captures — like in the first bird photo below, where you can easily make out individual feathers — it’s the authentic subject-background separation that only real optical glass can provide.

You can clearly see that depth across the sample gallery above, from the defined texture in the squirrel's bushy tail along the wooden railing to the details of nesting birds. The creamy background blur produced by this telephoto setup is remarkable, giving every frame a professional look without computational makeover. In fact, there are times when I genuinely struggle to tell the difference between these shots and those from a dedicated mirrorless camera.

After spending a full month with the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, it’s clear that groundbreaking mobile camera innovation is thriving outside the usual suspects like Apple, Samsung, and Google. Between its versatile triple 200MP sensor array, superb low-light and astrophotography performance, and a native periscope zoom capable of reaching out to a killer 120x, it delivers every bit of the flagship-tier performance I look for.

But it’s the modular Hasselblad telephoto converter kit that truly elevates this device from a fantastic camera phone into an unmatched creative tool — delivering authentic 10x optical reach, crisp framing, and stabilized long-range shots that genuinely bridge the gap to a dedicated mirrorless setup.

#3221. How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network

Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he says, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” says Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”

At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies

This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

To that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta says its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO

“We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” says Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The company is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, New York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

The top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.

Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.

The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.

The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.

On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.

The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”

“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”

A decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.

But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.

The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.

Because individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.

To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.

“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.

The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.

Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.

Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.

For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.

Beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.

“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.

Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.

There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.

According to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.

As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

That helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

In Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the company’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies

By contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

“One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” says Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them big. This limitation is from the batteries.”

In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies

Further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the company’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

Then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

This article was updated on 29 October 2026.

Tom Clynes, an IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, is a writer and photojournalist who covers science and the environment.

This sounds like a test plane more than a commercial one, but I guess that makes sense while companies are figuring out how to integrate new technologies into our existing safety regulations.The other thing that stands out to me is how the motors have redundant sub-systems. I can see the value, but it sure seems like a steep price to pay in terms of weight and complexity. Looking forward to seeing how that evolves.

#3220. Martin Marietta (MLM) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Lhoist lifts results while housing softness and diesel costs pressure margins.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Martin Marietta Materials, Inc. (MLM +2.35%) reported record financial results for the third quarter, primarily supported by the strategic integration of Lhoist North America and continued resilience in infrastructure and heavy nonresidential end markets. Management stated that the company's portfolio transformation into high-margin specialties and aggregates is intended to provide earnings durability across economic cycles. The company is currently executing a network optimization program to align production with shifting demand and reduce structural costs through plant idling and inventory management. While interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as single family residential construction have softened, management indicated that infrastructure investment remains supported by elevated state department of transportation budgets and multiyear federal funding programs.

I will now turn the call over to your host, Ms. Jacklyn Rooker, Martin Marietta's vice president of investor relations. Jacklyn, you may begin.

C. Howard Nye: Thank you, Jacklyn. Good morning, and thank you for joining today's earnings call. Martin Marietta delivered record financial performance in the third quarter while advancing the transformation of our portfolio. Importantly, we achieved these results in a more challenging macroeconomic environment as strong acquisition performance more than offset elevated diesel, and other energy related cost inflation. The completion of our combination with Lhoist North America or LNA marked a defining milestone in our company's evolution meaningfully expanding our differentiated upstream specialties platform and further diversifying our earnings and cash flow profile. LNA's performance since closing has provided early validation of the strategic and financial rationale for the transaction.

For the August 21 through September 30 period, the business generated revenues and cash gross profit of $216 million and $115 million respectively. Well ahead of our initial expectations. 75 days since closing, integration is progressing well, and we remain focused on capturing the synergy benefits of the combination while maintaining the business' operating momentum. I thank our teams for their tremendous dedication and hard work in supporting the successful closing and ongoing integration. Turning to our 2026 outlook, as announced in today's release, we are updating our full year revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoints to $7.8 billion and $2.48 billion respectively.

This updated guidance reflects stronger acquisition contributions partially offset by lower near term expectations for our heritage operations where softer shipment trends and current price cost dynamics are anticipated to persist through the fourth quarter. Looking toward 2027, our preliminary outlook anticipates mid to high single digit mix adjusted aggregates pricing growth reflecting already communicated January 1 pricing actions for fixed based customers, fourth quarter 26 pricing actions on new quoted work, and the midyear pricing carryover across acquired businesses.

Since the acquired operations have lower average selling prices in our heritage business, acquisition mix will temper headline reported pricing growth in the first half of 27 particularly through May 15, the 1 year anniversary of the New Frontier Materials acquisition. We thus expect full year reported ASP growth in the mid single digit range. Importantly, these acquired operations provide meaningful opportunity for continued pricing growth over time as we apply our commercial practices across the expanded network. Turning to the end market trends, infrastructure remains our most resilient and aggregates intensive end market.

At the federal level, current surface transportation programs have been extended through December 11, 2026, while work continues toward a longer term extension and, ultimately, the next surface transportation authorization. We continue to see broad bipartisan support for infrastructure investment Importantly, 40% of the infrastructure investment in Jobs Act funding remains to be spent. Providing a multiyear runway for transportation investment. At the same time, state department of transportation budgets across many of our key markets remain at historically elevated levels. More than 60% of funding across our top states is derived from state and other nonfederal sources providing a more stable funding base.

Private construction presents a more mixed outlook with Dodge Construction Network forecasting nonresidential square footage starts of approximately 1.2 billion square feet in 2027 approximately 24% below the 2022 peak While interest rate sensitive private nonresidential construction remains soft, data centers, power generation, and warehouse development remain areas of relative strength. Data center project shipments more than doubled in the third quarter, versus the prior year's comparable period. Our extensive distribution network, particularly in Texas and Louisiana, positions us well to serve the scale and logistical complexity of these often geographically remote projects with both construction aggregates and lime for soil stabilization.

Also encouraged by the ongoing recovery in warehouse construction building on the inflection that began in last year's third quarter. Michael J. Petro: Thank you, Ward, and good morning, everyone. Our core aggregates business generated record revenues of $1.7 billion an increase of 14%. Cash gross profit of $696 million an increase of 6%, driven by acquisition contributions that more than offset a $25 million decline the organic business. Excluding the diesel headwind, cost of goods sold per ton would have increased 3% or 2.6% on an organic basis reflecting disciplined controllable cost management by our operating teams. Most notably, organic labor cost per ton, our single largest cost category, declined modestly in the quarter and was roughly flat year to date.

Our specialties business delivered record quarterly revenues and cash gross profit of $362 million and $163 million respectively, LNA's $216 million revenue and $115 million cash gross profit contribution since the August 21 closing date further demonstrates the resilience of Lyme and the transaction's margin accretion to the enterprise. In a year characterized by significant acquisition and divestiture activity, related purchase accounting, and comparability impacts on reported results our record third quarter free cash flow of $426 million an increase of 18% demonstrates the strong underlying financial performance of the business. On a year to date basis, disciplined inventory management has unlocked $135 million while capital expenditures are $157 million lower than the prior year period.

These actions alone have contributed over $290 million of free cash flow improvement. Together with our strong year to date organic labor cost control, ongoing network optimization efforts, and other structural cost actions, we reaffirm our confidence in achieving $350 million incremental cash flow target discussed during the second quarter call. Turning now to our updated 2026 guidance and preliminary 2027 outlook. Our revised 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoint of $2.48 billion includes expected contributions from LNA and reflects year to date performance. October shipment trends and an assumed normal winter. The outlook also incorporates continued inflationary pressure across diesel and other energy related cost categories, as well as New Frontier's impact on reported volume and headline pricing.

In 2027, we expect margin expansion driven primarily by mid- to high single digit mix adjusted aggregates pricing growth combined with ongoing network optimization disciplined cost management, and a full year contribution from LNA, we expect these benefits to more than offset continued inflationary pressure. Turning now to the balance sheet. We funded the cash consideration for the LNA transaction with a $1.5 billion pre-payable term loan and $5.5 billion of senior notes issued across several maturities with a weighted average coupon rate of approximately 5.5%. As discussed when announcing the transaction, we are committed to deleveraging to our targeted range of 2 to 2.5x net debt to adjusted EBITDA and retaining our investment grade credit ratings.

With deleveraging supported by the significantly enhanced free cash flow generation of the combined business. Ward, back to you.

C. Howard Nye: Thank you, Michael. What distinguishes Martin Marietta today is the deliberate reshaping of our earnings profile. Through portfolio optimization, we have built a more resilient and diversified business with increased contributions from our central division, and our higher margin specialties platform. At the same time, we are optimizing our aggregates network, and aligning production with current demand conditions, creating a leaner cost structure and a more efficient operating platform. Combined with the pricing discipline that has long been a hallmark of Martin Marietta, these actions position us to expand margins, while continuing to grow earnings and cash flow. Operator, please provide the required instructions as we are now ready to take questions.

Operator: Thank you. If you would like to ask a question, please press star followed by 1 on your telephone keypad. Question and rejoin the queue for any additional questions. Our first question comes from Trey Grooms from Stephens.

Trey Grooms: Hey, good morning, everyone. Thanks for taking my question. So Ward, could you give us a little bit more detail on the puts and takes behind your preliminary 2027 pricing view of mid to high single digits, mix And what is your end market outlook? Could imply for organic aggregates volumes next year? And with this, maybe what your outlook is for the gross profit contribution from ags or cash gross profit contribution given your outlook for continued higher costs in 2027? Thank you.

C. Howard Nye: Trey, thanks for the question. Good morning to you. Trey, I will take you through several puts and takes on that. So let's start to your question with pricing. So currently, we see a nice path to mid to high single digit mix adjusted aggregates growth in 2027. And I think there is several reasons for that. Number 1, what we think we are going to see on January 1 price realization. I think that is important.

Number 2, what we are already seeing in quoting work that we are doing now in Q4 and on the 2027 projects that were coming next year, and then lastly, the carryover pricing on acquired volumes at the midyear price increases that we saw in the acquired businesses. As I indicated in the prepared remarks, those markets tend to be 50% or 25% below heritage Martin Marietta, So that is important that we got those in midyear. But equally gives us a nice track record going forward. What I will say relative to pricing, and I mentioned it briefly in the prepared remarks, cadence is gonna matter.

Because, obviously, as we anniversary both the Quikrete transaction in February and the New Frontier acquisition in May, you will see a nice bump those 2 anniversaries roll by. But keep in mind, if we are really thinking about the business in 2 different chunks, I would say this. The heritage business, about half of the shipments are fixed base and about half are quoted work. Again, if we are seeing nice quoted work pull through right now, I think that is important. Relative to the other part of your question with respect to volumes, I guess I would say several things. Number 1, the backlogs actually look very similar to what they did coming into this year.

I think that is a really good place to start. At the same time, as you and I discussed before, it is a dynamic market right now. So we are really just waiting to see the end of the year and have a much better feel on the precision of what volumes are going to look like. The thing that is important to remember relative to volume is we are gonna have a really tough Q1 compare. Because keep in mind, as we said last year, when Vale is having a bad winter, meaning they have no snow, we are having a great winter.

So keep in mind, the West and the central divisions came out of the box early in 2026 very, very aggressively. We do not anticipate that happening. Again, that goes back to Michael's comment. We are really looking for more normalized weather. With respect to the other part of your question on end market outlook, I would say several things. 1, think the best way to think about that is it continues to be relatively bifurcated.

And what I mean by that, residential and light nonres, simply remain pressured because of what is going on with interest rates and as we saw those rates move here in the second half of the year, we saw both of those hit a bit of an air pocket. Not a big surprise, You would have expected it. I expected it too. And, frankly, as long as mortgage rates remain above 7%, single family housing is just not gonna be in a terribly robust place. Now the converse of that is what we see going on in infrastructure and what we see in heavy non res.

So if we are looking at that, keep in mind those areas account for about half of our aggregates business. So when we are going into the new year with those performing well, I think that is important. So if we are looking at data centers, they remain an especially attractive opportunity. And what we are seeing is year over year, our data center volumes more than doubled year over year in the third quarter. And again, Texas is expected to represent approximately 30% of projected US data center capacity by 2028 And our leading position in Texas, not just in stone, but in lime today is gonna put us in a really attractive place for those multiyear projects.

But we have also discussed what is been happening relative to warehouse. We expect that recovery to continue. Again, if we are looking at warehouse and distribution construction, that is up approximately in our world by 51%. Year to date. And again, I mentioned what Amazon is doing between now and 2031, adding more than a thousand facilities. We think, again, that gives nice momentum going into the new year. And the last 1 I will mention, Trey, in response to your question, then I will ask Michael to come back and talk specifically about profit numbers that you have referenced. Is power generation.

And we are seeing that move in very considerable ways both relative to LNG and what is happening in portions of the Texas market, but more broadly, what is happening in data and data warehousing as well because we are seeing increasingly amounts of that going in behind the meter. So I have tried to give you a sense of what do I think is happening with price, what do I think is happening with volume, How are the end markets behaving that I think lead up to those? Then, Michael, I will ask you to come back and respond to the other portion of this question.

Michael J. Petro: Yeah, Trey, we will come back certainly with more specifics relative to our profit guide for next year. We are just given the preliminary pricing now. But as you know, pricing is the disproportionate lever for profit growth. And as Ward mentioned, we feel very confident about what we are going to be able to achieve January 1 there. So the mid to high single digits on a mix adjusted basis is definitely what you should be baking in. What I would tell you is inflation we expect continue.

Certainly with diesel where it is today, I think you can model a flat line there We are seeing all in with acquisitions about a $25 million headwind per quarter for diesel. So we will lap that in Q1 of next year. So we will have an incremental headwind going into next year in the first quarter until we start having same 1, same diesel comps. So think elevated inflation mid to high single digit pricing, and some of the commentary that Ward provided on volume out are able to get you to a preliminary profit number.

Operator: Our next question comes from Adam Thalhimer from Thompson Davis. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Adam Thalhimer: Hey. Good morning, guys. Nice job in a tough environment. Hey. Thanks. Can you update us on how the LNA integration is going? And why did they get off to such a fast start in Q3?

C. Howard Nye: Adam, thanks for the question. And look. that is obviously a bright spot in almost any circumstance. The integration is going just fine is the quick response. The work streams are well underway. The performance so far, to your point, has exceeded our initial expectations. The integration remains totally on track, so if you are really looking at what is happened in the 40 days since closing, cash gross profit was $115 million, adjusted EBITDA at $104 million, at 48-plus percent margin. And part of what I think people are now seeing is what we had long seen in that business and why we found it to be so compelling.

And keep in mind, we have not even started to get the additional contributions that we believe we are going to see as we continue to integrate this because we think the additional value creation that is going to come from cross selling in hot mix or Texas mega projects or otherwise is gonna be pretty considerable. So to your point, are we really remain focused on capturing those synergies just as quickly and thoughtfully as we can? We are. But here's the other piece that we are really focused on. it is a great business.

So the last thing that we want to do is do anything that takes a really good business, a high performing business, and puts it off track. The integration is going well. The synergy realization is going well. The cultures have come together. Actually very nicely. Their safety culture and ours aligned the way that we would hope Adam. So there is nothing that we are seeing in this that has been a negative surprise to us at all. And again, I think we will continue to have results that the street will see. And they will like and the merits of this transaction will simply become self evident. Thanks, Ward.

Operator: Thank you, Our next question comes from Kathryn Thompson from Thompson Research Group. Please go Hi.

Kathryn Thompson: Thank you for taking my question today. I appreciate your color on 2027 outlook and also for LNA. Congratulations again on closing that I think the next big subject are elections. So we wrapped up elections yesterday, and we are looking forward to hopefully, a reauthorization of the federal highway bill next year. Would like to get your thoughts in terms of how the elections may or may not impact this process. What you are seeing right now with states in terms of their spending and, you know, some of the inevitable things that happen such as holding up lettings, in advance of a highway bill? And are you seeing that in the states in which you operate? So much.

C. Howard Nye: Catherine, thanks so much. The question. I would say several things. 1, to your point, if we are really looking at states in the first instance and the fact that in our world, given the fact that we have tried to build our business in states that have really good fiscal conditions, The state budget circumstances matter disproportionately. And what we are seeing right now is very good, consistent, expected performance from the states. And what I mean by that is if I go in and look at. And states are important to us, which means now California, Texas, Georgia, Missouri, South Carolina, Colorado, Iowa, they are all maintaining or increasing transportation investment.

If we are looking at North Carolina and Florida, again, their funding is gonna be perfectly adequate for what we are looking to do next year. So as we are going into 2027, I do not see anything in the states that are disproportionately important to us that lead us to believe that there are gonna be any issues there. And to your point, have we seen any delay in lettings? The short answer is no. We have not. If we are looking on the other part of your question relative to what is going on from the federal level, Now keep in mind, when Build America 250 came out of the congress, it came out with 62-2 vote.

I mean, that tells us from the outset that this is a bipartisan bill. Look, do I think it is still possible that we could see something in a lame duck congress? Maybe. Do I think that is relatively unlikely? Probably. And do I think a democratic senate might push even harder relative to highways, bridges, roads, streets. And overall transportation? I think so. So long story short, do I think we should go ahead and plan for seeing probably a continuing resolution or 2 as the congress goes through that process. I think that is probably realistic. Is that something that concerns me? I would suggest to you frankly, not at all. Again, I think this is largely bipartisan.

I think we have got a group likely coming in who want to invest perhaps even more So, again, I am not seeing anything from the states that is concerning to me. I see a process going forward at the federal government, but I think we have seen before, and it is very navigable. The last thing that I would say, and I think this is important, if we go back and look at the last peak in aggregate shipments several years ago, You know what that was in the middle of? A continuing resolution.

And I think what happens is people oftentimes sit back, look at a CR, and wonder what is this going to mean for this very fundamental product that rolls out And the fact is, we simply go through these ebbs and flows, I think, in a very steady, very way. And I do not see anything at the federal level or the state level that makes me think otherwise, Catherine. So I hope that is responsive. that is very helpful. Thanks so much, and best of luck. Thanks, Katherine.

Operator: Our next question comes from Philip Ng from Jefferies. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Philip Ng: Hey, guys. I guess my question is for 2027 for either for Michael. If diesel prices and cost at these levels, is 3% to 4% cost per ton increase reasonable when we think about 2027? And then been really noisy this year. Outside of M&A, any callouts on mix and the loss or any noise in terms of that number as well? And I know they produce some construction grade aggregate as well. Yeah.

Michael J. Petro: No. Thanks, Philip, for the question. I think the short answer to your COGS per ton inflation estimate is probably in the general ZIP code. The best way to think about it for us on diesel is we will consume in the aggregates business all in with Quickrete and New Frontier. About 50 million gallons. You know, at current spot rates of about $4.70 a gallon. So that is gonna be the diesel comp that we will be looking at next year. And we are assuming planning purposes internally and for what we are doing relative to price, that type of diesel level for the for the balance of 2027. No, you were breaking up a little bit.

Philip Ng: Sure. From your from a mix standpoint for pricing, 2027, any callouts outside of M&A that could create some noise for 2027? Appreciate New Frontier and Quikrete and Lhoist, I believe they have some construction grade aggregates do not believe it is part of that equation, but does that have an impact in terms of we think about mix for 2027?

Michael J. Petro: Yep. No. So the Lhoist aggregates are certainly out of that. From a mix perspective in Q1, you will have the acquisition mix of New Frontier and 2 months of Quikrete. So on a reported basis, that will continue to be impacted by those tons flowing through. Of course, you get the benefit of the tonnage on volume in the Q1 comp on an as reported basis. Then in Q2, you have about 45 days of New Frontier.

So we begin to lap the acquisition comps midway through Q2 and that. that is generally speaking the mix from an acquisition perspective The other mix that we have had a lot of this year is the geographic mix on the organic business. That could very well turn into be a mix tailwind next year. As Ward mentioned, we do not expect we are expecting more of a normal winter. So we do not expect is for the central division and Colorado to come out of the gates with the volume growth that we saw those 2 divisions do. This year. So that means more contribution from the East and the Southwest, which tend to have higher average selling prices.

That said, that is why we are guiding preliminarily to a mix adjusted price metric of mid to high single digits. That would effectively capture all mix, whether it be organic and or acquisition.

C. Howard Nye: Hey, Let me come back and add 1 more thing too because the price conversation is really important. And thank you for the question. The other thing that I wanna make sure we do not drive by in this quote without talking about has been the cost performance of the business. Because I think our teams have done that in my view, extraordinarily well. So if we are looking at organic cost of goods sold, and I am going to exclude for these, external freight, it increased 5.1% of the quarter and 3.8% year-to-date. But excluding the diesel spike, and the corresponding increases were limited to 2.6% and 2.2%, respectively.

And 1 thing that I think is really important is if we are looking at labor cost per ton, which is our single largest cost category, that was flat for both the quarter and year to date. So I think your point's a good 1, and that is making sure you have your head around what is that pricing cadence next year. But keep in mind, the thing that we can really control within our gates is what is happening with respect to cost. And I like the setup relative to pricing, but I also like what I am already seeing relative to cost.

So forgive me for parachuting that in, Phil, but I think that is an important 1 to get Appreciate the color. Thank you, guys. You bet.

Operator: Our next question comes from Angel Castillo from Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Esther Osinaiya: Hi. This is Esther Osinaiya on for Angel Castillo. I just had a question on the aggregate sold to ready mixed customers. Is it mainly moved to April 1 increases. So do you see any changes in the ability to get price for ready mixed customers in 2027, like that timeline shifting to possibly twice a year versus that 1 time, April 1?

C. Howard Nye: Esther, thank you for the question. I would say several things. No. I do not. And what I think we are broadly seeing from ready mixed customers is as follows. I think some will be January 1, I think some will be April 1. I think there is just gonna be a primary difference in geographies. So think in geographies that are colder based, you will see April. I think in warmer based, you will see a January 1 price increase. And here's what we have heard very clearly from our concrete customers this year. It was very difficult for them given what was happening in private nonres and res markets to take a midyear price increase this year.

I think that is part of the pressure that you have seen this year. Their response has been I am seeing the same input issues you are. I know you are gonna have to go up in the New Year. Do this for me. Give me 1 price increase Hit me at the beginning of the year, and do not plan for midyear next year. I think that actually helps them in their planning. Frankly, from our perspective, moving that forward is very helpful as well. So I think your question relative to concrete is particularly well placed because I think that has been really 1 of the more challenging aspects of this year.

But, again, I think the answer is yes. We will see increases in some markets in January. Yes. We will see increases in some markets in April. We are gonna treat both of those relative to concrete as if that is going to be the only 1 during the course of the year. So, Esther, I hope that is helpful. Yes. Thank you.

Anthony Pettinari: Hey. So in the quarter, you saw ag's organic shipments decline and organic pricing up, I think, 2.7%.
