That you would call out when we look at 3Q and maybe think about 4Q.

C. Howard Nye: Yeah. I would I would say the primary thing that changed, Anthony, is number 1, the concrete guys could not take mid years this year. And just talk with Esther about that. So I think that is 1 thing. I do not see that persistent I think the other issue was, as interest rates moved. We simply saw the private work slowdown. And, again, not a big surprise. I think you have crossed the heavy side space.

I would be surprised if that is not a pretty consistent answer And part of what I think we are doing is we are looking at what happened with volumes because of that interest rate increase in September and then what we have seen in October. On a days affected basis. that is what is informed the way that we have looked at the balance of the year, particularly going into Q4. And again, last year, for example, we had a November that was a pretty heady November from a volume perspective. So, again, I think we are trying to just be very thoughtful. Maybe with a touch of conservatism. As we are looking at Q4 this year.

Okay. that is helpful. I will turn it over. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from Keith Hughes from Truist. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Keith Hughes: Thank you. When you were talking about 2027, you called out the dates. So specifically anniversarying New Frontier. And I guess, Quikrete, in getting their prices up towards the Martin Marietta average. I assume you are not gonna get it all the way. Do you have any feel for how much of the gap between the 2 entities pricing you will be able to realize as we hit the second half of next year.

C. Howard Nye: Keith, that is a great question. So thank you for that. So I would say several things. 1, did we see mid years at the Quickrete operations New Frontier this year even though we closed New Frontier after the mid year? The answer is yes. We did. Do I anticipate that those will likely be marked in which we will look for mid years again next year? The answer is yes. I think we probably will.

Think to answer your question more directly, typically, what we have seen Keith, is probably a 36 month runway from the time that we buy a business until the time that we can get it closer to something that looks like a Martin Marietta average I do not think these are gonna be dramatically different. And 1 reason I would say that in many respects is the markets that are really hitting it the hardest right now tend to be those markets in the center part of the country. So if we are looking in markets in Missouri and Kansas City or others, those are markets that from a volume perspective have done very, very well this year.

And again, back to the notion on backlogs. Our backlogs in those markets also look attractive So I think I have given you A, where they sit today, b, the timeframe that we think we are likely to see that gap closed, and what I think will happen in those markets with mid years in 2027. You are welcome, Keith.

Operator: Our next question comes from Avi Jaroslawis from UBS. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Analyst: Good morning. So I know you are expecting positive price cost for the year next year, but should we expect that the organic price cost is going to turn positive early in 2027? Or should we continue to see some headwinds there for some time into next year? Maybe until we lap some of the, higher cost comps from this year?

Michael J. Petro: Yeah. No. We would think on an organic basis, so ex the reported mix impacts from the acquisitions, should see price cost out of the gate next year. Okay. Got it. And just quickly, maybe what are you expecting on that front for Q4? It look similar to Q3 or any differences? Yeah. So on an organic basis, for Q4, what we are seeing is implied in the guide is down high single digit volume. Up on a reported organic basis about 2% pricing. So that is a step up from the 1% that we saw in Q3. So we are starting to see a little bit of momentum from the quoting work flowing through.

But we expect to continue to have the elevated COGS inflation in Q4. So we think Q4 is certainly still price cost negative, the inflection point being what we are going to do on January 1. Okay. Very helpful. Thank you very much. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from Jared Greenblatt from JPMorgan.

Garrett Samuel Greenblatt: Hi, thanks for taking my question. I just wanted to touch back on the Lhoist transaction and talk about some expectations between 2027 there. In terms of that, what is the cadence of when we should expect to see some of this cross selling volume start flowing through on the aggregate side? Maybe if you could talk about the timing of the royalty contracts you have. Then just on the price side of things, what are the dynamics or expectations you see for lime in 2027?

C. Howard Nye: Well, We will with the aggregate side in the fullness of time. I mean, those are contracts that are in place with companies that we and LNA have good relationships with, and we want to be very thoughtful. About those. If we start looking at really what we expect from LNA next year, part of what is going to be attractive about that business, we are anticipating about $820 million worth of EBITDA for 2027. And part of what is really appealing about that business is how steady we think that is going to look across the year.

And I think that is 1 of the things that we spoke up when we did the transaction because it adds such nice, stable, consistent predictable earnings. So if we think about what that is gonna look like, mean, this is pretty easy way to measure it. Probably 23% of profits will come through in Q1, 27%-ish in Q2, 27% in Q3, and then back to 23% in Q4. So really, you have got it bookended with 23%. You got 27% in the middle, which means you are getting about a 50/50 split. During the course of the year.

I think to the other part of your question, we are already having our sales teams working very collaboratively looking at either DOT jobs, data center jobs, etcetera. Because keep in mind, part of what is going to happen now on either Public Works or big heavy private nonres works is we can look at those jobs together. And in some instances, they are gonna want base stone, clean stone, etcetera. In other instances, they may want the lime, particularly as they are working through in some respects, unsuitable or challenging soils. Or in some instances, we may want to push them 1 way or another for various reasons that are to the customer's benefit.

So you will clearly see the benefits of cross selling coming through as we get into 2027. Frankly, I think we will start seeing some of that even here in the latter part of 2026. Again, I hope that answered your question.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ivan Yi from Wolfe Research. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Ivan Yi: Yes. Good morning, guys. Thanks for the time. You bet. You did not break out you did not break out specific the volumes and the pricing for the lime business, but can you speak directionally about how LNA tonnage and pricing trended in 3Q? And also, what are you seeing thus far in 4Q? Thank you.

Michael J. Petro: Yeah. No. We are we are still looking at ultimately what is gonna be the level of disclosure for specialties business as we balance providing appropriate visibility so that the investing community can make informed decisions versus disclosing anything competitively sensitive. So I think it is all part of the evaluation that we are taking a look at. But what I can say on volume and price just on a percentage basis, both were up nicely with revenue in the period that we ended in September was up about double digits. And I would say the trend in October on 1 less shipping day looked similar. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from Michael Dudas from Vertical Research.

Michael Dudas: Good morning, Jacklyn. Michael, and Ward. Good morning. Maybe this 1 for Michael. You highlighted some positive operating and free cash flow metrics in the quarter and your outlook for the year. Maybe you can early look on 2027 on CapEx, or can you continue to get some working capital tailwinds as we move to 2027? And, you know, looking at relative to what free cash flow generation could be versus what you had thought coming into the Lhoist acquisition?

Michael J. Petro: How's it played through? Yes. So the Lhoist business, as you know, is just a cash generation machine because it does not require a lot of CapEx given back to a question that we were talking about earlier. They largely outsource a lot of the mining. So crushing rock, it wears down crushers, conveyors, equipment, etcetera, is on a third party's dime. So extremely good cash flow conversion from EBITDA generated from LNA given the limited CapEx requirements.

C. Howard Nye: But I would say for next year, our CapEx guide when we do come out with it will include CapEx all in inclusive of acquisitions. But we still expect that to be within that guide that we provided at the Capital Markets Day, which would suggest about 25% of EBITDA. So we do not see any difference in that. Relative to working capital, we are getting a lot of the benefits this year. In terms of working capital inflows relative to inventory. What we are gonna look to do is stabilize that so that we do not have it swinging the other way into a working capital outflow. Moving forward.

So I would not expect the same quantum of cash flow impact as a result of inventory management, but I would not expect it to reverse and go the other way.

Michael Dudas: And we are looking at some tuck in acquisitions you made. You now close of 1 in September. How does that play out the next 12, 18 months given the deleveraging focus on top of what this. I am sure it is pretty interesting pipeline still for additions for your business.

C. Howard Nye: It is. And, Michael, thank you for the question on that. Actually, the way that we structured the transaction between cash and equity, was very purposeful because we did not want to have ourselves on the sidelines if we saw. If attractive bolt on acquisitions. Now that said, the delevering process is going to be important. And we are going to start that here in the fourth quarter with approximately $500 million of debt repayment coming up over the coming weeks. So I think you will see a nice blend. Will we invest in the business, to Michael's point, from a CapEx perspective? That we think is appropriate Absolutely. Will we be paying down debt? To be sure.

And will we continue to be in the bolt on business in. On the aggregate Just as you saw with the Fraser transaction that was announced, we will continue to do that and we have the ability to do it. So you for the question. Thank you, guys.

Operator: Our next question comes from Brent Thielman from Oppenheimer. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Brent Thielman: Hey, thanks. Good morning. Ward, maybe just on LNA, it looks like you were low 40% gross margin ex the markup on a shortened quarter. Can you just talk about your ability to protect those margins? Or even expand on those margins in a kind of a dynamic cost environment.

C. Howard Nye: You know, the nice thing about that business is, you know, a big piece of their cost is energy. They have looked at that from a very different lens than we have historically in aggregates. We looked at it 2 degree in this dimension in cement because there is some hedging that goes on with that. So again, it tends to be very, very predictable. The pricing in that space tends to be pretty constructive as new work comes up. And keep in mind, the other thing that is different about that business is in many respects, we have got contracts going forward that we know are in place that have built in inflators in them.

So, again, it is a business that we talked about before from quarter to quarter, from a year to year, and otherwise, you can actually model really very, very well. And yeah, I think having the business positioned in the Southern of the United States where we continue to see remanufacturing, where we continue to see significant energy work. Whereas I indicated in my prepared remarks, Texas is gonna have 30% of the data center activity over the coming years. We see something in that business that we believe is highly durable and highly resilient, and that was 1 of the reasons that we were so attracted to it. Frankly, for the last decade.

And, again, we have we have been watching that space. And keep in mind, even if you look at our heritage Woodville plant, I mean, that was the business that was seeing nice growth at the mid sing. #3218. Google will spend $15B on data centres in Malaysia over two years

New campuses in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan add to Malaysia's place as Southeast Asia's data centre hub.

Google plans to spend $15B in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028 on data centres, cloud operations, water, power and training. It will expand its Selangor campus and build new ones in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, where it is also funding a $160M water plant.

Google plans to spend $15B on data centres and cloud operations in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. The money will also go into local water supplies, power generation and training, the company said.

Google will expand its existing campus at Elmina Business Park in Selangor and build new ones in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, Malay Mail reported. The Elmina site came from a $2B investment Google announced in May 2024.

Alphabet chief investment officer Ruth Porat announced the plan at an event in Kuala Lumpur attended by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

“Our nation possesses the stability, the talent, the ambition to be a premier digital powerhouse in Southeast Asia,” Anwar said.

Google says building the campuses will support more than 37,000 local jobs a year and add about $1.1B a year to Malaysia’s economy. Once they are running, it expects them to sustain more than 9,000 jobs.

Water is a big part of the deal. Earlier this week, Google said it would fund a $160M reservoir and treatment plant in Negeri Sembilan. It will supply 65 million litres of drinking water a day to the data centre and nearby communities.

Water has become a flashpoint for Google elsewhere. Its $15B India data centre has faced protests over local supplies, and on Indonesia’s Batam island, near Singapore, residents have protested dry taps as data centres spread.

Malaysia has become Southeast Asia’s main data centre hub, thanks to low costs, reliable infrastructure and its closeness to Singapore. Oracle, Amazon, Alibaba and ByteDance are all expanding there. The country has more than 6 GW of planned capacity, the largest pipeline in the region.

More money may follow. In late October, Anwar said SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son plans about $50B of AI investment in Malaysia, though SoftBank has not confirmed the figure.

The deal mirrors one Google made in Europe. In September, it said it would put €13B into Finland over the same two years.

But while I’m gathering the ingredients to make homemade mincemeat, they’ve been checking the skies for snow and whether we’ll have a white Christmas this year.

According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) a white Christmas can be declared when their is at least one inch of snow on the ground on Christmas Day. It doesn’t have to snow on December 25th, as long as a decent covering remains.

Their newly released winter outlook divides the continent into starkly contrasting camps, with the chance of a white Christmas varying by region.

There are only three regions where the Old Farmer’s Almanac predicts a white Christmas for sure. If you live in the Northeast, the High Plains and Alaska, you can expect a decent covering of snow on Christmas Day.

#3215. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

#3214. Pangram’s new models spot AI fakes in images and video, it says

The AI text detection startup adds heatmaps, video uploads and browser alerts, but its accuracy figures are self-reported.

Pangram’s demo: a real photo of a restaurant whose wall mural is AI-generated (left), the Image 1.0 heatmap (centre) and the overlay (right).

Pangram launched Pangram Image 1.0 for AI images and the faster Image Flash 1.0 for video. It claims near-perfect scores on its own tests and 98.7% on the DF26 academic benchmark. Both are in its web app and API, and Image 1.0 is in its Chrome extension.

Pangram, a New York startup known for spotting AI-written text, has launched two models for detecting AI images and video, the company said on Wednesday. Pangram Image 1.0 checks still images, while the smaller, faster Pangram Image Flash 1.0 checks video frame by frame.

The image model can also draw a heatmap showing where AI content sits in a picture, such as a fake object added to a real photo. Pangram says it catches 99.2% of AI images and wrongly flags 0.27% of real ones.

In its own test, Pangram made AI copies of 100 real photos with 12 leading image generators, using prompts that closely matched each original. Image 1.0 scored 99.96% accuracy on that set. The test was designed by Pangram, not by outside reviewers.

For video, Pangram used DF26, an academic benchmark of 2,691 clips of people speaking to camera, published in September. Its authors found that both people and leading detectors did little better than chance at telling real clips from fakes.

Pangram says Flash 1.0 scores 98.7% on DF26, 29 points ahead of the next-best detector.

The new models also work on smaller images, down to 256 by 256 pixels from 512 by 512. Results below 512 pixels carry a lower-confidence warning. Pangram says it trains the models to see through compression, blur and noise, which platforms and people trying to fool detectors can add.

Image 1.0 now runs in Pangram’s Chrome extension, which flags AI content on social media, shopping and rental sites. Users can also upload videos in the web app, and the API now handles both images and video. Platforms are cracking down too: Snapchat has stopped recommending AI videos on Spotlight.

Pangram raised $9M in a round led by Menlo Ventures in July, when it first previewed image detection. Its text detector already runs on Substack.

AI detectors still make mistakes. In August, Pangram’s text tool flagged a Berkeley professor’s op-ed as partly AI-written, which she disputed.

Even Meta’s own image detector missed cropped fakes from its generator more than half the time in Reuters tests. On YouTube, a network that paid real actors to read AI scripts beat its detectors.

#3213. Security Bite: The record $6.3B Binance heist started with a fake Homebrew install on Mac

Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history.

At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.

I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here.

Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook.

The attack basically transpired in two steps.

According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1.

Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions.

Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed.

It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything…

This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run.

Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them.

I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Follow the show so you don’t miss that.

#3212. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

The Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra is coming in early 2027, and while we haven't heard a lot about the phone so far, it looks like the floodgates are starting to open. The latest leaks seem to reveal more details about the phone's design, as well as a possible performance change that could prove very disappointing for those of you hoping to pick up the new S27 Ultra.

We've already seen design leaks that showcase the Galaxy S27 Ultra's new look, swapping the vertical camera array for a horizontal camera bar — which is reminiscent of the "Raised Plateau" Apple debuted on iPhone 17 Pro Max. Now dummy units of that design have appeared online courtesy of Android Headline, letting us visualize that design as a real phone.

Dummy units are, of course, no substitute for the real thing. However they do give us an idea of what using these phones might be like.

Takeaways from the dummy units include changes to the camera, which includes removing the 10MP telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. The telephoto does look quite small, but that's only because the S26 Ultra's telephoto had a deceptive design. So it's unclear what this means for the camera hardware.

The actual dimensions of the phone haven't really changed. The S27 Ultra dummy unit measures 163.76 x 78.25 x 7.97mm (6.44 x 3.0 x 0.31 inches), compared to 163.6 x 78.1 x 7.9mm on the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Which means the size difference is barely distinguishable. So really, the main visual changes come in the form of the camera setup.

Android Headline also notes that the design includes a built-in S Pen, alongside magnets to facilitate full Qi2 wireless charging. I don't see the magnets on the dummy unit or the CAD renders they're based on, so take that particular rumor with a healthy dose of scepticism.

Those of you hoping for a super-powered S27 series may be disappointed, though. While we fully expect that the Ultra model will come with the newly-unveiled Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 (or a custom "for Galaxy" variant), the same may not be true of the S27 Pro.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Notebookcheck recently uncovered listings for all four Galaxy S27 models in the import-export database NBD. It reveals that the S27 Pro may come with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the successor to the current Elite Gen 5 chipset in the S26 series. This chip is still being build on a 2nm process, with all the performance and efficiency benefits that affords, but it's not the absolute best chip Qualcomm will have on offer.

The Extreme Gen 6 chip is supposed to come with better computing, graphics and neural performance, as well as the ability to record videos in 8K resolution at 60 frames per second.

The regular Elite Gen 6 is limited to 30fps, and while the ability to record in 8K isn't going to appeal to everyone, it shows that the Extreme chip is the superior option. Certainly from a performance point of view, and that could be enough to push people away from the Pro model.

That said, a less impressive chip is likely cheaper, and means Samsung could be trying to avoid unnecessary costs that would need to be passed on to the consumer.

The listings also reveal that the international versions of the S27 and S27 Plus could run on the Exynos 2700 chipset, rather than a Snapdragon chip. Though Samsung has been doing that for years, and it's not really that surprising.

The same listings feature screen size too, with the S27, S27 Plus and S27 Ultra offering the same 6.3-, 6.7- and 6.9-inch displays as their predecessors. Meanwhile the Pro is set to offer a 6.5-inch display, and sit between the S27 and its plus-sized counterpart.

The Galaxy S27 series is expected to arrive in January, and we here at Tom's Guide will be watching for all the latest news and rumors to keep you up to date. Stay tuned for more.

#3210. Mayville Engineering (MEC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Data center projects lifted sales, but startup and labor costs squeezed profits.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Mayville Engineering Company, Inc. (MEC -0.31%) reported that third quarter results were driven by project volumes in the data center and critical power end market and improved demand in commercial vehicle segments. Management stated that the company is currently navigating a transitional period characterized by significant investments in new capacity and the absorption of startup costs for recently secured programs. The company indicated that operational performance across its manufacturing footprint varied as teams responded to evolving customer schedules and labor constraints in rural facilities. Leadership noted that capital allocation remains focused on expanding organic capacity, specifically through the recent acquisition of a manufacturing facility in the Southeastern United States.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the 26 Third Quarter Mayville Engineering Company Earnings Call. After today's prepared remarks, we will host a question and answer session. Please press *1 to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press *1 again. I will now hand the conference over to Stefan Neely with Vallum Advisors. Please go ahead.

Stefan Neely: Thank you, operator. On behalf of our entire team, I would like to welcome you to our third quarter 26 results conference call. Leading the call today is MEC's President and CEO, Jagadeesh A. Reddy and Rachele Lehr, Chief Financial Officer. Today's discussion contains forward-looking statements about future business and financial expectations. Actual results may differ significantly from those projected in today's forward-looking statements. Due to various risks and uncertainties, including the risks described in our periodic reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Except as required by law, we undertake no obligation to update our forward-looking statements. Further, this call will include the discussion of certain non GAAP financial measures.

Reconciliation of these measures to the closest GAAP financial measure is included in our quarterly earnings press release, which is available at mecinc.com. Following our prepared remarks, we will open the line for questions. With that, would like to turn the call over to Jagadeesh.

Jagadeesh A. Reddy: Thank you, Stefan Neely, and good morning, everyone. Our third quarter results were in line with our expectations reflecting strong demand and accelerating project volumes within our data center and critical power end market. Net sales increased approximately 18% year-over-year. This was supported by the continued growth in data center and critical power the ongoing recovery in commercial vehicle and sustained demand in construction and access. In data center and critical power, additional programs reached full production during the quarter improving capacity utilization and driving a sequential improvement in adjusted EBITDA margin of approximately 190 basis points.

At the same time, remain in the early stages of ramping the more than $145 million in projects secured in this end market over the past year. The pace and the scale of customer requirements continue to place significant demands on our people, equipment, and organization. On October 1st, we closed on the acquisition of a manufacturing facility in Thompson, Georgia. Executing the capacity strategy we outlined following our second quarter equity offering. I will discuss the facility and our plans with it in more detail shortly. Operational performance across our plants remained uneven during the quarter for 2 distinct reasons.

First, at the facilities supporting data center and critical power, customer program timelines, continue to evolve rapidly, requiring our teams to adjust production schedules, and resources in response. We also incurred approximately $3 million of data center and critical power project launch and outsourcing costs along with premium labor costs supporting other customer programs. Second, facilities more heavily weighted towards agriculture and power sports are operating below efficient utilization levels, as customer volumes in those end markets remain soft. We are actively shifting programs across our footprint to better balance workloads, and align our cost structure. This rebalancing takes time, and the resulting underutilization weighed on margins in the quarter. These costs were in line with our expectations though.

As discussed on our last call, we continue to view them as temporary. Expect them to moderate gradually as demand continues to accelerate and new awards continue to enter the launch cycle. We expect these ramp related costs to decline through early 27 as equipment on order is delivered outsourced production returns in house, and we continue to fill open positions. Importantly, we are absorbing these near term costs deliberately because the programs we are launching today are accretive to our long term margin profile. Finally, the demand we see today reflects a multiyear investment cycle and we believe MEC remains in early stages of that opportunity. Our products are typically in the later stages of a data center build.

This means the programs we are producing today support infrastructure investments that broke ground roughly 3 years ago. Level of investment already committed across the industry combined with our less than 5% penetration among our OEM customers, gives us confidence in the long term demand outlook. While near term sentiment around the data center construction may fluctuate, we remain confident in the durability of this demand and the multiyear growth opportunity ahead of MEC. Moving on to some of our key end markets. Commercial vehicle net sales increased nearly 35% year-over-year, reflecting improved customer demand supported by an increase in North American Class 8 production. ACT continues to project Class 8 production growth of over 8% in 2026.

While its outlook for 2027 has moderated, ACT still expects production to increase approximately 9% in 2027. We remain encouraged by current build rates and the activity we are seeing from our customers. In construction and access, net sales increased approximately 9% year-over-year on continued improvement in nonresidential construction demand. We expect this end market to remain a steady contributor as nonresidential activity continues to improve. In power sports, net sales decreased by approximately 27% year-over-year, driven by continued soft customer demand as OEMs in this end market realigned global supply chains. This trend is consistent with our expectations and is likely to persist into 2027.

Military remains constrained by ongoing program transition delays and agriculture, remains in a cyclical trough with no near term inflection expected. Both are consistent with the outlook we have shared previously. Within data center and critical power, net sales increased approximately 65% reflecting accelerating demand from current customers and new project launches. This end market represented approximately 22% of total net sales in the quarter. During the quarter, we secured approximately $45 million of new data center and critical power project awards, while our qualified opportunity pipeline now exceeds $200 million. With growing demand, we continue to evaluate opportunities for customers to reserve dedicated capacity as well as arrangements where customers fund certain capital investments required to support their programs.

We will continue to manage capacity and production priorities with a focus on sustainable, diversified, and profitable long term growth. These awards secured during the quarter reflect a combination of new customer wins, and continued expansion with existing major customers. These programs span a range of power gen enclosures, switchgear, switchboard enclosures, and uninterrupted power supplies. We continue to expand our share with key commercial vehicle customers as they prepare for upcoming product launches tied to the 2027 EPA regulatory changes. These programs are expected to begin entering production in late 26 and continue ramping into 2027.

Beyond commercial vehicle, we secured new business tied to model introductions with an our sports customer while also expanding our business with an agricultural customer. Turning to capital allocation, our focus remains on 3 priorities. Investing in organic growth, continuing to reduce leverage, and pursuing selective accretive acquisitions. First, organic growth. Based on our awarded programs and pipeline, we currently expect to reach full capacity within the next 18 months. We are deploying capital now to expand our footprint ahead of that point. On October 1st, we closed on the acquisition of our Thompson, Georgia facility.

Located in the Southeastern United States closer to key data center and critical power customers, this facility establishes a platform for growth in a region where our capacity has been constrained. Together with planned equipment investment, we expect this facility to add approximately $50 million of annual revenue capacity by 2028. This will extend our total revenue capacity beyond the approximately $850 million we previously disclosed. Rachele will cover the associated capital spending, and the return criteria we apply to these investments. Second, deleveraging. We ended the quarter with a net leverage of 2.9x and our long term target remains 2.5x.

As volumes ramp, and profitability improves, we expect earnings growth and cash generation to drive continued progress toward that target. Third, accretive M&A We will remain opportunistic in pursuing acquisitions that strengthen our competitive position expand capacity, and support long term value creation. Looking ahead, we are confident in the opportunity in front of us and in our ability to deliver profitable growth in 2027 and beyond. Before I turn the call over to Rachele Lehr, I want to address the trajectory of our margins as we navigate this period of transition for MEC. In the past, we have pointed to an approximately 15% adjusted EBITDA margin as the target for our business.

We continue to see a clear path to that level and potentially beyond. That path rests on 4 drivers each of which are already in motion. First, the moderation of ramp related costs as equipment on order is delivered. And placed into service and outsourced work returns in house. Second, improved absorption and operating leverage as our data center and critical power programs continue to ramp toward full production. Given the scale of demand in front of us, we are intentionally adding people, equipment, and capacity ahead of our current levels. As volumes catch up to that resource base, we expect operating leverage to significantly improve. Third, the continued build out of our workforce.

Labor availability remains tight in certain facilities. As hiring catches up, we expect to reduce our reliance on premium labor and overtime. Lastly, the normalization of demand in our agriculture and power sports end markets. Lower customer volumes in these markets are pressuring margins through underutilization as I noted earlier. Footprint rebalancing already underway should help offset that and a recovery in those volumes would provide additional margin support. These 4 drivers combined with the continued mix shift toward higher value data center and critical power programs as this end market moves towards 25% of total revenue gives us confidence in that trajectory.

We expect to make measurable margin improvement over the next 12 to 18 months and I want to be clear about the shape of that progress. These drivers work on different timelines. Ramp related cost, should moderate first beginning in early 27. Hiring absorption improve as programs reach a run rate over the course of the year. And the timing of recovery in agriculture and power sports will be determined by demand in those end markets. As a result, we expect 2027 to be a year of continued growth with margins improving sequentially rather than in a single step. The benefit of this work will be most visible as we exit the year and move into 2028.

We will provide our formal outlook for 2027 on our fourth quarter call. We believe these actions position MEC to deliver attractive sustainable returns on invested capital as we capitalize on a multiyear secular growth opportunity. With that, would like to turn the call over to Rachele.

Rachele Lehr: Thank you, Jagadeesh A. Reddy, and good morning, everyone. Total sales for the third quarter increased 18.1% on a year-over-year basis to $170.4 million Manufacturing margin was $18.8 million or 11% of net sales, compared to $15.9 million or 11% of net sales in the prior year period. The year over year increase in manufacturing margin dollars was primarily attributable to improved capacity utilization driven by higher sales volumes in data center and critical power as well as growth within commercial vehicle and construction and access end markets. This increase was partially offset by $3 million of data center and critical power launch and outsourcing costs and premium labor.

Other selling, general, and administrative expenses were $8.8 million compared to $10.5 million in the prior year period. The decrease primarily reflects a decrease in nonrecurring acquisition related expenses and the realization of synergies associated with the AccuFab acquisition. Interest expense was $3 million compared to $3.4 million in the prior year period, due to decreased average borrowings under our revolving credit facility partially offset by higher interest rates in the current period. Adjusted EBITDA was $17 million or 10% of net sales, compared to $14.1 million or 9.8% of net sales in the prior year period.

The increase was primarily due to higher sales volume and improved capacity utilization, partially offset by data center and critical power project launch and outsourcing costs and premium labor. On a sequential basis, adjusted EBITDA margin improved by approximately 190 basis points. Turning now to our cash flow and the balance sheet. Free cash flow during the third quarter was a use of $3.3 million as compared to a use of $1.1 million in the prior year period. The decrease was primarily driven by higher capital expenditures related to equipment needed to support rapidly accelerating demand in the data center and critical power end market, partially offset by higher cash flow from operations.

As of September 30, our net debt was $146.6 million The ratio of net debt to trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA calculated per our current credit agreement, was 2.9x. Now turning to a review of our updated outlook for the full year of 2026. For the full year of 2026, we currently expect net sales of between $630 million and $640 million adjusted EBITDA of between $48 million and $50 million and free cash flow use of between $6 million and $16 million This outlook assumes a full year of AccuFab ownership, incremental cross selling revenue, and continued recovery in commercial vehicle and construction and access. Partially offset by ongoing softness in our agriculture and powersports end markets.

Our guidance also incorporates the impact of continued launch and outsourcing costs associated with data center and critical power programs along with premium labor. Our updated outlook reflects 2 factors. First, as Jagadeesh noted, customer program timelines in data center and critical power continue to evolve, and the timing of certain project volumes has shifted into early 27. Second, mix within our legacy end markets is weighing on margins. Strong growth in commercial vehicle is occurring alongside continued softness in agriculture and power sports. Where lower volumes are leaving portions of our footprint underutilized. As a result, we expect fourth quarter adjusted EBITDA margin to be modestly below the third quarter level.

We view this as a transitional quarter and it does not change the path Jagadeesh outlined. With ramp related costs beginning to moderate in early 27 and margins improving sequentially from there. Free cash flow guidance reflects working capital investment and planned capital expenditures of $25 million to $35 million including the initial investment in the Thompson, Georgia facility. As Jagadeesh mentioned, on October 1, we completed the acquisition of our Thompson, Georgia facility. Inclusive of the purchase price, facility improvements, and production equipment, we currently expect to invest a total of $25 million in the location through 2028.

Of that amount, we currently anticipate approximately $10 million of capital expenditures in 2027 with the remaining to be invested in 2028. When fully deployed, the investment is expected to approximately $50 million of annual revenue capacity. The timing of the spending will be aligned with equipment lead times customer demand, and the ramp of awarded programs. We will continue to evaluate each phase of the investment against our established return criteria including an internal rate of return of at least 15%. This phased approach allows us to add capacity as demand develops while maintaining discipline around capital deployment and cash flow. In summary, our third quarter reflected the dynamics Jagadeesh A. Reddy described.

Strong volume growth and improving utilization in data center and critical power partially offset by launch costs, and softness in a couple of our legacy end markets. Looking ahead, our focus remains on converting higher volumes into improved profitability and cash flow. While we are not providing 2027 guidance today, we expect that improvement to build gradually over the course of the year. Ramp related costs should moderate first, with the full benefit of improved fixed cost absorption, operating leverage, and footprint rebalancing becoming more reflected in our results by late 27 or early 28. Users can turn a prompt or photo into a GIF, then change its speed and edit single frames.

The ChatGPT app open on an iPhone, its dark start screen showing the OpenAI logo.

OpenAI is adding animated GIFs to ChatGPT with a new image model, Images 2.6. Users can make a GIF from text or a photo and edit its frames. Developers get two new API models, and OpenAI says people now make over 4 billion images a week.

OpenAI is rolling out animated GIFs in ChatGPT alongside a new image model, Images 2.6, The Verge reported on Wednesday. Users can turn a written prompt or an uploaded photo into a GIF.

Once a GIF is made, users can change how fast it plays, look at and edit single frames, and share it. Until now, ChatGPT could not make a GIF in one step. The feature arrives months after OpenAI shut down Sora, its AI video app, in March.

OpenAI says Images 2.6 also makes image generation in ChatGPT faster. It is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users on the web, desktop and mobile.

Developers get two new API models: GPT-Image-2.6 Flare for speed and GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst for quality. They follow the split OpenAI introduced with Images 2.5 in September, when Adobe put one of its models into Firefly.

Use keeps growing. OpenAI says people now make more than 4 billion images a week across ChatGPT and its API, up from 3 billion in September. The figures are OpenAI’s own and cover all image use, not only GIFs.

OpenAI has updated its image tools often this year. Images 2.0, launched in April, was its first image model that reasons before drawing. Last month, OpenAI began testing ads inside image generation in the US.

Similar to what’s available on iPhone Duo, the animated artwork for what’s playing now bleeds further into the lyrics view. It’s a great look that’s now coming to all iPhone models.

#3207. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.
