Moving to slide 11, you can see that we generated operating cash flow of $256 million in the third quarter, and after CapEx, free cash flow was $221 million, up significantly from the prior year. From a capital allocation standpoint, we returned $89 million of cash to shareholders through share buybacks and dividends in the third quarter. Note that we have approximately 9 million shares remaining on our repurchase authorization. Looking at the balance sheet, we ended the third quarter with net debt to adjusted EBITDA at 1.7x, which is an improvement from last quarter, driven by higher EBITDA and debt paydown. Now let's turn to the current outlook for full year 2026 with a summary on slide 13.

Starting with the bottom line, we are increasing our adjusted earnings per share outlook to the range of $6.35-$6.50, which represents 20% growth at the midpoint versus 2025. With respect to net sales, we expect total revenue to increase approximately 5.5%, unchanged versus the midpoint of the prior range. Organically, we are reaffirming our outlook for revenue to be up 3.5% at the midpoint. Currency translation is estimated to contribute around 1.25% to sales for the year, up slightly from the prior guide. M&A is expected to add 0.75% to full-year revenue on a net basis. The Bijur Delimon acquisition continues to perform well, while the updated outlook now reflects the impact of the belts divestiture on the fourth quarter.

The current earnings outlook implies that our 2026 consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin will be in the mid-18% range at the midpoint, slightly higher than the prior guidance, to primarily reflect the third-quarter performance. Moving to free cash flow, we expect to generate $375 million-$400 million in 2026, unchanged from the prior outlook. On slide 14, we provide an updated view on our 2026 organic sales outlook by end market sector, which includes the impact of both volumes and pricing. Again, we are reaffirming the full-year organic sales growth rate of 3.5%. You can see that we upgraded our outlook for the automation and industrial solutions sector, while we reduced our outlook for the power and electrification sector.

Note that our outlook assumes that sales in the China wind market decline again in the fourth quarter, both sequentially and year-over-year. Keep in mind that our China wind business is expected to be only a low single-digit percentage of total company sales in 2026, with the run rate in the second half of this year now below prior trough levels. As a result, we would not expect this business to have a significant impact on the full-year 2027 outlook, and supports the step-up in the organic sales outlook for next year that Lucian highlighted earlier. Moving to slide 15, here we provide a bridge of the increase in our 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook at the midpoint.

Most of the increase is driven primarily by our outperformance in the third quarter, including the impact of the tariff refunds. You can also see that we are adding $0.08 per share to reflect a lower net interest expense outlook for the year compared to our last guide. In summary, Timken delivered solid results in the third quarter, including double-digit earnings growth and strong cash flow. We have a strong balance sheet, significant capital deployment optionality, and are well-positioned to achieve strong earnings growth again in 2027. Let me turn it back over to Lucian for some final remarks before we open the line for questions. Lucian?

Lucian Boldea: Thanks, Mike. Let me reiterate that we are focused on delivering a strong finish to the year while making continued progress on our Elevate to Outperform strategy, which is a multi-year transformation. In 2026, we have taken significant actions to transform the core of our business, to reduce complexity and exit non-strategic underperforming businesses, refocus our resources on strategic verticals, and integrate our Timken operating system. As a leadership team, we take our commitments very seriously and will continue to work relentlessly to deliver what we committed to. Our plans are on track, and we remain confident that our strategy will accelerate growth, structurally increase margin, and drive significant shareholder value over the coming years.

Mike Discenza: Thanks, Lucian. This concludes our formal remarks. We will now open up the line for questions. Operator?

Operator: Gentlemen, thank you. To our phone audience joining today, at this time, we will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, you may press star and then the digit one on your telephone. If you are using a speakerphone today, please pick up your handset prior to pressing the keys. If you would like to withdraw your question, repeat the steps. Star one will also remove you from the queue. We will take just a moment to pause momentarily while we assemble our roster. First, from the line of Bryan Blair with Oppenheimer.

Bryan Blair: Thank you. Good morning, guys.

Bryan Blair: We know your Q4 organic sales outlook is unchanged, similar growth to Q3. Maybe offer a little more color on how orders trended through October and how we should think about core growth by segment in the fourth quarter. I assume that China wind is a little bit less of a, quote-unquote, "bad guy" on the Engineered Bearings side, and the comp is obviously a bit healthier for Industrial Motion.

Lucian Boldea: Thank you, Bryan. I think when you look at you have to look at the context of Q3 and Q4 in everything that we're doing to transform the company. You're a little bit looking at not going across the water and not everything that's happening beneath the surface. We're definitely focusing our resources where we said, and you look at the early wins, we alluded to that in our prepared remarks, where our pipeline sat year-over-year. Our pipeline is up in Q3, mid-single digit. What's more exciting is the percent increases that happen in that pipeline in our focus verticals. Whether you're talking about automation and robotics, or we're talking about aerospace and defense, where there are significant double-digit increases.

Those happen in Q3 in the pipeline. Obviously, they will continue to happen. We expect for them to continue to happen in Q4 as well. The demand picture externally, we don't see that being dramatically different going from Q3 to Q4. The undercurrent from all this is also, obviously, we have an automotive OE unwind that is already having a little bit of volume impact that we're offsetting with growth. There's a lot of churn in here that we're doing to really deliver on a number and on a commitment that we have made.

I'm proud of the team that we have done that, and we're trying to give that same kind of appropriate guidance for Q4 on what we believe we're going to do. The pipeline order book that we're looking at, all the indicators say that we're headed in the right direction. It is going as planned. There are no big surprises. Assuming the market just holds the way it is and continues to stay where it is, then we feel very good about our ability to deliver similar performance in Q4. We've already given a little bit of a view into 2027 without really giving a guide, but that's where we are.

Bryan Blair: I appreciate the color. You did offer a segue to the preliminary 2027 outlook there, so have to dive in a bit. Is it fair to assume that, consistent with the medium-term framework you've put out there and performance through 2026, that you're contemplating high single-digit Industrial Motion growth next year, more low single on the bearings side? If we look across your major end markets, I think you alluded to some of these dynamics in your prior answer, but how would you rank order growth expectations given current visibility?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah, absolutely. I think if you look, I think what you said is appropriate. Obviously, now we focus on finishing 2026 strong, but the destiny for Q1 is pretty much set during Q4, so we definitely are focusing on both. I think it's a little early to comment on 2027 with a lot of certainty, but expecting organic sales to increase by mid-single digits is still the case. Our strategic initiatives are starting to drive incremental growth, and those will, of course, only accelerate as we move forward. The markets that you were asking about, absolutely, automation and robotics is very much the leader in driving that growth, but right behind it is A&D.

In both of these, we're seeing increases in our pipeline of double digit year-over-year, and it's not a low double digit number. It's a very healthy double digit number. That gives us a lot of confidence that we will be able to start benefiting more and more from pivoting that portfolio. Obviously, there's still pricing. I'm sure there'll be other questions on pricing later, but to tease that a little bit early on, our price minus cost in Q3 was positive on a year-over-year basis. It was positive sequentially. We expect the same in Q4, both year-over-year as well as sequentially from Q3. So, that says that our discipline around pricing is there.

Our track record is now there, so we feel good about that being additive to our organic, to our volume growth going into 2027. There's 80/20, obviously, that's going to start being a beneficiary not only to the bottom line, but to the top line as we focus on customers. So, that will help as well. On the margin side, belts, you're going to start seeing that already in Q4, and really we feel good about seeing a significant impact to that in 2027. We've committed to more than 200 basis points of Industrial Motion margins, so that's a third of the company. So, take a third of that number, 60 to 70 basis points from the belts.

So, again, all those actions that we have taken without really providing a formal outlook make us confident in our ability to achieve stronger performance in 2027 as we continue to build upon what we're executing today.

Bryan Blair: Understood. Thank you again.

Operator: Our next question will come from the line of David Raso at Evercore.

David Raso: Hi, thank you for the time. I was curious, you spoke of auto OE exits as part of the fourth quarter comments, but when you speak of organic sales next year, mid-single digit growth, is that including with some of the auto exits or excluding? Just to level set, and I have a follow-up.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah, what we've committed to is a net number. Absolutely. Yes.

David Raso: Okay, so the mid-single digit is even with, and I'll put a number around it, $100 million of revenue backed away from an auto. Even with exiting that, you still look at mid-single digit. It includes the exiting, just to be clear.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah, I'll remind you that the exit is, the majority of the revenue exit is not in 2027. That happens in 2028. But there is a number in 2027 as well. It's smaller than what you mentioned. It's a part of the total, but the majority is in 2028. But yes, the number is a net number, is the answer.

David Raso: Okay, helpful. Because I'm just trying to understand. I thought the China wind business, the comp gets easier in the fourth quarter to the extent where EB this quarter would have been like 3.8% organic without the China wind drag. That's why I'm just curious if that's sort of the bogey and the wind year-over-year. If I remember correctly, it's not much of a decline. If you kept it, like China wind, I guess sequentially, are we now kind of flat-lining a little bit sequentially? Because if that's the case, I think the comp becomes almost nil.

David Raso: Why would EB go from 3.8% ex-wind to still sub three in the fourth quarter? I'm just trying to get the confidence on EB showing any growth into 2027, and why is that a credible view?

Lucian Boldea: Right. No, that's very fair. Again, we can go into more detail on China wind, but what I would tell you is at a high level, there is another step down sequentially going from Q3 to Q4. But when you look at it at that point, it really becomes low single digit percentage of the total, so it's no longer that significant. Having said that, if you'll recall first half of 2026, we had pretty strong performance. It was also in the back half of 2025, so there was about a 12-month period that was pretty strong.

China wind tends to be a little more cyclical, a little more lumpy, and there's nothing that says that overall demand is going away or that we're not competitive or any of that. What the reality of that market is, it does tend to be a little more cyclical, and so we're now in the down cycle. But yeah, it's a little bit down. Q4 versus Q3 is another step down sequentially.

David Raso: And one last thing, sorry if I missed it. The mix issue that hurt the. When I do price cost, I also include the mix in it, and that mix was the real drag when we look at price cost. I am excluding IEEPA. The mix was very different in this quarter. It was a negative two, and last quarter, I think it was a positive $13 million. Did I miss it? What was the big mix change?

Mike Discenza: No, you are right, David. You did not miss it. It was primarily in the Industrial Motion segment where we had the larger mix impact, and it really is just the shift in where the growth was. So, we grew still in some of the higher margin businesses, but grew at a slower rate in the higher margin businesses and a little bit faster in some of the lower margin businesses. So, it really was just a mix. And think, the highest margin businesses, lubrication, linear motion, et cetera, are Philadelphia Gear business, and then lower margin businesses like chain and some of the more OE-focused markets.

So, it really was just a shift between the markets and the growth rates between the quarters.

David Raso: Thank you. I appreciate the time. Oh, sorry, again, Lucian.

Lucian Boldea: Thank you. No, and I was also going to add regionally, I think if you look at where our slow growth was, Industrial Motion has a very heavy European footprint, Europe being down in Q3, and really almost all of that happened in the month of August. That also weighed down that mix from a regional standpoint.

Operator: Our next question will come from Angel Castillo at Morgan Stanley.

Oliver: Hey, good morning, guys. This is Oliver on for Angel today. Maybe just

Oliver: when we look across. Good morning. When we look across kind of organic growth across your peers, I mean, do you feel like you have a mandate to go and take more price? Or maybe are we making some sort of strategic choice here in terms of price cost? I mean, just hoping you could help us understand kind of confidence in re-acceleration going forward.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Look, really appreciate the question. As I said, we're in the midst of a pretty significant transformation on how we're thinking about our business, how we're. On one hand, yes, you think of the three pillars of the strategy and how we're trying to focus on the right verticals. We're doing 80/20 to focus on our 80s customers to get more share of wallet, to be a little bit less cyclical than we are today, and to really be more resilient and more efficient in our growth. We've also started now to do is we set up a Chief Operating Officer organization, and we're frankly looking at our assets differently.

We are taking that sweat the assets mindset, which means leveraging that fixed cost. It's a two-step process. We look in the mirror, we look at our cost structure, we build a competitive cost structure, and then with confidence, we go out and compete, and we use the capacity that we have. When the capacity is not competitive, then we take action and we reduce that capacity. But it's our job to maintain the capacity that's competitive, then once we have it, we use it.

Aligning those P&Ls with the factories and really having that sweat the asset focus is going to get additional opportunity to do some of the things that you are talking about, especially on the Engineered Bearings side, where you're more fixed cost intensive, and so that fixed cost leverage does create a lot of value.

Oliver: Understood. Maybe just to follow up on that, I mean, One Timken, it's helped you drive some early wins here. You're able to combine some different capabilities. I mean, the question is the sum greater than the parts here? Is there some margin uplift or maybe some revenue uplift that's maybe we're not fully appreciating?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Look, the sum is much greater than the parts, and the sum is greater than the parts both in how we operate, but also how we present ourselves to the market. One Timken sometimes is a big word, and people take it to the extreme that it means every product line to every customer. Clearly, it doesn't. But if you look at data in any pick-the-random company, what you will find is if you take one customer that does business with three or more business units inside a company, that customer is more loyal, that customer is more sticky, you have more ability to collaborate with that customer in innovation.

It's just everything gets better with a multi-business line customer. And that doesn't happen if you leave it kind of to one business at a time, everybody for themselves. If you present yourself to that customer as one company, then you can combine the appropriate value, the appropriate offerings, so that the sum of the parts is greater. It also allows you to bring more of a solution in. We used the example in the prepared remarks where we were talking to somebody in the space industry, and they were an existing customer using one of our legacy solutions in their gen one product.

They were moving to a next-gen product where the precision of what they required was far greater. The good news is, as we looked at our Cone Drive technology that they were using originally, we were able to shift them over to cycloidal gearbox through Spinea. That's a little higher cost technology, but much higher precision, which met their need. So that generated a higher value opportunity for us with the same customer. In addition to that, we were able to then convince them to sell them the subsystem instead of just the gearbox, which generated really 2.5, almost three times more revenue than the opportunity would have otherwise.

So we took something that was business at risk and turned it into a much bigger opportunity than it was before, but much more importantly, built credibility with that customer that we actually can provide a solution instead of what we would have done in the past, maybe try to negotiate the price on a technology that really didn't meet their need going forward. It's just an example. When you step to the back of the store operationally, there is even more opportunity there. You go from very simple things like, why would you not buy airline tickets, hotel rooms, and rental cars, and all that one single way? Why would you buy steel two different ways? You wouldn't.

Or how would you manage real estate? You'd manage it all together. That's all kind of table stakes, obvious. Some of that we've already been doing. We're going to do more of it more deliberately. But then how do you take 100 plus operating locations and establish playbooks by archetype? They're not all the same, but they're not all different. Are there four or five different archetypes that you can then establish unique KPIs for those, an automation strategy, and operating those, and then finally sweating those assets? So, the sum of the parts is definitely greater here as we move forward. I'm convinced of that. I'm convinced of that both operationally, but especially in front of the customers.

As we engage with these 80s customers and with our key account plans, we've done a few by now, and wherever we go, we see value. We have to see one yet where we walk home and say, "Well, that was not a good idea." It's working. The early indications are there. Obviously, this takes time. You don't show up the first day and land a bunch of revenue that afternoon. But we do see early wins, we see pipeline, we see orders, we see all the indications that we need to see that give us a lot of confidence that we're headed on the right track.

Operator: Our next question comes from Rob Wertheimer at Melius Research.

Rob Wertheimer: Hi, thanks and good morning.

Rob Wertheimer: I had one kind of in a similar vein, morning, to what David asked. As you've worked through 80/20 and opportunities and things you might cut, is there any other drag in 2027 from fading smaller products that had low volume, et cetera? Then I had a follow-up if I can. Thank you.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Thank you for the question. The short answer is no drag from 80/20 in 2027. We think the drag is behind us, for it was more of an investment. We're now at a point where we're at least paying for that investment through the early actions. I gave some examples in the prepared remarks, and the benefits are starting to flow in as you enter into 2027, where 80/20 is a net benefit. I say that from a cost side, from the cost of implementing 80/20, the cost of training, the cost of all that's a net benefit.

The bigger benefit, obviously, it's called 80/20 and not 20/80 because the benefit doesn't come from the 20s, the benefit comes from the 80s. The benefit comes from growth. That's what's most exciting to me about 80/20, is this engagement with our key customers, key account plans, bringing more than one Timken business to bear to solving a customer problem. That's what will change our trajectory. Frankly, that's what's already helping our Industrial Motion. Our Industrial Motion business now has several quarters in a row where we're growing very nicely in the mid to high single digits. That's expected not only to continue, but to start accelerating that number.

Rob Wertheimer: Perfect. Thank you. Maybe it's small, I don't know, but the electroadhesive acquisition is not one I expected. I wonder if you could expand for a second on how that fits into current either technology or end market. Then does that significantly kind of signal an expansion of your acquisition play field or TAM? I'll stop there. Thank you.

Lucian Boldea: Right. No, look, it's a great question. I have to confess, when it was introduced to me a while back with that name, electroadhesive, I said the same thing. What is mechanical engineering or tribology or precision machining in there? Let me give it a layman's explanation at least that I think of on this technology. Basically think of an e-brake that holds position without consuming electricity. On a humanoid, if it has to pick something up and then it has to hold that position very firmly without really consuming battery life, that's what this technology does. The application, really, humanoid is a great application, but you can think of this as also in other industrial applications.

It's not a brake in the sense of a car, so it doesn't slow something down. It holds position locked. It's either on or off, but it does it in a very energy efficient way. Where battery life is very important, we think this technology is a big enabler, again, in conjunction with actuators, in conjunction with some of the other offerings, because then we'll do the go and we'll do the stop at the same time with equal precision and in an energy efficient manner. That's the idea of the technology. It's part of the overall solution being more of a systems provider.

Operator: Our next question will come from Kyle Menges at Citigroup. Please go ahead.

Kyle Menges: Thanks. Maybe a follow-up on Rob's last question. Lucian, I think you made comments about starting to build up an M&A pipeline, and would just love to hear just anything you can share on maybe how that M&A pipeline is building, areas of focus, and are we still thinking about bolt-ons or could there be potential for anything larger?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Let me start with the last question because that is the easiest one. Yes, still bolt-ons, not something larger. How we think about our M&A pipeline is really way more strategically aligned with the verticals. One of the things that we try to do at Investor Day is to really lay out very, very clearly our roadmap, how we are trying to grow, where we are trying to grow, how we are trying to win. So also the both the where to play and how to win. We articulated the key verticals, and what that means is really we expect our M&A pipeline to really be aligned with those key verticals.

What I will tell you is there would be probably two types of M&A. One, you can think a little bit in terms of the Bijur Delimon being an example. How do I further the technology platforms that I have, continues to solidify my leadership? How do I add more complementary offerings in these key markets that really work with the solutions that we already provide? Then there is a smaller subset which is similar to this investment in this technology, which is R&D make versus buy.

We might do an acquisition that maybe does not have a lot of revenue, but you acquire a technical capability that then you can leverage in the portfolio to bring your current solutions or pull others through the market, but would have to be pretty well aligned with our focus markets and with where we are trying to go. The other part that we are developing and have now developed this playbook of regionally translating our existing acquisitions, that we have 22 of those that we have made in the last 10 years, depending on how exactly, how granular you get with the count, and most of those are regional in Industrial Motion.

So, how we translate those from one region to another will become a playbook for a future M&A as well, where we will be in a great position to buy a single region play that then we can very quickly copy, paste, translate into other regions. That is another avenue to create value with M&A that we now have in place.

Kyle Menges: Got it. That is helpful, Lucian. It seems like since the Investor Day, you continue to talk about 80/20 initiatives and maybe some organizational changes as well, that at least some of which feel somewhat incremental. Would love to just hear what you feel like you have been doing on 80/20 and any other restructuring initiatives that you would say are probably incremental from what you laid out at the Investor Day.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Look, I think if you polled 19,000 people today, I would bet you won't find many that say it's incremental. We've made a lot of changes in the company. If you think how we were operating a year ago, we had an Engineered Bearings segment that was running like a vertical P&L, and then Industrial Motion running separately. We've turned that basically 90 degrees on its side. We have a single Chief Operating Officer that runs a single customer-facing organization that's regional first, but inside those regions, it's verticalized. It's not territories, it's not product lines, it's verticals, it's industries.

The entire sales force went from, you had an EB sales force, and then you had a dozen IM sales forces. Now you have a Timken sales force. If you go to Europe, you have a Timken sales force that might be focused on automation, you might have one that's focused on aerospace and defense, and they're specialized in that area. That transformation on the customer-facing side is dramatic. We have a technology organization under a Chief Technology Officer that now includes the entire company. It's not independent organizations inside the P&L, so that's pulled together. On the operations side, we have a single COO that includes bearings, includes Industrial Motion.

Inside the P&Ls, we used to have the P&Ls aligned by market. They're now aligned with the factories. We would have a rail P&L in bearings and aerospace one. Now, they'll share the factory. By the way, that's no longer the case. I have a small bore and a large bore P&L ownership in bearings that basically is aligned with a network of factories that then can be leveraged so they can sweat the assets. There's been very significant changes under the surface to really operationalize this. The more significant change, and Steve Ribaudo is driving even more of that, as he joined our COO, is that's the hardware, the org structure.

The software obviously is the operating model, that discipline, that cadence. We now have a cadence every month. We call it business decision week. That's where it's a prescribed agenda. It happens the same day every month. It's the same system. It's the same reporting, just new numbers every month. We refer to what did we do, what did we say we were going to do, did we get it done, what are we doing to mitigate? All that is very transparent, very prescribed.

There's a substantial amount of operationalizing the strategy that's happened, some before Investor Day, but most of it after Investor Day, and it's now really taking shape on the back of the store with Steve Ribaudo joining in September as COO.

Kyle Menges: Great. That is helpful. I guess this was all kind of within that plan that you shared at the Investor Day?

Lucian Boldea: Yes. It is within the plan, but some of it, that Investor Day was a plan. It is now past tense actions.

Kyle Menges: Got it. That is helpful. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question will come from Steve Barger at KeyBanc.

Steve Barger: Hey, thanks. Really nice to see the positive backlog trend. How much of the mid-single-digit backlog growth is OEM versus aftermarket and distribution, and where are you seeing the most acceleration in OEM schedules?

Mike Discenza: Yeah. Hey, Steve, Mike here. Thanks for the question. I will come at that question a slightly different way, because we don't really classify the backlog by channel. What I would say is that our channel partners, we feel confident that the inventory levels are at a good place. So, the backlog is commensurate with kind of the sell-through rate, if you will. So, in order intake, strong there, commensurate with strong sales growth. on the OE side, Lucian Boldea referred to where we are seeing the strength, but maybe to get one level more specific, we saw strong order book growth in our infrastructure market, which would include things like heavy industries, off-highway, et cetera.

Of course, aerospace has been growing strong and continued to grow strong, and that's in both segments, both Industrial Motion and Engineered Bearings, see continued backlog growth there. General industrial, which again cuts across a lot of the lighter, say, industrial markets. The one place where we obviously are struggling from an order book standpoint was wind energy, which was down substantially, and we already said would be down again in the fourth quarter. So, hopefully that helps give a little color.

Steve Barger: Yeah, I appreciate that. Lucian, you said that early minimum order and customer segmentation actions are improving profitability without affecting revenue. Are the benefits that you're seeing so far from a better price versus cost to serve, or are you already driving incremental growth and share of wallet with the high-priority customers?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Both are already happening. I think that we have a few examples now with larger customers where really probably September was the first month where I could really hang my hat on a significant number that made a difference to say, "Okay, yes, this is starting to pay off." I can identify discrete opportunities at these large customers that were directly related to opportunities we got through a different level of engagement. I think that started really in earnest in September, and then as we expand that effort, I'm optimistic, obviously, that's going to grow not only with the customers we've already engaged, but also as we expand the customers.

The minimum order value that came from, when you do 80/20, you do a zero-up, and you kind of look in the mirror and say, "Okay, what does it actually cost me to process an order?" It's not a small number. Then you realize that maybe you were processing orders that were below the revenue that it costs you to process the order, and why on earth would you do that? Also recognizing that, by the way, the customer that places the order, it's not free for them either to place that order, and it just doesn't make any sense. We have a minimum order value now that's going to allow us to be more efficient.

We will, for the time being, what that does in the immediate term is it frees up the resources to serve those 80s customers better, because obviously when we engage with those 80 customers and we say, "We need more from you," that means we will do more for them. We will give them better service, we will give them better lead times, we will give them better visibility, and as a result, they will give us more of their share of wallet, but that requires people as well. That's that redeployment of fewer orders to process because there's fewer smaller ones, more time for the big customers.

But as we continue to do this, there will be some productivity opportunities. Obviously, there will be a net benefit from a margin standpoint.

Mike Discenza: Yeah, and maybe Steve, just a reminder of what we have said all along, which was 80/20, the first half was a drag on the company. The second half, which we are squarely in right now, those benefits are really offsetting some of those costs. Then we will expect to see that drop-through on the margin really as we get into 2027. We spent the last almost a year now, we have been doing this for a little less than a year, doing a lot of learnings, and Lucian Boldea has referenced several of the tools that we have put in place. There are many tools. Each business, as we have segmented, has different needs.

So, a lot of activity going on there, deploying the tools, then looking for that to start delivering results next year, both top and bottom line in a meaningful way.

Operator: Next, we will hear from the line of Tim Thein, or Thein rather, at Raymond James. I hope I said your name correctly, sir. Please go ahead.

Tim Thein: Yeah, that was a good effort. Yeah, just on a question is on kind of the visibility you have for 2027. Some of your longer cycle business or longer cycle, larger backlog-based businesses that you called out earlier is driving a lot of the kind of the order momentum. So, A&D and as well as automation and robotics. I mean, it is nearly 40% of revenue. So, just as you kind of exit the year, I am just curious if you could speak to where you expect to exit the year.

It's the undercurrent of we're exiting a market, we're doing divestitures, we're doing growth at the same time. What we said we're doing, what we said we're working on is working. It's working very well.

The early indicators are very positive that we're headed on the right track, and that's why we're sitting here earlier than normal, reaffirming our views on 2027 without doing a firm guide, but getting as close as we can to that.

Mike Discenza: The other thing just in our control and that we've communicated is pricing. We said we included 100 basis points of pricing in our long-term targets and expect to be able to deliver on that promise as well. We have that in our control to help with that growth.

#3190. Android 17 adoption hits a staggering 1% – why you really should update now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Only a quarter of Android phones have even made it to Android 16.

Android 17 adoption hasn’t been speedy. According to the most recent data from heise.de via Android Studio, as reported by Android Authority, Android 17 has reached just 1% of active devices since its release in June 2026.

While Android 16 is finally the most used Google OS for Android devices, at 25.4% of active Android devices, these distribution figures indicate that getting users to upgrade to even newer software is an uphill battle.

It’s true that Android 17 has had less time to reach devices than Android 16 did when the previous distribution snapshot was published, but the minuscule adoption rate underscores how slowly the latest release is infiltrating the Android ecosystem.

Also: How Android 17 stops network snoops and SMS blasters now

Plus, the data show that more Android users than not are running versions that are many years old. I’m all for not fixing what’s not broken, but when Android 14 is the second most widely used version (15.% of devices are still running it), while Android 15 trails not far behind at 14.7%, there’s a pretty large chunk of individuals who may be putting themselves (and their data) at risk.

And it doesn’t end there. Android 13 and Android 11 are still on the table for 11.8% and 10.1% of users, with almost another 10% still using Android 12. That’s about another 30% of users still running Android 13 or older.

Though the numbers indicate that almost 60% of active Android devices are running Android 14 or newer, about 40% of users haven’t even upgraded to Android 14 or later.

Also: This Android 17 setting logs suspicious activity on your phone for troubleshooting

While the numbers are staggering, they’re not surprising. Android updates typically lag behind iOS updates. While the iPhone and its software are both designed, controlled, and distributed by Apple, Android updates must roll out from a single starting point to a wider array of mobile devices and systems to reach users. While Google is responsible for the core of the Android system, those updates must then be curated, reviewed, and pushed to every device that uses Android. This includes phones from Google, Samsung, Nothing, and more, which usually requires adaptations from each manufacturer. Apple’s updates are often adopted faster because there’s no middle entity between iOS and the user, while Android’s process is rather fragmented.

Keep in mind that Google no longer publishes a regularly updated public distribution chart, so this data isn’t from a real-time survey of every Android device. There’s only cumulative adoption data through Android Studio, and these estimates are derived from those figures and cover devices that contacted the Google Play Store during a seven-day period.

It’s always good practice to keep your device updated to the latest available software that your system allows. There are a few great reasons why those eligible for Android 17 should upgrade, including improved features — like the ability to “bubble” apps and stop network snoops and SMS blasters.

Also: I enabled Android’s new security feature that detects fake cell towers – here’s why

Plus, it’s the most proactive thing you can do for your device. Software updates usually include improvements to your phone’s operation, speed, security, and more, and it’s an easy (and free) way to keep your phone healthy.

#3187. Apple’s HomeView may double as security camera – watch out Ring, Nest, and Wyze

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple’s HomeView smart home hub could soon double as an indoor security camera via HomeKit Secure Video, according to settings discovered by a Reddit user pdfu.

Also: 5 ways HomeView could make me switch from Echo

Once these settings are enabled, users can configure HomeView to detect motion, stream real-time video, and record video. These strings appear in HomeView software version 27.2, suggesting that Apple will wrap this feature into an upcoming software update. Still, there’s a possibility that this feature gets delayed to an even later software release.

Via HomeKit Security Camera, only users registered to the home can view HomeView’s video streams and recordings. Additionally, a green status light will appear, and a chime will sound to alert house dwellers that HomeView is recording or someone is starting a camera stream.

Finally, all members registered to the Home app will receive a notification when someone else changes HomeKit Secure Video settings, such as allowing HomeView to detect motion or record video.

HomeView may have four video options: Off, Detect Activity, Stream, and Stream & Allow Recordings. With Detect Activity, home members would be alerted to motion but won’t be able to rewatch who or what triggered the notification.

Stream would allow users to stream video from HomeView in real time, but the home hub won’t record the livestream. Finally, Stream & Allow Recordings would allow home members to stream video from HomeView in real time, with all members able to access its recordings.

Also: Hold onto your old HomePod – an upgrade is on the way

Code strings also point to customization options, such as allowing HomeView to detect motion, stream, or record video only when you’re home, away, or asleep, using home members’ iPhone or other device locations to determine proximity.

Apple’s bottom-up ecosystem control gives it an advantage over competing home security brands like Ring, Nest, and Wyze. Users can easily access their HomeView camera stream without a third-party app or delayed notifications.

However, Apple’s greatest advantage may be HomeView’s potential versatility; instead of purchasing a separate camera device, HomeView lets users interact with Siri while cooking, be used as an intercom throughout the house, lock and unlock compatible smart locks from its display, and view an in-home camera feed all from one screen.

Also: Renting? These Apple smart home devices are worth it

Furthermore, Apple typically extends the lifespan of its smart home hardware through software updates, so users may not need to upgrade for six to ten years, as evidenced by the 2020 HomePod receiving the latest smart speaker feature upgrades in HomePod 27.2.

I'll now turn the presentation over to Mr. Stratos Desypris, Navios Partners' Chief Operating Officer. Stratos?

Efstratios Desypris: Thank you, Angeliki, and good morning all. Please turn to Slide 9, which details our operating free cash flow potential for Q4 of 2026 and full year 2027. For the fourth quarter of 2026, we fixed 80% of available days at a net average rate of $31,837 per day. Contracted revenue exceeds estimated total cash operating costs by $133.6 million, and we have 2,713 remaining open or index-linked days, offering additional upside. Even for 2027, our contracted revenue already exceeds estimated total cash operating costs by $4 million. We have fixed 56% of our available days at a net rate of $29,605 per day, and we still have 25,220 days open or index-linked that will provide significant additional free cash.

Every $1,000 per day on those days creates over $25 million of additional free cash. Moving to Slide 10. Our contracted revenue backlog provides strong earnings visibility. Taking advantage of the current strong rate environment, we continue to grow contracted revenue. Since the start of the third quarter, we added approximately $735 million: $537 million from 8 containerships, $145 million from 4 tankers and $53 million minimum revenue from 2 dry bulk vessels. Total contracted revenue reached a record high $5 billion: $2.1 billion for tankers, $2.6 billion for containerships and $0.3 billion for dry bulk. Charters are extended through 2037 with a diverse group of quality counterparties. Slide 11 summarizes the fleet developments for Q3 and Q4 quarter-to-date.

We agreed to acquire four scrubber-fitted and shore-power-fitted newbuilding 10,100 TEU containerships with delivery expected in the second half of '28 and first half of '29 for $488 million. We also agreed to acquire one newbuilding scrubber-fitted VLCC expected to be delivered in Q4 of 2029 for $124 million and two newbuilding scrubber-fitted MR2s for $91.2 million with expected delivery in the second half of 2029. We also sold a 17-year-old capesize vessel for $30.8 million.

Additionally, we took delivery of two newbuilding vessels: one MR2 vessel, which is chartered out for about 5 years at a net daily rate of $23,400, and one 7,900 TEU container ship chartered out for about 4 years at a net daily rate of $42,463. We continue to actively renew our fleet to maintain a young age profile. We have 34 newbuilding vessels delivering to our fleet through 2029, representing $3.1 billion of investment. We have mitigated the residual value risk of our newbuilding program with long-term creditworthy charters expected to generate about $2.3 billion in contracted revenue over a 5-year average charter duration. Moving to Slide 12. Our diversified fleet provides both revenue visibility and market exposure.

For 2027, we have 57,947 available days, of which 56% are fixed and 44% are open or indexed. Our chartering strategy takes advantage of each segment fundamentals. Containerships are 98% fixed, anchoring our cash flow. Tankers are 72% fixed, providing stable healthy cash flows, but also significant upside optionality. Dry bulk is also where significant upside sits. 87% of our 2027 dry bulk days are open or indexed, which is nearly 80% of all our open days. That reflects our approach. We fix long term when the market pays and we stretch short when it does not. Dry bulk rates were weak for a prolonged period, so period charters made little sense.

As charter rates improved, we have begun adding cover, such as the 5-year capesize newbuilding charter with a floor of $26,000 per day plus profit sharing. I now pass the call to Eri Tsironi, our CFO, who will take you through the financial highlights. Eri?

Erifili Tsironi: Thank you, Stratos, and good morning all. I will briefly review our unaudited financial results for the third quarter and the first 9 months of '26. Financial information is included in the press release and summarized in the slide presentation available on the company's website. Moving to the earnings highlights on Slide 13. Total revenue for the third quarter of '26 increased by 25% to $432 million compared to $347 million for the same period in '25 due to higher fleet combined time charter equivalent rate. Our combined TCE for the third quarter of '26 increased by 26% to $30,371 per day, while our available days slightly increased to 13,479 days compared to Q3 '25.

In terms of sector performance, the TCE rate for our dry bulk fleet and tanker fleet increased by 43% and 38% to $25,708 and $36,183 per day, respectively, compared to Q3 '25. The TCE rate for our container fleet was 1% lower at $31,619 per day. EBITDA, net income and earnings per common unit for the third quarter and the first 9 months of '26 were adjusted as explained in the press release and the slide footnote. Adjusted EBITDA for Q3 '26 increased by $78 million to $272 million compared to Q3 '25, mainly due to the increase in revenue.

Vessel operating expenses increased by $3 million due to an 8% increase in daily OpEx rate to $7,320 due to higher maintenance, repair and spares expenses, partially mitigated by a 4% decrease in OpEx days. Adjusted income for Q3 '26 almost doubled to $164 million compared to $84 million for the same period in '25. Adjusted earnings and earnings per common unit for the third quarter of '26 were $5.7 and $6.4, respectively. Total revenue for the first 9 months of '26 increased by 23% to $1.2 billion compared to $979 million for the same period in '25 due to higher combined time charter equivalent rate despite lower available days.

Our combined TCE rate for the first 9 months of '26 increased by 24% to $28,209 per day, while our available days decreased by 1% to 39,735 days compared to the same period in '25. In terms of sector performance, our TCE rate per day was higher in all three sectors as follows: 45% increase to $22,332 for our bulkers, 29% increase to $33,897 for our tankers and 1% increase to $31,504 for our container ships compared to the first 9 months of '25. Adjusted EBITDA for the first 9 months of '26 increased by $198 million to $718 million compared to the same period in '25. The increase was primarily driven by the increase in revenue.

Fleet OpEx daily rate was 4% higher than 2025 levels at $7,223 due to higher maintenance, repair and spares expenses. Adjusted EBITDA was also negatively affected by a $17 million increase in time charter and voyage expenses primarily reflecting additional insurance premiums reimbursed by the charterers and a $4 million increase in general and administrative expenses, mainly due to higher prevailing euro-dollar exchange rate as well as the increase in legal, professional and audit fees during the first 9 months of '26. Adjusted net income for the first 9 months of '26 doubled to $396 million compared to $196 million for the same period in '25.

Adjusted earnings and earnings per common unit for the first 9 months of '26 were $13.6 and $15.8, respectively. Turning to Slide 14. I will briefly discuss some key balance sheet data. As of September 30, '26, cash and cash equivalents, including restricted cash and time deposits in excess of 3 months were $508 million. In addition, we had approximately $150 million available under two revolving facilities. During the first 9 months of '26, we paid approximately $290 million under our newbuilding program, net of debt, and we concluded the sale of 5 vessels for $185 million, adding about $160 million cash after debt repayment.

Long-term borrowings, including the current portion and the senior secured bond net of deferred fees, increased by $87 million to $2.25 billion following the delivery of 8 newbuildings during the first 9 months of the year. Net debt to book capitalization improved to 29%. During the first 9 months of '26, we voluntarily repaid approximately $170 million of debt, including $90 million paid in Q3 '26 relating to 7 vessels, which are currently debt-free. Slide 15 highlights our debt structure. At quarter end, we had 62 debt-free vessels, including 18 vessels securing our unutilized revolving credit facilities.

We have a diversified financing base consisting of leasing structures in Japan and China, more than 15 active banking relationships and a $330 million senior unsecured bond trading in the Oslo Bors. In addition, 44% of our debt is fixed at an average interest rate of 6.3%, while 52% carries no loan-to-value covenant. We have also partially mitigated higher interest rate costs by lowering the average margin on our floating rate debt and bareboat liabilities for the in the water fleet to 1.7%. I would like to note that the average margin for the committed floating rate debt of our newbuilding program is 1.4%.

Our maturity profile is staggered with no significant balloons due in any single year until 2030 when the bond matures. Finally, recently, we concluded the financing of 3 newbuilding LR2s for a total amount of $136 million. I'll now pass the call to Vincent Vandewalle, Navios Partners' Chief Trading Officer, to take you through the industry section. Vincent?

Vincent Vandewalle: Thank you, Eri. Strait of Hormuz closure has created a major energy and shipping shock, affecting about 20% of the worldwide crude product and LNG flows. The disruption has tightened tanker availability and driven freight rates for all sizes sharply higher. Rates for VLCCs hit all-time highs, reaching $1.4 million per day and remained elevated even as all flows out of the Middle East returned to pre-war levels. Increased crude volumes from the U.S.A., Brazil, Venezuela and Guyana heading to both Europe and Asia are adding more ton miles as worldwide stocks have been drawn down and oil demand continues at high levels.

Product tanker rates have also risen with the Baltic Clean Tanker Index reaching an all-time high of 3,015 points last week, 264% higher than long-term average of 826. Higher fuel costs and security of supply concern continue to drive the purchasing and transportation of commodities and finished goods. This has raised rates for dry bulk assets for both Capes and Panamaxes and has continued to support container time charter rates. The conflict in Ukraine and effects due to El Nino will also add ton miles for most vessel types. We expect coal imports to continue at elevated levels, while LNG passage through Hormuz remains restricted.

With negotiations between the U.S. and Iran at an impasse and increasing attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and Southern Red Sea, vessel utilization will continue to run at high levels, supporting elevated rates for the near term. Medium-term trade adjustments depend on how long oil prices stay elevated. And, for example, whether decreased fertilizer availability affects crop supply later this year. Strategic and commercial crude and product reserves will need to be restocked, which should keep tanker rates elevated over the longer term. However, prolonged Hormuz closure could still trigger a global slowdown or a recessionary demand shock, which could affect all shipping markets. Please turn to Slide 18 for the review of the dry bulk industry.

Demand growth for dry bulk trade has been relatively stable over the last 25 years at about 4% compound annual ton-mile growth. The current order book stands at about 15% of the total fleet and is expected to remain low due to high newbuilding prices, uncertainty about new fuel regulations, yard availability and general market outlook. The fleet is aging quickly with 39% of the vessels 15 years old. With older vessels far exceeding those on order, supply should be constrained over the medium term. Please turn to Slide 19. The main driver of dry bulk demand will be strong Atlantic Basin iron ore growth over the next several years with new projects in Guinea, Brazil and Liberia.

The largest new project is Simandou in Guinea, which started shipments at the end of last year and is expected to ramp up to 120 million by '28. Mid-October year-to-date shipments were about 20 million long-haul tons from 0 last year. Vale in Brazil has three new projects totaling 50 million tonnes expected to start exporting by the end of '26 and Liberia will add 10 million tonnes of exports in '26. Other African iron ore exports projects have been announced, but awaiting final investment decisions. In total, these 180 million tonnes are all long-haul ton miles trading, creating demand for an additional 249 Capes.

With the current order book of only 228 Capes due by '28, a further tightening of supply and demand is expected over the next few years, benefiting rates. Overall, the dry bulk market looks positive based on steady long-term demand growth and a constrained supply of vessels. Please turn to Slide 21 for the review of the tanker industry. As to supply, we see a tanker order book of 26%, about 50% of the fleet is already over 15 years old, rising quickly in the next few years. With older vessels exceeding the order book and yards offering first deliveries in '29 or '30, supply is set to be tight for several years. Please turn to Slide 22.

VLCCs reached record spot earnings of $1.4 million a day recently as a portion of the fleet has been sanctioned, damaged, restricted in trading or dedicated to ship-to-ship shuttle service through Hormuz. In all, 28% of the VLCC fleet has been restricted from normal operations, leading to exceptional spot and long-term charter rates. Please turn to Slide 23. Middle East crude oil flows have recently returned to pre-war levels, although their composition has shifted significantly. Increasing use of ship-to-ship transfers, along with exports out of the Red Sea and via pipelines have created more inefficiencies and led VLCC rates to the current extreme elevated rates. This has also helped Suezmax and Aframax crude tanker rates to rise across the board.

The tanker market also looks positive over the medium term based on a low order book compared with an aging and reduced fleet due to sanctions. Please turn to Slide 25 for the review of the container industry. After the COVID pandemic, containership orders were mainly for the biggest units with fleet expansion in large vessels set to continue at a high level. Currently, 73% of the order book is for ships with 9,000 TEU capacity or greater and only 23% of the order book is for 2,000 to 9,000 TEU capacity where Navios is most active. Note that by '29, more than 50% of the 2,000 to 9,000 TEU fleet will be 20 years or older.

Small segments of the fleet are well positioned to take advantage of shifting trading patterns. As shown on the right-hand graph, growth in non-mainlane trades generally exceed the traditional mainlane trades to the U.S. and Europe due to tariffs and higher growth in developing economies, notwithstanding Iran war-related dislocations this year. Trades involving the Southern Hemisphere, mostly served by smaller-sized vessels, are expected to see continued healthy growth as this trade shift continues. Overall, Navios Fleet is well positioned within the container market and continues to benefit from long-term employment with our high-quality charters. This concludes our presentation. I would now like to turn the call over to Angeliki Frangou for her final comments. Angeliki?

Angeliki Frangou: Thank you, Vincent. This concludes our formal presentation. We open the call to questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And we'll take our first question from Omar Nokta with Clarksons Securities.

Omar Nokta: Clearly, you have very strong results and you continue to reinvest in the business, divesting older vessels, acquiring newbuildings primarily with long-term charters. I think, obviously, a real significant thing that's developed here recently is at least one of the many things has been the reduction in your net LTV. You've gotten it down to 23%. That's your long-term target of trying to get it to that 20% to 25% range. So congratulations on that. So I guess now that you're here, is there anything that changes the business approach? Your market footprint has generally stayed the same within the three main aspects of your business. But does anything change from here? Do you look to be more acquisitive?

Is there a target you want to keep through the cycles with this net LTV? Yes, any color you can give on anything that changes from here based on you reaching your target?

Angeliki Frangou: Number one, I'll say the target is one thing, but also you can see that we care about return to our investors. As you know, I'm a 20% owner of the -- almost 20% owner of the equity. So we are fully aligned here. Important thing is you have to see what we have done with our cash this year. In 2026, we spent about four, $450 million cash for newbuildings. We prepaid in order to reach our LTV numbers about $170 million accelerated debt repayment. And we returned so far about $40 million return of capital to our investors, $660 million up to now.

As we are -- the year is finishing in Q1, we will recalibrate our return of capital and seeing the conditions at the time. But one thing we have done is we built NAV and also by pushing NAV, we get a share price to chase this NAV.

Omar Nokta: Angeliki, no, that's good context. And so we'll stay tuned on things as they develop. And maybe just kind of as a follow-up, you've had this long-term exposure to the three main segments of shipping of tankers, containers, dry bulk. And you obviously invested within all three and recycled proceeds into new ships in those markets. But as you kind of think about where things are, I know there's a lot to think about, you have plenty of flexibility. But do you see investment opportunities for Navios outside these three core areas within shipping perhaps or any other segments that look interesting from an investment standpoint?

Angeliki Frangou: Listen, the beauty of our platform is that we are able to take advantage of any market. And this is what it makes it unique. And I think this is something that we like to stress. I mean it allows. We have $1 billion in platform on EBITDA generation LTM. We have a very low leverage. And we have the ability and we have been expanding and building NAV while we are deleveraging. So that platform -- and we have a contracted revenue of about $5 billion that allow us to have contracted revenue beyond 2030.

So this kind of a platform allows you to be able to be opportunistic on the -- on what we see as an area to expand. And one thing I want to say, we are very mindful of our investors. Think about we completed $100 million of a buyback, and we have already announced a $200 million buyback. What we have done, you have to see it over a period of time. We have -- over the last 5 years, we more than doubled our NAV. So we are chasing. This is our success. We are building that NAV. On the same time, we have done -- we have grown -- our share price has increased over 300%.

So this is not one quarter, not one year. It's multiple years of effort to provide results.

Omar Nokta: Indeed, we can see it. So well done. Congratulations on the latest, and we'll see how things develop from here.

Operator: We'll move next to Stephanie Moore with Jefferies.

Stephanie Benjamin Moore: I guess just as you think about your Q4 VLCC days are fixed at just over, I think, 70%. How are you thinking about spot versus term coverage from here? I would love to hear your thoughts just given where we are in the market and then appetite as we think about more days are open into 2027.

Angeliki Frangou: Thank you. This is a good question. The nature of our platform allows us to have flexibility. So this depends on the sector and part of the cycle. So, you will see that the contracted revenue allows us to be totally non-biased on where we take the exposure. If you see for this year and Stratos had analyzed very well is we have a lot of exposure on our dry bulk capesize vessels. We see an opportunity here and why we keep larger vessels on the tanker segment, VLCC exposure. So we are opportunistic on where we see the exposure.

On the container side, on the other side, we see the nice cash flows as a good bedrock for our visibility.

Efstratios Desypris: Just one quick add-on here, Stephanie, on the exposure that we have on the tankers. -- as Angeliki said we have covered -- we have a lot of contracted revenue on the tanker side, about $2.4 billion of contracted revenue. But what we have opened is about 1/3 of our days, which are open for next year. And basically, you will see that these are mostly the VLs that are on spot exposure because there, we see the bigger volatility and the bigger upside. And again, if we also drill down on the other sectors on the dry bulk, where you do not have a lot of very healthy contract -- long-term contracted revenue.

Now we see the market picking up and we see availability of longer contracts. You see that the exposure there is mostly for next year is about 90% and the vast majority of it is on capesize. And containers, of course, as Angeliki said, I mean, we are almost fully fixed for next year because there, we capitalize on a very strong market.

Stephanie Benjamin Moore: Really helpful. And then just as a follow-up, you booked, I think, over $63 million of sale gains year-to-date. And as I think look at tanker values here that are up well over 40%. Maybe with your vessels that are over 15 years old, should we expect asset sales to be up into 2027? Or how should we think about overall sale potential there?

Angeliki Frangou: I think, Stephanie, you have seen we are very opportunistic on that. Earlier in the year, we sold VLCCs that were 17 years old. Today's environment, you are actually generating -- in a month you're generating such numbers that don't make sense; you're making multiples of the value. So it depends on the situation. Where we see value, we will automatically do it. And we have been very -- this is a continuous process. So I cannot tell you the moment. It depends on the market versus chartering, which we are very disciplined and we will always do. And even if the chartering opportunity to the market value of the vessel may be equal, we will sell one, keep one.

We have this continuous program. And we have done that. We have sold over $1 billion almost $1.2 billion on vessels. This is a continuous effort.

Operator: And this does conclude the question-and-answer portion of today's event. I would now like to hand the call back to Angeliki for any additional or closing remarks.

Angeliki Frangou: Thank you. This completes our Q3 results. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. This brings us to the end of today's meeting. We appreciate your time and participation. You may now disconnect.

Apple gave me the OLED iPad mini of my dreams, but the budget tier dies with it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I recently called out Apple’s new “why not” era under CEO John Ternus — a chaotic, experimental chapter bringing us the $2,000 iPhone Duo and $3,000 touchscreen MacBook Pros. Well, the iPad mini 8 just arrived, and it perfectly encapsulates the dark side of this new philosophy.

I just finished reading Tony Polanco’s review of the new mini, and I completely agree with his assessment: it is a stunning piece of hardware. That new OLED panel is a visual marvel, the IP67 water resistance is a massive structural win, and it is undeniably one of the most capable tablets Apple has ever made.

And then, I looked at the pricing ladder, and realized it revealed something grave. The iPad mini 8 is proof that Apple’s “budget” tier is officially dead, replaced by sneaky paywalls, binned silicon and a display refresh rate that would have been considered “old” back in 2018.

By stuffing flagship features into a smaller chassis, compromising weirdly in some areas and passing the skyrocketing component costs directly to you, the message is clear: buying into the Apple ecosystem today comes with a pro tax.

If the $699 starting price wasn’t concerningly high enough, Apple has incorporated tantalizing silicon upgrades into its price ladder.

In all the marketing, the Cupertino crew boasts that the new mini is powered by the 2nm A20 Pro chip from the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and Duo. But what you don’t see until you actually head to the shop is that if you buy the base model, you aren’t actually getting the full chip. You are getting a slightly nerfed version.

In fact, if you take a closer look at the specs (5-core CPU, 7-core GPU and 16-core Neural Engine vs the 6-core CPU and dual 16-core Neural Engine), something struck me. This sounds like the difference between the A18 and A18 Pro of last year — knocking a core off.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The entry-level and mid-tier models are locked to this binned option. If you want the actual A20 Pro, you’re forced to drop $1,000 on the 512GB version.

Now, is this something most people are going to feel? No. But it’s something worth noting. Apple is holding the true A20 Pro performance behind a massive storage paywall. You’re paying MacBook Air to get the real thing.

Many folks at this point will immediately point to the supply chain, and that’s fair enough. We are in the middle of a brutal global memory shortage driven by the AI data center bubble — Ternus himself said it’s “unprecedented” in Apple’s most recent earnings call, and the A20 Pro requires RAM overhead to run Apple Intelligence.

But the solution to this component inflation is rather telling. It’s something I’ve talked about with the MacBook PROLED and Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20. I’m gonna call it the OLED facade.

Rather than eating a margin hit to protect entry-level consumers, or finding a way to build a highly capable device with slightly older silicon, Apple’s gone the luxury route — packing an OLED screen into a re-engineered body and jacking up the price.

As David Naranjo, Associate Director at Counterpoint Research, told me when we predicted the price of the new MacBook Pros, OLED is “becoming a way for PC makers to justify higher prices as memory and component costs go up.” Companies are “using these premium displays to protect their profits and balance the rising costs."

They aren’t just adjusting for inflation; the idea of an accessible budget-friendly tablet is slowly but surely being abandoned.

But what I find most frustrating reading Tony’s review is what Apple’s left out here.

If you’re going to lure people in with the $699 tablet, and FOMO upsell them to the fully unbinned processor and enough storage, the device needs to be a flawless flagship experience. Yet, despite the price hike, Apple still locked the display to a 60Hz refresh rate.

And despite moving the front-facing camera to the landscape edge (giving more room around the side of the camera for extra tech), there’s no Face ID.

Why? Well, I can only theorize, and that’s where I take you back to the product ladder of the iPads. If we got an iPad mini 8 with 120Hz ProMotion and Face ID, that would nerf the larger, more expensive iPad Pro. It feels hamstrung to protect that pathway to one of its $1,300+ flagships.

The iPad mini 8 is a brilliant, powerful and gorgeous device, which is why I felt so conflicted writing this. For most folks buying this, you’re going to have a great time. But it does represent an Apple that is moving away from affordability (along with the wider tech industry).

Consumers didn’t necessarily need a mini tablet capable of running a dual neural engine with an OLED panel. But in the same vein, they feel necessary in Apple’s “why not” era of building premium, experimental hardware.

John Ternus’s vision for the future is coming into focus fast, and you better start saving up because the entry-level Apple experience is quickly vanishing in the rearview mirror.

The Blaugrana host Unai Emery's improving Villains.

Spanish giant Barcelona will look to get back to winning ways in the Champions League on Tuesday as it faces a free-scoring Aston Villa team at Camp Nou.

Barca crashed to its first defeat of this year’s competition last time out, losing to defending champs Paris Saint-Germain 4–2. Hansi Flick’s squad followed up that loss with a stinging domestic defeat to rivals Real Madrid in El Clásico but bounced back in style at the weekend with a comprehensive 6-1 drubbing of Alavés in La Liga on Saturday.

After a summer of much upheaval, today’s match meanwhile marks a good indicator of Aston Villa’s recent progress under Unai Emery. The Villains have responded well to losing a host of key players such as Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Emiliano Martínez during the summer, winning all three of their UCL games so far against Club Brugge, Fenerbahçe and Viking.
