#3173. Trump Asked Grok AI About Invading Venezuela. Democrats Want His Chat History

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

An AI chatbot was consulted about military action, raising questions about security risks, sycophancy and hallucination.

House Democrats are trying to force the White House to turn over President Donald Trump’s conversations with AI chatbots, including when he consulted Elon Musk’s Grok about deposing Venezuela’s former president Nicolás Maduro at the start of the year.

In a joint letter to Trump last week, Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, and Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat, argued that the president’s AI prompts — and the responses he received — should be considered public records under the 1978 Presidential Records Act. Lawmakers also raised ethical and security concerns about the president’s reliance on “unsecured, privately operated AI systems” to carry out foreign policy decisions, alleging that Trump consulted Grok, but not Congress, on military deployment to Venezuela.

According to public reporting cited in the letter, in December 2025, just weeks before ordering the military operation and Maduro’s arrest, Trump spent multiple hours prompting Grok about how Venezuelans would respond to the leader’s capture. Trump reportedly “came away thinking Grok was ingenious.”

Garcia and Raskin argue that Trump’s use of AI “exposes the country to malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties.” A January executive summary of a General Services Administration report, reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, concluded that xAI’s Grok “does not meet the safety and alignment expectations required” for general federal use and may pose a security risk in classified settings.

Using Grok as an informal policy adviser also raises questions over Musk’s political influence over a system he owns and has repeatedly altered to reduce content filters. “If the American President is relying on the policy advice of a Musk-designed, Hitler-friendly chatbot with a predilection for child pornography in order to carry out his official duties, Americans have a right to know,” reads the joint letter (PDF), referring to Grok’s infamous antisemitic episode in 2025 when the chatbot referred to itself as “MechaHitler.”

The letter also refers to the White House’s ongoing use of AI chatbots in military adventures abroad, including in the war with Iran: “If the United States military killed dozens of innocent schoolchildren based on the faulty advice of an AI chatbot, we have a right to know that too.” In June, months after the US military strike on an Iranian elementary school killed at least 123 children, the Pentagon’s artificial intelligence chief said the Grok chatbot’s continued operation was “a matter of paramount national security.”

Reached for comment, the White House referred CNET to the Pentagon, which didn’t immediately respond. Rep. Garcia’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The case for using an AI chatbot for tactical decision-making is usually framed in terms of efficiency. But large language models, or LLMs, are merely probabilistic text generators that can often sound authoritative while producing biased or fabricated information. In a military context, those failure points can end in missile strikes, arrests and civilian deaths.

AI models are also known to amplify existing biases, feeding users with responses that agree with their strongly held beliefs. This sycophancy often leads to answers that mirror those found in an online echo chamber. One journalist found that previous Grok models had “tripled” sycophancy rates compared with popular ChatGPT and Claude models, representing a shift in “behavior that MIT researchers identify as actively harmful.”

In other words, if the president believes he has a brilliant invasion plan, it’s Grok’s modus operandi to serve as a “yes man” and validate that course of action.

Another problem with using an AI chatbot for military decisions is the material on which a model is built. An LLM is a compilation of code that produces contextual responses based on its massive training data — a wealth of information scraped from the internet, including (but not limited to) blog posts, scientific papers, legal documents and code. Grok models, in particular, are also trained on the public interactions from X, a platform infested with bot farms and right-wing engagement bait.

When Trump was prompting Grok in December 2025, officials alleged that the chatbot told the president “that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall.” In the wake of the Venezuelan invasion, X users continued to prompt Grok about the operation, asking if the South American country “deserved” to be bombed.

The other problem is what’s commonly referred to as “hallucination.” LLMs are known to invent outputs if they don’t have the information necessary to respond to a particular prompt. From fabricated cases in legal briefs, phantom citations in government reports and other serious documents bungled by AI, there’s no way to completely prevent false intelligence from trickling through.

Earlier this year, according to reporting cited in the letter, US military officials received an intelligence report alleging that a Chinese vessel in the Middle East was carrying components for a nuclear weapons program. Only as the military prepared to intercept the ship — an action that many say could have escalated into a confrontation with China — did officials discover that the report’s author had relied on an AI chatbot and misidentified the cargo. The error didn’t cause a war, but it revealed how dangerously a fabricated AI output can slip into a military decision chain.

Moreover, if the president or his advisers use a consumer AI product rather than a hardened government system, those chats could be processed by a private company’s infrastructure. Garcia and Raskin have asked the White House to explain whether it restricts classified information from AI chatbots and whether vendors, subcontractors or other external parties can access prompts, outputs, logs or metadata.

Trump’s use of AI in the Venezuela operation would be concerning even if it were isolated. But Garcia and Raskin argue that it fits a broader pattern of AI entering high-stakes government decisions without adequate safeguards.

The Pentagon said in a sworn statement (PDF) that xAI’s latest models enabled US forces to deploy over 2,000 munitions to target 2,000 different locations within 96 hours during Operation Epic Fury, the US campaign against Iran. Grok isn’t the whole story. Palantir’s Maven Smart System, which integrates intelligence from satellites, drones and other sources to identify military targets, reportedly played a central role in the US campaign against Iran. The Defense Department has also awarded contracts worth up to $200 million each to Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI to accelerate military adoption of advanced AI.

Globally, AI systems are being used to make decisions about who lives and who dies. Researchers have regularly pointed to Israel’s indiscriminate bombing of Gaza as a clear example of AI-first warfighting. According to analysis cited by Georgetown Security Studies Review, Israel’s Lavender system marked roughly 37,000 Palestinians as suspected Hamas or Islamic Jihad operatives early in the war, with an estimated error rate of 10%.

The Lavender system “dramatically expanded” Israel’s kill list by relying on signals such as communication patterns and group-chat membership, producing misidentifications that included Palestinian police, aid workers, relatives of militants and people with similar names or nicknames. A related Israeli system, “Where’s Daddy?” tracked marked Palestinians and alerted the military when they entered their homes, striking multiple private family residences.

While the political shock of an AI chatbot influencing military strategy dominates the headlines, the real battleground is legal. Demanding that President Trump’s AI chatbot prompts and outputs be marked as official government property under the Presidential Records Act would turn AI conversations into public records, opening the door for Congress to subpoena the executive branch. Raskin and Garcia are requesting a full description of the president’s personal use of the technology and a closed-door briefing by Nov. 11 to review the administration’s AI protocols and cybersecurity safeguards.

Regardless of how the legal side shakes out, the question is no longer whether AI will be used in war, but whether the public will be allowed to see where AI begins and human responsibility ends.

#3172. Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The partnership could provide one of the nation’s largest AI companies with a bevy of personal medical data.

A major US healthcare technology provider just teamed up with Anthropic to connect patient health records with Claude.

Athenahealth, a healthcare technology provider serving over 20% of the US population, launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) compatible server that connects to Anthropic’s Claude. The server, named AthenaPatient MCP, allows the AI model to gather information from health records and answer related questions. The process is secure, according to Athenahealth, and requires patients to sign in with their account credentials.

AthenaPatient MCP is available only to Claude Pro and Claude Max users, which cost $20 and $100 per month, respectively. Not all Athenahealth patients will have their data shared with Claude, and not all Claude Pro and Claude Max users must opt in. Users must give Claude their authenticated Athenahealth credentials, can choose which health information Claude can access, and can revoke access at any time, according to the press release.

Also: The wearable health boom is creating a data overload for doctors – what happens next

Once authorized, Claude takes patients’ information like lab results, vitals, medications, health conditions, immunizations, visit history, diagnostic reports, allergies, procedures, and care plans into account when answering questions.

The AI partnership does not provide medical advice, according to Sam Lambson, vice president of product management, data & ecosystem at Athenahealth, who responded to ZDNET in an email. It also should not replace a clinician’s professional judgment or medical advice. “Patients should contact a qualified healthcare professional with questions about diagnosis, treatment, or changes to their care,” Lambson said.

It appears that the AthenaPatient MCP tool is designed to help patients better understand the information provided by health professionals, rather than to give them medical advice. So, one may ask AthenaPatient MCP about their latest blood test results, such as “What was my most recent red blood cell count?” but users shouldn’t expect Claude to explain how an abnormally high or low count may affect them.

Athenahealth says that the agreement prohibits Anthropic from using data accessed through this connection to train its models or improve its products.

Partnerships between big tech and big healthcare aren’t new. In fact, the collaboration between Athenahealth and Anthropic follows a larger trend across the health tech industry. Earlier this year, Microsoft teamed up with Mayo Clinic to develop an AI model for healthcare; Boston Children’s Hospital forged a partnership with OpenAI to develop an enterprise AI system for use across research, clinical, and administrative teams, according to a press release.

Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

A growing number of Americans are consulting AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. This partnership makes the process slightly more secure by authorizing patient account credentials before granting the model access to health records.

Health data is extremely valuable, and tech companies are increasingly interested in partnering with healthcare providers to access it. Much of the “AI could cure cancer” messaging we hear relies on these humongous companies obtaining enough health data to train their AI models and link disease data to patient data. This is not to say, however, that solving this complex issue is the motive behind the partnership between Athenahealth and Anthropic.

Also: Asking AI for medical advice? There’s a right and wrong way, one doctor explains

A more reasonable explanation for such a partnership is that an AI that can answer patient queries could eliminate some of the admin work doctors do between patient visits, like answering questions about test results, giving Athenahealth doctors some time back.

Will partnerships like Anthropic and Athenahealth’s improve patient outcomes? That remains to be seen, but a recent survey by Pew Research Center found that Americans aren’t that confident on the matter. The largest shares of respondents still preferred that a human oversee AI when it’s used in a clinical context.

Some of the biggest names in travel are turning to “practical AI” to simplify trip booking and planning.

Between Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s, it’s the time of year when your luggage stays packed. With millions of Americans planning to travel sometime between now and the end of the year, it’s time to start thinking about how to make the most of your trip.

Right on time, Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo just rolled out more than 30 new travel features. Expedia Group, which owns all three brands, said the goal is to make trip planning and execution easier with practical AI.

“Travel is a series of decisions, and travelers want the joy of discovery and planning to last through every stage of the journey,” Shilpa Ranganathan, chief product officer at Expedia Group, said. “That’s why we’re building AI-powered experiences across our brands that help travelers make informed decisions, give them flexibility and value, and personalize every step of their trip. And when travelers need a person, our human agents step in with the full context to make things right.”

Here’s what’s new from each travel brand.

Expedia says it’s introducing a more personal homepage, flexible travel packages, more straightforward bookings for families, interactive maps of your travel destination for easier planning and expanded airport perks like Clear Plus discounts and free lounge access for flight delays.

Two new AI-powered products are also rolling out to make trip planning smoother once a trip is already booked. Expedia’s new Activity Planner is an AI-powered conversational shopping assistant that can find and book activities, restaurants and events based on your itinerary. You can also receive tailored recommendations based on your preferences.

Another is a Property Expert, which lets you ask questions about a business and get AI-generated insights on the property, reviews, reservations and other details.

The platform is improving its AI Compare experience to help you compare multiple hotels in one place. The comparisons are personalized to your interests and preferences for location, amenities, price and policy details.

The Hotels.com homepage will also adapt to the type of trip you booked, such as a vacation or work trip, and include suggested links tailored to your booking, like options to extend your stay and access to receipts for easier work-trip expenses.

The Airbnb rival is launching several new features and services, including a tool to make group bookings easier to manage, an option to reserve now, pay later, and enhanced customer support.

With Vrbo’s natural language search, you can describe in plain language what kind of rental property you’re looking for. Rather than spending hours researching options one by one, you can simply say you’re looking for a beachfront home in South Florida with a kitchen and outdoor gathering space that’s dog-friendly. The enhanced search feature allows you to narrow down your options without relying on traditional filters.

Vrbo’s Arrival Experience is getting an upgrade to make your rental details more accessible. Key property information, such as check-in and checkout times, door codes, directions and house rules, will now be aggregated in one place, so you can stay on top of your booking without searching through multiple emails or messages.

Loan resolutions and deleveraging took center stage amid lingering macro headwinds.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Claros Mortgage Trust, Inc. (CMTG +66.67%) reported third-quarter results focused on the resolution of watchlist loans, the repositioning of real estate owned assets, and the deleveraging of its balance sheet. Management reported resolving $3.8 billion of loans and reducing indebtedness by $2.9 billion since Jan. 1, 2025. The company is directing proceeds from recent asset sales toward paying down its secured term loan to reduce its highest cost of capital. The company reported that its current portfolio has been reduced to 21 loans and eight REO investments, which management stated increases transparency and reduces variability in book value calculations. #3169. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

‘A Dog’s Perfect Christmas’ is cozy but no Christmas classic

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Netflix’s holiday movie slate for 2026 begins its rollout this week, starting with “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas,” a streaming original that so rigidly sticks to the genre conventions that it is as predictable as unwrapping a Christmas present from that one relative who always gets you an Axe body spray gift set. Within seconds, you know exactly what you’re getting.

All the trappings of a family-focused festive-themed comedy-drama are here. By the end, everything is wrapped up in a neat bow, all to send viewers into the credits with a warm fuzzy feeling. It’s a safe holiday movie created in a tinsel-laden laboratory, where artistic merit is not the end goal. Instead, the objective is to create a product palatable for all ages.

But if “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” proves anything, it’s that throwing a couple of cute canine companions into the mix can make even a Christmas movie this flavorless at least tolerable. Which isn’t to say it has any original musings on the special connection between household pets and their owners. It doesn’t even break from the weary formula established in other dog movies like “A Dog’s Purpose” and “A Dog’s Journey.”

However, the dogs were lovable enough to thaw out even my cynical soul. It might not be a future Christmas classic — the likes of “It’s A Wonderful Life” and “Elf” will not fear their place in any family’s annual seasonal watchlist being pinched by this new Netflix movie — but dog lovers everywhere will probably find this film cozy enough to watch, if only once.

Based on the novel by W. Bruce Cameron, author of “A Dog’s Purpose,” this movie focuses on the Goss family. Their holiday festivities are already off to a rocky start, with grandpa Sander (Dennis Quaid) grieving the loss of his wife two years prior, husband Hunter (Milo Ventimiglia) putting work first, and mother Juliana (Kathleen Rose Perkins) struggling to find common ground with her moody teenage daughter, Ello (Brooke Lena Johnson).

Things take a further turn when a medical emergency throws the family into turmoil and threatens to bring a swift end to any lingering holiday cheer. It’s up to the Goss' wise old dog, a basset hound named Winstead (voiced by Thomas Haden Church), and an energetic new arrival, a Corgi puppy named Ruby (Sadie Hatch), to bring the humans back together.

I really cannot overstate just how generic “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” is. All its narrative beats have been seen in countless other holiday movies, and it has no desire to rework the genre trappings. But whether you demand, or particularly look for, originality in your holiday watchlist is a matter of personal preference. If you want a cozy family comedy, it’s a suitable way to spend 100 minutes, and it'll probably make for great background noise while putting up your own seasonal decorations, if that's your thing.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

It’s been suggested that Netflix has a mandate that its movies need to reiterate key plot points for viewers only half-watching, and while the streamer denies this, 'A Dog’s Perfect Christmas' is evidence to the contrary.

Another notable area where “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” comes up short is in its insistence on over-explaining. It’s been suggested that Netflix has a mandate that its movies need to reiterate key plot points for viewers only half-watching, and while the streamer denies this, “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” is evidence to the contrary. Characters often speak unnaturally, regurgitating facts as if they know a third party is watching their holiday season unfold and might need a reminder (or three) to follow along.

But even if “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” will no doubt be forgotten long before you take down your tree and household decorations for another year, in the moment, it’s by no means offensively bad. It’s just bland. But above all, the two dogs at the heart of the holiday crowd-pleaser are very cute and given enough screen time to make their presence felt.

“A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” celebrates family, especially these four-legged members of our homes who are just as important to the unit as any human. That’s a message that dog owners everywhere will relate to, and it gives this Netflix movie a crowd-pleasing quality. I guess it really does prove that the inclusion of a dog (or two) can make anything watchable.

#3167. Apple Is Putting an Age Limit on Falling in Love With AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Dating and AI companion apps have new age gate restrictions, while apps that share your location will have to disclose it.

Practicing flirting using Replika's AI system.

Falling in love with artificial intelligence raises a lot of questions about loneliness, human connection and what the heck we’re doing as a species. Apple has a more immediate concern: Are you at least 18?

The company is tightening its App Store rules, requiring dating apps and AI companions that offer romantic or sexual interactions to carry an 18-and-over age rating. The change applies whether you’re looking for love with another human being or flirting with a chatbot that never leaves you on read.

In a notice to developers on Monday, Apple said it will introduce two new content descriptors on Nov. 16: “Dating and Relationships” and “Shared Location.” Developers will have to disclose whether their apps offer dating features, including romantic or sexual interactions with virtual companions, or whether they allow users to share their real-world locations with others.

Location-sharing features may also affect age ratings, depending on the country. In Brazil, for example, apps that allow users to share their locations must carry a minimum age rating of 16, while dating apps require an 18-and-over rating. Developers have until Jan. 12, 2027, to complete the new disclosures for all their apps.

Most major dating apps, including Tinder and Hinge, already require users to be at least old enough to vote (in the US, that is). The more interesting part is how Apple’s rules could affect AI companions, which have become increasingly popular.

Last year, Character.AI, a platform where users can create and interact with fictional AI personalities, removed open-ended chats for users under 18. The company continued offering other features to younger users, but the decision came amid growing concerns about the emotional and psychological risks of forming relationships with AI.

A 2026 Common Sense Media report, which surveyed more than 1,000 children ages 9 to 17, found that many were already treating AI as a confidant. An earlier 2025 study found that nearly three-quarters of teens had used AI companions, with a third choosing chatbots over humans for serious conversations. The nonprofit has warned that such relationships can pose risks to minors, particularly around emotional attachment and dependency.

Apple’s announcement also follows the company’s expanded parental controls in iOS 27, which gave parents more control over their children’s apps, browsing and screen time. The update introduced features that let parents approve websites before their children visit them, set time limits for app categories and restrict access to potentially harmful content.

However, an “18-plus” rating doesn’t automatically mean everyone has to verify their age. The labels work with parental restrictions, while Apple may require users to confirm they’re adults before downloading those adult apps in certain regions.

So the new rules won’t necessarily stop teenagers from finding a digital soulmate. They should, however, make it harder for apps offering romantic AI relationships to slip past age-based content restrictions — regardless of whether a chatbot says you’re mature for your age.

Currently, ChatGPT’s desktop app features a ChatGPT and Codex section, and within the ChatGPT section, you can find the Chat and Work tabs. It’s not especially easy to navigate, and OpenAI is looking to change that.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

“Starting in December, Plus, Pro, and Business plans’ usage allowance will be shared across ChatGPT and Codex as we bring the agentic capabilities of Work into the main ChatGPT experience,” OpenAI detailed in its note entitled “Understanding ChatGPT and Codex usage limits.”

An email was also sent to current users, sharing similar information, according to TechCrunch. The email confirmed the merger of the Chat and Work tabs, adding that the integrated experience will be available to select users for feedback before it is made more widely available.

“This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app,” the email said.

OpenAI said the transition will allow both ChatGPT and Codex to draw tokens from the same allowance pool. While most customers won’t be affected, depending on usage and model, some users may need to wait for resets more than usual.

“Your usage for ChatGPT and Codex will be measured in tokens, the units of information a model processes and generates. How much of your allowance you use will depend on the model you choose and the task you ask it to do. More advanced models and complex tasks generally use more of your allowance. Instant chat will not draw from your usage,” OpenAI said in the online note.

In September, rival Anthropic merged Claude‘s chat and Cowork functions into a single screen. OpenAI said that they don’t expect the upcoming change to disrupt users’ current experience.

“We’re preparing carefully for this transition to help prevent disruption to your workflows. We expect most users won’t need to wait for their usage to reset more often than they do now,” OpenAI said.

Some Roku users are about to feel like fish out of water. Fans of the platform’s classic Aquatic Life screensaver are discovering that the animation will soon be unavailable.

The popular animated screensaver featuring realistic aquarium life will be replaced by the Roku City screensaver on Dec. 1. Roku City is the platform’s signature purple skyline, featuring rotating digital billboards packed with brand sponsorships and clever pop-culture Easter eggs. (Seattle’s short-spined raccoon, Jimothy, has made an appearance.)

That doesn’t mean all fish-filled options have been flushed. Several third-party Roku wallpaper apps offer a variety of aquarium options to choose from. But if you’re sticking to what Roku itself provides on its streaming boxes, the move away from the aquarium screensaver also means switching to an alternative that’s filled with advertising.

“It seems like this is a way for Roku to convert a popular screensaver into a way to make money, or at least generate more engagement, via the Roku City version,” said CNET Senior Editor Ty Pendlebury, who covers home entertainment options including the Roku streaming boxes.

A Roku representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Viewers who miss these specific fish can still watch a YouTube version of Roku’s Aquatic Life screensaver for as long as the company chooses to keep this nearly 3-minute video on the internet.

#3163. I tested the RedMagic 12 Pro – and it’s the fastest Android I’ve ever seen

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

If it's possible to release a flagship phone while at the same time making it appear more like a midrange phone, Red Magic has found a way.

RedMagic just announced the international launch of the RedMagic 12 Pro — its latest flagship phone. Typically, the company releases devices in China first and then slowly rolls them out to the rest of the world. This time around, the company knew it had a phone that could compete with other flagship devices.

Also: I’ve been a Google Pixel fan for years, but this $500 Android phone is giving me pause

RedMagic’s phones are high-performance devices known to do one thing especially well: mobile gaming. The RedMagic 12 Pro is no exception. It houses a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 CPU with up to 5.01 GHz, which is paired with the RedMagic R5 Gaming Chipset, and I can honestly say it’s the fastest Android phone I’ve ever tested.

After the initial setup, I installed Geekbench 7 to benchmark the phone and compare it to my Pixel 9 Pro. As for the latest iPhone, according to Geekbench, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes out ahead in single-core performance, but it just barely falls behind in multi-core performance.

The RedMagic 7 Pro nearly doubled the Pixel 11 Pro’s multi-core score. And Google’s device couldn’t beat the single-core score either. As I said, I’ve never seen a Geekbench score this high.

Real-world usage confirms these numbers, because the phone reacts faster and behaves more smoothly than any Android device I’ve owned or tested. It’s so smooth and fast, it feels like magic. But it’s not just the speed that makes this phone special.

First off, I’ve always liked RedMagic’s Android “skin.” As you use it, it seems to be some amalgamation of Android and iOS. RedMagic is essentially doing what Google’s been trying for years: making the smoothest possible animations on Android.

Also: I switched to an Android with liquid cooling for a week – now I wish every phone had it

The interface is as elegant as any I’ve seen on a mobile device. Pull down the notification shade, and it glides down like it was made of silk. Tap on an app launcher, and it opens immediately. Switch between apps, and there’s zero lag or jitter. On top of that, there’s hardly any bezel to speak of — the display goes nearly to the edge of the device.

There’s also no indication of where the front-facing camera is. There’s no pinhole (as you’ll find with many Android devices), and there’s no island (like on iPhones). It’s just a solid display with no interruptions.

The Pro 12 also feels really good in the hand. Both the back and the front are glass. Yes, it invites fingerprints, but it feels so smooth. The back of the phone also has that typical RedMagic look and feel with integrated RGB lighting zones. You can customize the lighting zones for things like fan on/off, game key atmosphere, media atmosphere, incoming calls, charging, and the alarm clock.

Also: This 15-inch portable monitor solved my big issue with cheaper models – and rivals my Mac display

Everything, and I mean everything, about this phone is fast.

The RedMagic 12 Pro is 100% a gaming phone. I installed “Diablo: Immortal” and found it to perform better than the last RedMagic gaming-specific tablet I tested. Not only was it fast, but the graphics were gorgeous. Crisp, smooth, and responsive.

Since the RedMagic 12 Pro is advertised as a serious gaming phone, why does it include preinstalled games that are decidedly non-serious?

On this powerful gaming phone, you’ll find apps like Puzzle Spark, Mahjong Blast, Bolt Twist, GoGo! Blast, and Little Kitty, Big City preinstalled. These are not serious games. In fact, these game titles sound more like they belong on a list of malicious apps (they aren’t).

Also: This 9-inch tablet singlehandedly changed my mind about gaming on Android

I would rather see the Red Magic 12 Pro have zero preinstalled games than the collection it ships with. Yes, you can easily delete those apps, but their being on the phone kind of cheapens it. Given how amazing this phone is, I think RedMagic could get away with shipping a bit less cheese, and a lot more wine.

Either way, the RedMagic 12 Pro is a phone that belongs at the top of the heap among flagships, even above every Pixel phone ever released. If there is a phone that can impress me more than the RedMagic 12 Pro, I’ve yet to see it.

Suncor Energy Inc. (SU -4.52%) reported record financial performance for the third quarter, driven by physical integration between its upstream production and downstream refining assets. Management executed on strategic portfolio pruning by announcing the divestiture of non-core offshore East Coast assets for $1.2 billion while maintaining its long-term free funds flow growth targets through 2028. The company utilized record upgrader utilization and optimized refining throughput to capture synthetic crude oil price premiums and expand global export volumes. CFO Peter Zebedee indicated that the company's strengthened balance sheet, with net debt reduced to $1.8 billion, supports a significant increase in capital returns through a 10% dividend hike and expanded monthly share repurchases.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Suncor Energy Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker, Suncor Energy's Director of Investor Relations, Mr. David Johnson.

David L. Johnson: Thank you, operator, and good morning. Welcome to Suncor Energy's Third Quarter Earnings Call. Please note that today's comments contain forward-looking information. Actual results may differ materially from expected results because of various risk factors and assumptions that are described in our third quarter earnings release as well as our current annual information form, both of which are available on SEDAR+, EDGAR and our website, suncor.com. Certain financial measures referred to in these comments are not prescribed by Canadian generally accepted accounting principles. For a description of these financial measures, please see our third quarter earnings release. We'll start with comments from Rich Kruger, Chief Executive Officer; followed by Peter Zebedee, President and Chief Financial Officer.

Also on the call are Adam Albeldawi, Executive Vice President, Upstream; David Oldreive, Executive Vice President, Downstream; and Shelley Powell, Executive Vice President, Development and Projects. Following the formal remarks, we'll open the call up to questions. Now I'll hand it over to Rich to share his comments.

Richard Kruger: Thanks, David. Our third quarter involved completing major maintenance for the year, positioning for a strong finish, and maximizing value in today's business environment. We accomplished all 3. We also announced the sale of non-core offshore East Coast assets and a series of senior leadership transitions, actions that will position us well for the future. I'll discuss operational highlights, and Peter will follow with financial. Starting with safety. The third quarter was our safest quarter of the year for both personnel and process safety. But rather than recite data, I want to recognize an employee, Emma Todd, Projects Manager and EHS Leader.

Emma was recently awarded the Alberta Mine Safety Association's 2026 Trailblazer Safety Leader award, recognizing her passion and commitment in leading people to work safely. Emma first came to my attention a few years ago on a project that was struggling. She rolled up her sleeves, put her boots on the ground and got things back on track, but most impressive was that Emma knew by name every contractor on site. She epitomizes safety leadership at today's Suncor, and we are extremely proud of her.

Upstream production, 853,000 barrels a day in the quarter, a rebound of 92,000 barrels a day from a very wet second quarter and our second highest third quarter ever, only behind last year's record, achieved despite Syncrude's 47-day coker turnaround, which was successfully completed in the first half of October. Upgrader utilization, a very strong 98% in the quarter and 96% year-to-date. Base plant in Q3 achieved an exceptional 107% of nameplate capacity. Syncrude was 88% given the coker turnaround performance, which is extremely valuable, given today's synthetic price premiums. Refining throughput 488,000 barrels a day in the quarter, on par with last year's best ever. Here again, performance delivering tremendous value in today's business environment.

95% utilization in 3Q, throughput 28,000 barrels a day higher than our internal business plan and consensus, achieved despite a 37-day turnaround at Edmonton and a 31-day event at Montreal and despite temporary curtailment at Sarnia due to Line 5's unplanned outage. With all this activity, how did we achieve this exceptionally high throughput? Story time. Historically, a turnaround of the Edmonton refinery's fluid cat cracking unit would require reduced crude throughput and equal to about 30% of the refinery's capacity or 45,000 to 50,000 barrels a day. Because when this unit is offline, there's no ability to process the heavier gas oil stream coming off the larger crude distillation unit. This is where the story gets interesting.

[Jewel Amond] downstream production coordinator, came up with the idea to temporarily store gas oil and to blend it with production streams from our oil sand upgraders, 400 kilometers away in Fort Mac, creating a new marketable sweet synthetic crude. This innovative idea enabled full crude throughput during the entire turnaround, preserving 46,000 barrels a day of throughput that historically would have been curtailed. Adding 3% to Edmonton's annual average utilization rate and 1% to Suncor's overall utilization rate. The best part, it generated in excess of $50 million in incremental free funds, $50 million, one idea by one person, [Jewel], embraced and implemented by our team, leveraging Suncor's fundamental competitive advantage, our unparalleled physical integration.

This idea wasn't in our annual business plan, and it wasn't in our March investor deck. It illustrates our culture to continually add value and compete. My thanks to [Jewel] and his upstream and downstream colleagues. You guys rocked it. Product sales, 677,000 barrels a day in the quarter, a record by a whopping 30,000 barrels a day and nearly tied with our highest quarter ever, continuing a string that every month in 2026 has achieved a new sales record. Now the ninth quarter in a row above 600,000 barrels a day after never reaching 600,000 barrels a day in any previous quarter. Retail, our highest value channel with #1 market share. Year-to-date, volumes are up 4.3% year-on-year.

Jet sales at 38,000 barrels a day are up 65% year-on-year and exports at 75,000 barrels a day are up 80% year-on-year. We continue to operate at industry-leading refining utilization to meet our customers' needs, achieving both value and record sales in Canada as well as in thirsty global markets. The third quarter was a big turnaround quarter for us. You'll recall, historically, we spent $1.25 billion per year on turnarounds. In 2024 on our I-Day, we committed to reduce turnaround cost by $250 million a year over 3 years. We achieved that commitment in 2 years. In mid-'25, we increased our ambition by another $100 million to $350 million a year in reductions. We achieved that this year.

2026 being a big year with the third quarter being a big turnaround quarter, Edmonton and Montreal, the largest events in the downstream and Syncrude in the upstream. Results, Montreal, best ever cost and duration, Edmonton, best ever cost and duration. Syncrude best ever cost and duration. Three for 3 is Suncor hat trick. 2026 is now the third consecutive year with turnaround cost below $1 billion. Our schedule performance has improved from third and fourth quartile to first and second quartile in North America. Cost has similarly improved with further improvement planned. Specifically, we have an additional $150 million reduction included in our 2028 targets.

On October 4, we announced an agreement to sell our interest in Terra Nova, White Rose and West White Rose to Ithaca Energy plc for $1.2 billion in upfront cash and potential additional payments of up to $350 million based on future oil prices over a 27-month period. With the transaction, Ithaca assumes all future obligations associated with the assets, including a $500 million regulatory well compliance program starting in 2027 at Terra Nova and estimated abandonment liabilities, which total $1.4 billion. Through the first half of 2026, these assets contributed about 18,000 barrels a day or 2% of our upstream production. But most importantly, this transaction is consistent with our strategy and our value proposition.

We create value through our unparalleled physically integrated upstream and downstream asset base underpinned by large long-life Oil Sands resources. These assets certainly of value, frankly, were not in that family photo. In Ithaca, we found a buyer whose strategy and core competency is aligned with these assets and consequently was willing to pay us accordingly, win-win for both parties. As stated in our press release, our 2026 I-Day commitments to grow free funds flow by an additional $2 billion a year and reduce our WTI breakeven by a further $5 per barrel through 2028 remain unchanged, reflecting our confidence in continuing to deliver exceptional shareholder value.

A quick wrap up, Suncor remains focused to excel, to compete, to win with best-in-class operating performance ambitions, definitive value-based priorities and plans, organizational alignment top to bottom, and a team-based results-oriented culture, delivering reliable and ratable high-performance literally built to win in any and all business environments. With that, I'll turn it to Peter.

Peter Zebedee: Well, thanks a lot, Rich. And wow, what a quarter for me to begin my role as CFO. As I reflect on the quarter, I'm incredibly proud of the progress we've made over the past 4 years. That hard work has fundamentally strengthened the business and positioned us to maximize value in today's commodity environment. Not only have we improved our resilience in lower priced environments by reducing our WTI corporate breakeven by more than $10 a barrel, we've expanded our earnings power at higher prices even more significantly. The third quarter of 2026 was proof of that. We delivered a record $6.7 billion in adjusted funds from operations and a record $5.2 billion in free funds flow.

Those exceptional results, however, only tell part of the story. To fully appreciate how much this business has changed, let's compare where we are today versus 2022 when we also had record high AFFO and free funds flow. Let's start with Oil Sands. Through the first 9 months of 2026, the benchmark crude prices for WTI, SYN and WTS averaged roughly 15% below 2022 levels. On price alone, that would have reduced Oil Sands AFFO by $1.5 billion. And yet today, our Oil Sands AFFO increased by $160 million to $11.1 billion. How do we do this? Higher production, higher margin, pure performance. The improvement in the downstream was even more remarkable.

Through the first 9 months of 2026, New York Harbor 2-1-1 crack spread, net of RVO, averaged 16% higher than in 2022. Yet downstream AFFO grew by over 60% to an astounding $7.9 billion. How do we do this? Record throughput and a much stronger margin capture in a business that many had thought was already at the top of its game. The value we've created is clear. Q3 year-to-date AFFO, 15% higher than 2022, free funds flow 18% higher. On a per share basis, both were roughly 40% higher. We are generating more cash flow and significantly more value per share, and it's not simply the result of commodity prices. This is the result of a fundamentally stronger business.

The value we create extends well beyond our shareholders. When Suncor succeeds, Canadian government share in that success. Q3 year-to-date, our operations have paid nearly $8 billion in income taxes and royalties to Canadian governments, reaching record high levels. This equates to about 40% of our free funds flow, pre-royalty and pretax. This performance reflects years of improving reliability, strengthening integration across the value chain and capturing higher margins from every barrel we produce and refine, and we're not done yet. There is no finish line when it comes to improving this business. Every improvement creates the opportunity for the next one.

And this is precisely why we did not change our normalized free funds flow growth or WTI breakeven reduction targets even with the sale of Terra Nova, White Rose and West White Rose. We have a clear line of sight to delivering those targets. So let me highlight a couple of examples on how the team keeps finding new ways to raise the bar. At our Canadian West Coast Burrard Terminal, we have more than doubled our export capacity, helping Canada supply much needed energy to global trading partners and giving our teams greater flexibility to capture value. Between Burrard and Montreal, we exported 92 cargoes over 9 months.

That's nearly 60% higher than in all of 2025 and at much lower contracted costs than the freight rates we saw in the market. At our refineries, we continue to find and capture improvements across the business. In July, the Commerce City team identified and addressed the constraint of the Plant 3 furnaces after never having run above 38,000 barrels a day. The unit is now operating at 43,000 barrels a day, a full 5,000 barrels a day increase to throughput. That improvement alone is expected to generate roughly $50 million of value in the second half of this year.

We have built a business that is consistently finding and capturing opportunities beyond what was visible only a few short years ago. And that same discipline extends to how we manage the balance sheet and allocate capital. We ended the quarter with $1.8 billion in net debt, and I know many on the call today are forecasting a net cash position by the end of the year. This is an exceptionally strong balance sheet. During the quarter, we returned over $2 billion to shareholders, including $1.4 billion of share buybacks and $700 million in dividends.

Beginning in October, we increased our monthly buybacks from $500 million a month to $750 million a month, reflecting our ability to sustain that level for an extended period of time. On the dividend, our philosophy remains unchanged. That is to sustain our integrated asset base, deliver a reliable and growing base dividend, return capital through consistent and ratable buybacks and invest in high-growth opportunities. We look to give long-term investors a predictable framework that they can count on through the cycle. To be very clear, every member of our Board and our executive team treats our dividend as an unbreakable promise to our shareholders.

The only way to grow it is by building a stronger and more resilient business, and that's exactly what we've been doing. The 10% dividend increase we announced is underpinned by structurally higher earnings power, a materially lower share count and confidence in our Investor Day plan. The absolute dividend level will remain fully sustainable through the cycle. With sizable increases in both dividends and share buybacks, we are on track to deliver record annual shareholder returns in 2026. Today, Suncor is generating more cash, maintaining a stronger balance sheet and returning more value to shareholders. And with that, I'll turn the call back over to David, and we can take some questions.

David L. Johnson: Thanks, Peter. I'll turn the call back to the operator, and we can go to the questions.

Richard Kruger: Greg, I'll take a shot at it, and then I'll ask Dave to comment further. What -- again, what makes us different is this uniquely physically integrated upstream and downstream. Dave Oldreive: I think you covered it well, Rich. Maybe I'll share a couple of examples of some of the things that we're doing to give some color to where we're finding value. And in addition to that, we're getting more diesel yields out of these units for a total of $140 million of value at Edmonton so far year-to-date. And I would say that's not done yet. Richard Kruger: I think, Greg, cutting through that is, when you have technical and operational teams that have provided the right focus and leadership, they continue to find opportunities, and we're beyond scratching the surface, but we're far from done. Greg Pardy: Yes, the downstream is super impressive. The overall business is super impressive. But also related to that, back at your Investor Day, you framed a very, very large resource base as well as upstream growth optionality. I'm just wondering -- pretty open-ended question, but just wondering how those pieces fit together?

Richard Kruger: Sure. We do have a huge high-quality resource base. And in many instances, it has advantages, synergies because of our existing footprint, whether that's Lewis, expansions at Firebag, et cetera. The -- if you talk about growth in general, we're less concerned about what today's oil price is and more concerned about what will the oil price be 5 years, 10 years, 15 years from now. So in high prices, inevitably, questions come up about growth and are you changing it? The question we ask ourselves is, has the world fundamentally changed? And we don't know if it has yet. There's a lot of theorists and so-called experts.

I haven't met anyone in my career, Greg, who can accurately predict long-term oil prices. So we look at generating attractive returns through mid-cycle prices when we can enjoy good business environments and we can withstand weakness. Now as it relates to the MOU and the interactions between the industry and the government, I think it's important to step back. What's the goal? The goal is that Canada is globally competitive on a fiscal and regulatory risk framework so that we can attract and incent capital. That's the goal. So the MOU has many components to it, the so-called 3Ps, pipeline, production, pathways. We've seen some things occur, the new Mega Deduction.

There seems to be some momentum on the West Coast pipeline. There's -- we're all anxiously waiting to hear more from the province on royalties and incentives there. The parties are all sleeves rolled up, meeting endlessly, working hard together, but that goal is the global competitiveness of the industry. And from a Suncor standpoint, we would far rather have a good deal when we're ready or versus a bad or an incomplete deal at an artificial date or deadline. So we're working hard. And the days on the calendar are just other days to me, November 15 is coming up.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Dennis Fong with CIBC.

Dennis Fong: And congratulations on a solid quarter. My first question here follows along the lines of, I guess, Greg's first question but kind of expands on some of the prepared remarks there. And further, I think in Q3, you were able to showcase how that interconnection was helpful with respect to obviously, your refining turnarounds and so forth.

My question here is, what are you looking to do to bolster that physical interconnectivity beyond what has already been outlined like ore sharing at Fort Hills or interconnect pipeline and/or obviously, the physical connection between your Fort McMurray Oil Sands and Edmonton and your Eastern refineries?

Richard Kruger: Adam, you want to -- you just -- at the end, you linked into the refining, but Adam, why don't you start out in terms of kind of the vision and our priorities in the upstream overall.

Adam Albeldawi: Yes, happy to do that. Dennis, you actually captured one of the main things that makes us quite unique in the upstream. And that is the ability to have physical integration across all of our assets in the upstream. So whether that is Firebag bitumen going to the base plant upgrader, whether that's Firebag bitumen going to Syncrude, whether it's Fort Hills bitumen going to the base plant upgrader or [sours] in between Syncrude and base plant. So when you take a step back and take a look at what makes us unique, that is one of the main things that makes us incredibly unique in the upstream business. So how do we leverage that?

There's a couple of ways we leverage that. The first way is when you look at the performance in our upgraders over the last several years, one of the main focus areas for us has been increasing the utilization. And as we increase the utilization, clearly, that increases the bitumen feed that we need from our mines and from our in situ assets. So the physical integration that we have across the assets enable us to actually continue to increase upgrading rates. And that's where you see some of the higher price realizations that you saw in Q3. The second main way we take advantage of this is during maintenance events.

So when there's maintenance events at our mine production assets, we now have the ability to move bitumen from different in situ assets to the upgraders to keep the upgraders full, again, ensuring we maximize value from those big, big money makers. So there's a couple of examples of how we leverage the integration that we have. As we look forward, we are always looking to see how we can maximize that even further.

So for example, the record transfers that you're seeing from Fort Hills to the base plant upgrader is a result of the continued debottlenecking activities our team has done to maximize PFT bitumen to the base plant, and we are continuing to find opportunities to do that even further.

Richard Kruger: I think a key part of all this is as we have improved underlying asset performance, now we can continue to optimize and create incremental value. But when you have assets where you have too much variability in their performance, you can't optimize. And I'll take just the tail end of your question and extend that to the downstream. I would bet a week's pay, I think the Edmonton refinery is the only refinery in North America that runs 100% on feedstock from the refinery's owner. I would guess, if not it, there's -- it's probably a -- Dave will kick in part of that week's pay.

But -- so what we were able to do is Edmonton with its pots and pans, primary units, secondary units, we can literally moderate what Edmonton can maximize value on from our upstream operations. Sarnia, far further away, runs with well over half of its feedstock with Suncor crudes. As you get further away to Montreal, the percentage goes down, but that interconnectedness is still a key differentiator with us, and that allows our upstream and downstream teams to work hand-in-hand, maximizing every dollar and every barrel. That is at the core, that is what makes us different and unique relative to a broader peer set.

Dennis Fong: Great. My second question. Can you talk towards maybe from taking a step back and thinking about this strategically, how kind of a combination of logistics, global marketing, obviously, the tanker capacity that you have time contracted as well as your ability to expand kind of your network to market globally, how that's really improved, we'll call it, market intelligence, your ability to act more opportunistically, especially given the volatility of the market and what that maybe means for kind of value generation for both upstream and downstream?

Richard Kruger: This has been a really fun area. And of course, it gets back to that, again, the predictability and stability of the underlying assets. And sometimes, Dennis, we'd rather be lucky than good. And in this case, we -- a few years ago, we started to look at the opportunities beyond our core domestic markets. You've heard the story about how Dave came in and we philosophically changed our strategy on sales and said, run our facilities full out, we will find profitable homes for that. That extended beyond Canada, whereas in the '24 I-Day, we said we could market in 21 countries. This year, we said 45 countries. Did we have a vision that we would necessarily do that?

No, not necessarily. But with events in the world, started by Russia, Ukraine, now in the Middle East, as we've had those opportunities and as we've locked in logistical capabilities, not only pipeline access to the coast, but you mentioned time charters. We've got what now 9 time charters that can be in crude or product service off of the coast. I mentioned how export volumes are up 80% year-on-year. These have -- where typically an export market is a market of last resort. You kind of get your barrel there because you don't have a better home for it. Those markets now have been particularly valuable because of acute shortages.

So that this full holistic integrated model extends well beyond upstream and downstream. It is logistics. It is markets, it's customers abroad, and that is an area we have changed materially. But here again, our rallying cry is we're not done yet. We keep seeing opportunities. Our traders, both particularly in Calgary and Houston, we've got some folks in London as well. They're extremely sophisticated on the markets we compete in. We're not trying to be a global trader, but the markets we compete in, they're extremely knowledgeable, seeing opportunities. And it's one of the reasons you see if you start doing realizations per barrel, this and that because those profits we put back into the business that generated them.

You have seen and you will continue to see premium prices for Suncor production and products because of that level of sophistication. It is -- we have a lot of fun with it, candidly. And we have -- we believe we'll continue to create more value that our peers are unable to replicate.

We -- if you take 2028, the assets that we are looking to sell will be about 40,000 barrels a day of our -- of the grand total. And then so the 100 becomes 60. And our confidence in either the breakeven or the free funds growth remained because on May -- March 31, folks saw a snapshot in time, but this organization continues to work and make things better.
