Or is it the debottlenecking and the capacity that's actually increased in which case, what does that imply for your dividend breakeven trajectory? That's 2 questions, I guess.

Richard Kruger: Thanks, Doug. Every time I go out there and make a commitment, these son of the guns that I'm sitting around the table with prove me wrong because they do better. We rerated our downstream flow 466,000 barrels a day to 511,000, the full capacity. And this guy sitting next to me to the left, he's been telling me that lately we've had days north of 520,000. And it was like I thought capacity was 511. So things keep getting better. But you're exactly right. As that continues, that breakeven, which for us, of course, includes our full dividend, we continue to drive it down. The downstream kind of subsidizes or enhances that breakeven.

So as we said the new year -- new plan this year was going to be going from around 43 to 38 this year, in part because of some special circumstances, we're going to achieve more than we thought we would have achieved this year. We're not necessarily sure if those will -- that will endure over time. But these fundamental improvements, whether it's debottlenecking, those incremental barrels, they greatly add to our ability to drive down that breakeven. And I think the 10% dividend increase is illustrative of the confidence that we have going forward. We've been kind of 5% year after year, roughly equal to the fraction of shares we've been buying back.

So Peter ramped up the buybacks to $750 million here. The dividend is going up by 10%. The 10% probably is a pretty good indication that with the amount of shares we think we'll be buying back and our confidence in the underlying business, the -- you can continue to expect further shareholder returns, whether it be a dividend and/or buybacks.

Douglas George Blyth Leggate: I guess we'll wait for the update. But Rich, my follow-up, I'll try and ask this as succinctly as I can. But years ago, we all used to think about pre-royalty and post-royalty payouts and how they were ring-fenced and so on. And with the tax change in September, clearly, you're getting accelerated -- I don't want to call it tax shield, but depreciation that maybe makes the previous discussion somewhat less relevant. And I guess what I'm going with this is when you laid out your strategy through 2028, you didn't have that tax treatment in your capital plan.

So I'm wondering in the context of what you just answered before about maybe you want to look at growth options, has the tax treatment changed your thoughts on how you -- whether you decide to go after more growth?

Richard Kruger: What the tax treatment fundamentally does, we're -- under current rules or we're able to ultimately depreciate our investments. It's just the time at which we can depreciate them. So if you do that over a 10-year period or a 3 -- I'm making this up or a 2- or 3-year period, it enhances the calculation of a rate of return, and it can accelerate a payout of an investment. So fundamentally, these accelerated depreciation rules help derisk long-term capital-intensive investments. Are they game changers in terms of do you do something or not do something? Maybe, but I don't think it fundamentally changes the long-term investment profile, say, wow, we will now do a whole bunch more.

But if you couple accelerated depreciation with an incentivized royalty system that starts to do some of the same things, if you clear up some of the regulatory complexities that would extend approval time frames upfront, you start coupling several of these things together, which are all part of the component parts of the MOU. Now you're changing the fundamental underlying fiscal and regulatory regime. And yes, that, in aggregate, can lead us to be more ambitious, more aggressive on long-term capital investments. Any one item is nice but probably on its own, not sufficient to materially alter the capital allocation framework.

Operator: One moment for our next question, and that will come from the line of Menno Hulshof with TD Securities.

Menno Hulshof: I'll start with a question on your global markets push. It didn't look like you were impacted in any significant way by the spike in freight rates in the quarter. And you did touch on some of this, but can you just elaborate on how the freight rate risk is currently being hedged out through contracting and how that challenge is generally being managed? And while we're at it, could you maybe put the bookends on sort of the number of cargoes that potentially get shipped in Q1 and -- call it, Q4 and Q1? And anything else within your global marketing push that you would want to flag?

Richard Kruger: Dave, why don't you take that? You and your team manage those for us.

Dave Oldreive: Yes, sure. And thanks, Menno. Rich mentioned our 9 time chartered vessels, which we fortuitously locked in before the rates went up dramatically. We're able to use those vessels for crude, particularly off the West Coast that goes to typically China or into the California markets. And we're seeing massive savings relative to current spot freight rates, and we take that back as our netback. We also have 4 MR vessels. Those are 300 kbd product vessels, mostly working off the West Coast to move diesel to markets. And same thing, we're seeing much lower freight rates, which helps us with our netbacks. Combine that with our advantaged logistics, we get really good value for our diesel sales.

If you think about export cargoes, we exported 92 cargoes year-to-date. That's about 60% more than we did in 2025 as a whole. What we do is we optimize based on our product netbacks, our alternatives domestically, and we balance between diesel and jet mostly. There's very little gasoline that we export. And we will optimize that based on price, based on market conditions and hard to say what Q4 and Q1 will bring, but we will make sure we optimize that to maximize value to Suncor in the current market.

Richard Kruger: Without saying, it's been a huge part of our performance this year.

Richard Kruger: Having that level of flexibility. And although the terms on those time charters are proprietary just for competitive purposes, they don't go forever. But we have that well into next year, we'll still have those before any of those will be looked at being renewing and things. And that gets back to that comment I made earlier. Sometimes we'd rather be lucky than good, and we took a lot of these actions, not anticipating the unique benefits we'll see now, but they have been extremely valuable for us. And I think in the quarters ahead, they're going to continue to be.

Menno Hulshof: Okay. And then I guess the second question is for Peter on the balance sheet. You talked about net debt falling a lot in the quarter. Like a lot of everybody else, we have clear line of sight to a net cash build. And given I've chatted with you about this in the past, but it seems like that is more of an output rather than something that the company wants to get to. So how are you thinking about sort of free cash allocation to the extent that oil prices and crack spreads remain elevated? I think there's probably limits to how much you want to grow. You recently increased the monthly buyback to $750 million.

How should we be thinking about that into 2027?

Peter Zebedee: Yes. Thanks a lot, Menno. And obviously, the balance sheet is in exceptional shape right now. And as we spoke about before, our philosophy on share buybacks has always been to buy back proportionate to our overall dividend. We're certainly doing that right now. And so that philosophy remains unchanged. We believe in returning excess funds to shareholders. We're always going to maintain the flexibility to respond to any material changes that may happen in the market. But this is the power of Suncor. This is the power of the integration that we bring to the table, and that's to provide reliable and predictable and ratable shareholder returns through the cycle, and you can count on us to continue that.

Richard Kruger: And Menno, maybe if I just add one other point to that. If we choose to grow faster than we outlined in our I-Day plan, the incremental capital that we're looking at is not overwhelming in any regard. So if the business environment stays strong and we would choose to invest more in the near term, the ability to return cash, the reliable and growing dividend and material buybacks, we think we're going to be able to do all of that. We don't have any particular goal or driver to build up a war chest of cash for any particular reason with a net debt at or near or below 0.

We have a lot of flexibility for whatever we choose to do. So you can interpret that as there'll be continued material cash return to shareholders, in particular, that incremental dollar via buybacks.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Manav Gupta with UBS.

Manav Gupta: Rich, you kind of talked about who made the family photo and who did not, but there were a couple of assets, I think, Hebron and Hibernia, which did make the family photo. And I'm trying to understand what drove the decision to keep those members in the family photo.

Richard Kruger: Hebron and Hibernia, of course, they're non-operated. And a big part of who's in the family photo and how close you snuggle up to me and my wife is what do you bring to the party? And can we add value to what you do? Hebron and Hibernia bring a lot to the party. They're longer life. They're a stable operation, a rock-solid operator who knows how to operate in the offshore quite well. And the -- fundamentally, we cash dividend checks each month from them, and they run it really well. So they add material cash flow. It's not to say the other -- the assets we're looking to sell don't, but they're not our core competency.

I don't think people buy Suncor because we operate a single FPSO off of the East Coast. So there are some distinctions there. And we've always talked about the East Coast is really a tale of two cities. There's the platforms that have run in Hibernia and the floaters, and we make -- we look at them in different ways and make different decisions based on how we see them.

Manav Gupta: My quick follow-up here is we are seeing WCS differentials widen. But given your refining capacity integration and the diesel margin, the impact of those differentials will be minimal for you compared to your peers. Can you talk about that?

Richard Kruger: Yes. You hit on it well. Our level of sensitivity or immunity to differential is uniquely low relative to a peer set. And the -- everyone is talking about what's going on. It's not so much that there's -- the pipes are overstuffed, so you can't get more out. It's some of this unique freight situation you're seeing in the Gulf Coast. There's a Venezuelan crude. There's a number of other factors here. So yes, they've certainly widened. Although the underlying WCS price, still at a historic level is quite high, we don't see this as kind of the new norm. We don't see these widening differentials as enduring.

But while they do, we are less affected by them than the rest of our peer group. Again, keep going back to that unique construct of our upstream and downstream asset base.

Operator: And one moment for our next question. That will come from the line of Patrick O'Rourke with ATB Cormark.

Patrick O'Rourke: Obviously, you've covered a lot of ground throughout the entire business, particularly the downstream. So that's been terrific. Maybe I'll keep it brief here then. When I look at year-to-date capital spend and we think about the normal cadence for Q4, it seems like it puts you down 1 or 2 paths here. One path where you're at or below the low end of your full year CapEx guide or another path where maybe you start preinvesting in 2027 and some of the strategic initiatives you've spoken to. I guess as of where we sit today, which path would you think you'd prefer to deviate down?

Richard Kruger: Yes. Fair question, Patrick. And we are tracking toward the low end of guidance on the capital. And in part, we didn't talk about it a lot in the second quarter, but these unique rain events also slowed some of our capital activity that involves moving dirt, things because of the weather conditions. So we're tracking to the low end. Given where we are, we've been asking ourselves some of the monies that we had planned on spending in '27. Does it make sense, given we have the capacity to move some of that to '26? If it makes sense, we've been looking to do that. That's probably lost in the round off, though, it's not big, big numbers.

But we're -- we have said that we're planning a future at or below $6 billion in capital. That's still where we are. We'll have guidance here in about a month for the next year. I think you can probably guesstimate what you might see on the capital side of it. So we're just looking at are there good, thoughtful, wise things to do versus macro changes. And part of that -- make no mistake, part of that coming on the low end of guidance is continued good performance. We've talked about turnarounds. I just flagged 3 of them that were best ever.

So our organization continues to do a good job of being very thoughtful, frugal and wise with capital allocation, and that's part of the reason we're tracking to the low end.

Patrick O'Rourke: Okay. Great. And then just thinking -- you touched on it a little bit, but WCS differential here. You've touched on your time charters. I mean, typically, the locational discount has been sort of between Hardisty and the Gulf, but now it's between the Gulf and maybe other waterborne crude markets. Based on the assets you have to move barrels here, what sort of ability do you have to mitigate WCS differentials by, say, pushing those heavy barrels that are not upgraded further out the value chain here in the fourth quarter and into 2027?

Richard Kruger: Dave, do you want to comment on that?

Dave Oldreive: Yes, sure. Patrick, as you know, we export off of the West Coast on our TMX volumes, and we get to capture full market value for those products. We have commitments on pipe into the Gulf for some of our volumes. But at the end of the day, really -- and we'll maximize into our refineries. But make no mistake, we're always maximizing heavies and sours into our refineries regardless of where the diff is. It's pretty much always economic for us. So really, we see ourselves continuing to do more of the same in that space. And like Richard said, we're pretty indifferent to the WCS diff overall.

What we -- if the diff is wider, we make it up in the refining business or we make it up in our upgraders. We see it as pretty indifferent to our operation through the fourth quarter.

Richard Kruger: Because of those time charters, when and how we contracted them, we don't have that same exposure to the differentials on the heavy crudes that are exported because of our freight rates. That won't last forever, but we also don't think the current world we're in will last forever either.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Travis Wood with NBC Capital Markets.

Travis Wood: Apologies if this was touched on, I logged in a bit late. I think in the opening remarks, and you've done this last quarter as well, just continue to talk about efforts to capture global pricing largely through the refined product market given where global cracks are. But could you walk through some of the detail and maybe some color around what that is exactly and what you're debottlenecking, whether it's kind of egress to Tidewater to be able to export to those markets? And then what type of volume would we be thinking about in the product sales for Q3?

And what do you think that contributed on the margin for the quarter as well without giving away too many of the trade and marketing secrets, obviously?

Richard Kruger: Sure. Travis, we're going to cut you some slack for joining us late as long as you go back and listen in to the earnings call song on your own time. You've got to hear that. It's one for the ages. Dave, you want to comment on that?

Dave Oldreive: Yes. So Travis, we optimize our exports off both coasts, and we have some unique efficient logistics with rail to the West Coast and then ability to trade direct to customer through our own chartered -- time chartered vessels on the West Coast as well as the same thing on the East Coast. We have niche markets that we deliver to where we see a unique value for our products, which tend to be lower cloud into Alaska on the West Coast, and Scandinavia, Iceland, places like that on the East Coast. And then there's a big short in Central America that we have an established relationship with some counterparties there that is very profitable for us.

We see our ability to grow that materially. We've grown it already, particularly the West Coast volumes. And it has historically been a rail loading and unloading constraint, and we've been busting through that, and we think we have more room to go on that through the -- into the first quarter.

Richard Kruger: And then the setup you have, Dave, again, not to get into commercial terms, but that getting products railed to the West Coast, the way your team has set that up, that's quite competitive with pipe products to the West Coast.

Travis Wood: Okay. And are you able to share what type of volume we're thinking about versus kind of domestic consumption like using the 677 of sales for this quarter, how much would reach the Tidewater of that number approximately?

Dave Oldreive: Yes, Travis, we exported about 75,000 barrels a day year-to-date.

Richard Kruger: Out of the [600-plus] still more than 10%.

Dave Oldreive: And we have an opportunity to do more if the market directs us in that direction, we have opportunity to do more, and we have an opportunity to flex between diesel and jet molecules as well, depending on where the market goes.

Travis Wood: Round numbers, we'll give a little more -- round numbers of that. A little less than half of that export has been -- if I have numbers right, has been crude and a little bit more than half products. Is that about right?

Richard Kruger: That's the product volume, sorry.

Dave Oldreive: The crude volume is in addition to that.

Richard Kruger: You're using ships for the crude, that's just the product.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Lydia Gould with Goldman Sachs.

Lydia Gould: Could you talk more about costs and how you're driving improvements in your operating costs across assets or any other areas of the business where you see opportunities to take out costs or drive structural efficiencies?

Richard Kruger: Sure. I'll make a general comment, and then I'm going to turn it to Adam, particularly in the mining side of it. We recognize you got -- you have to identify who you are, what you are. We're a global commodity that is cyclical in nature. We generally can't control the prices of our products. So we have to just have an endless, ruthless, unwavering commitment to cost management. For us, our refineries are extremely competitive. Our upstream is 2 components. It's a large and growing in situ and it's the large mining. The mining has a higher ongoing operating cost structure.

So Adam, why don't you share some of the things we're doing there to just contain, control, reduce cost in the upstream mining sector in particular.

Adam Albeldawi: Yes. So in the upstream, and Rich spoke about this already, when you look at the 2 main businesses, the in situ and the mining pieces, the in situ assets are already at a very competitive top quartile cost perspective. There is always work we are doing to continue to drive that down. But the big opportunity for us in the upstream is in the mining business. And when you look at the cost that we have in the mining business, there's a number of things we are doing to drive those costs down further.

I could speak about a number of examples to increase our productivity, but perhaps the example I'll speak to is the work we're doing to scale our autonomous haulage system. So you may recall that we have scaled and we have deployed AHS, autonomous haulage system, at our base plant operations. We have around 140 trucks or so ultra-class trucks fully autonomous. In addition to the increased safety performance we get from that, we are seeing a reduction in our operating costs resulting from the deployment of AHS. So the decision has been made to now deploy AHS and scale AHS at the Syncrude Mildred Lake facility.

We currently have just under 30 trucks kitted up with AHS at Mildred Lake. And by the end of this year, we will have close to 40 trucks kitted with AHS and in operation. So that is an example of the work we're doing in our mining business to continue to drive our productivity up and reduce our costs.

Richard Kruger: Yes. Thanks, Adam. So just to add to that, really 2 big levers, productivity in mining, little things make big differences with a large fleet and then technology. AHS is a technology on it. So those are the 2 big levers we're operating, and we know and internally, our mining has to be cost competitive to attract capital. And the teams understand that and are working hard to do that.

Operator: I'm showing no further questions in the queue at this time. I would now like to turn the call over to Mr. David Johnson for any closing remarks.

David L. Johnson: Thank you, everyone, for joining the call this morning. If you have any follow-up questions, please don't hesitate to reach out to our team. Operator, you can end the call.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you all for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3160. AI Data Centers Have a PR Problem. OpenAI Is Proposing a Rebrand

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

As part of the company's post-midterms marketing campaign, data centers could be called “AI compute campuses.”

OpenAI is shifting its marketing strategy after the US midterm elections conclude this week, proposing to rebrand its data centers as “AI compute campuses.” The creator of ChatGPT is preparing a public relations campaign that could include regulatory lobbying and efforts to rehabilitate AI’s image, according to Axios.

The push coincides with a potential blue wave in Congress. OpenAI Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane is reportedly trying to steer the AI policy debate and to send a message that “AI should be built by and for people,” as Axios reports.

The effort is a response to an increasingly enraged electorate, as backlash to AI data center construction becomes a unifying issue across party lines. A July Gallup poll found that as many as 70% of US adults are opposed to local data center construction, including Democrats, Republicans and independents.

Supporters of AI data centers often argue that the construction and operation of these massive AI server farms bring job growth to local communities. But studies show that employment is limited, and in some cases temporary. Residents continue to rally against the environmental impacts of water contamination, the burning of fossil fuels and noise pollution.

Lehane told Axios that OpenAI views the conversation as healthy and that “communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects.” The company is trying to reframe AI adoption as a means to access economic opportunities.

OpenAI’s new PR campaign aligns with Silicon Valley’s effort to repackage the controversial technology so it can move full speed ahead with building more data centers, which the White House has touted as vital engines for the US economy. President Donald Trump’s recent move to rename AI as “super intelligence” was another bid to dress up the capabilities of frontier labs, which have been under increased financial scrutiny by investors.

A representative from OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

OpenAI’s post-midterms marketing package includes implementing speed limits and mandatory safeguards for AI model development, largely echoing Anthropic’s “pacing” talking points. The company is also trying to shape the international standards that dictate the technology’s development.

Up to now, a lack of regulatory oversight has left top AI labs largely unchecked, leading to incidents where frontier models slipped past flimsy safety guardrails and caused real-world disruptions across the web.

OpenAI’s lobbying strategy for an alleged “human-centered” path based on “trust” fits squarely in the company’s data center rebrand — all calculated to help deflect public criticism. If the company publicly advocates slowing its own AI development, it can be more effective in what critics call “regulatory capture,” a tactic that gives large AI companies significant advantages.

In other words, if OpenAI helps write the rules meant to govern the industry, it can shape regulations to protect its market dominance. If frontier labs are considered the experts in constraining the industry, they can create a legal moat around themselves, making it more difficult for smaller competitors to enter the AI industry, while protecting their bottom lines from any real damage.

The Trump administration has been a major boon to the “Magnificent Seven,” the group of major tech companies that heavily influence the S&P 500 and global financial markets. After cozying up to the White House during the past two years, the most influential figures in Silicon Valley have been rewarded with a lax regulatory environment and expensive federal contracts.

Many of the biggest tech and AI companies donated millions of dollars to the president’s inaugural fund and, more recently, to his $330 million White House ballroom project. (Apple and Nvidia were among the top contributors, at $25 million each.)

As it stands, Trump is working directly with AI companies to define security threats and respond on their own terms. If the political tide turns in DC, however, it would make sense for Big Tech to make contingency plans for operating in a potentially less favorable environment. Democratic politicians have generally eyed the AI gold rush with greater outward skepticism and scrutiny, with some members of Congress even backing a resolution opposing AI company bailouts in the event of a financial bubble popping.

Lehane told Axios he believes AI will be the primary issue voters care about in the next presidential election cycle, and that the midterms are a “bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028.” If nothing else, OpenAI is angling to make new political alliances before that time comes.

#3159. Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.

I review the cameras, drones, instant cameras, and everything in between here at Tom's Guide. Everyone needs an easy-to-use, no-frills camera for capturing life's candid moments. The Kodak Charmera is a cute little camera that you can take practically anywhere with you. CFExpress cards are essential for videographers, too, so I'd highly recommend grabbing one for them.

Before you ask, no, you cannot have "too many SD cards" in your life — trust me, I have at least four and wish I had more! It's compatible with most camera shoulder strap loops thanks to its double-ended metal connecting O-ring, and it looks really good and premium, too.

Some photographers prefer a wrist strap over a neck strap as these straps keep the camera in or near hand at all times, and the K&F CONCEPT Camera Wrist Strap is a solid choice. It has a non-chafing design, and the anti-release quick release buckle stays locked while you shoot. It also enables you to quickly switch between handheld, tripod and chest mount setups.

The DJI Mic Mini is the ideal first microphone upgrade for new content creators who want to boost the quality of their audio, and a fine choice for more experienced creators who need a tiny microphone. This mic system is modular so can be scaled to your needs. It packs two levels of noise cancellation, and its omnidirectional mic works great for general content creation.

Every photographer needs a backpack that can safely store their gear and make it easy to transport. This K&F CONCEPT Camera Backpack is lightweight, durable, and multi-functional. It's small and compact, so can be stored easily in a backpack.

ND filters come in various levels of light reduction. This one from K&F CONCEPT is available in lots of thread sizes for different lenses, so make sure to find out the thread of your photographer buddy’s favorite lens.

Every photographer needs a camera and lens cleaning kit, and this one from Altura Photo is a great choice. Here's a silly, whimsical gift for the photographer in your life who already has everything: a lens-shaped coffee mug! I've always wanted one, to be honest, and might have to share this gift guide to drop a hint to my partner...

Because drones are small, they use microSD cards to store footage on, and trust me, you don't want to be caught out in the field without one. The SanDisk Ultra microSD Card 256GB is a great gift for pilots, offering read speeds up to 150 MB/s. It's compatible with most modern drones.

If you or your loved one want to display your instant prints around your house, now you can. The Orga'Neat Picture Holder is spacious enough to hold a 2x3-inch mini print, and it has a see-through case so everyone can admire the time you went skydiving in the Maldives.

The Polaroid Now and Now+ Filter Set is perfect for those who own either of those cameras. There are five creative filters in the box, including starburst, red vignette, orange, blue and yellow, and these can help photographers get creative with their shots.

If you've got a teen in your life, and they love LED lamps and instant cameras, you can combine their adoration for both with this 50 LED 5m Photo Clips String Lights set. It's battery powered and comes with a remote that lets you swap between different lighting modes.

Who says your furry friend can't join in on the holiday fun? This Dog Harness GoPro Mount is ideal for those with dogs (or cats, even) and a GoPro action camera. Your pet can wear it and then record the world from their POV. Trust me, it'll make for very cute videos.

#3157. This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You won't see the 'suspended' sign because it's not meant for you.

KELA researchers have exposed an active financial-scam infrastructure that hosts hundreds of fraudulent websites capable of faking their own suspensions to stay online. As of Oct. 25, 2026, 248 financial scam and phishing domains tied to 189 major US banks and financial services have been linked to the same infrastructure.

According to the cybersecurity firm’s report, published on Tuesday, the “Suspended” infrastructure operation runs websites that have cloned the official domains of victim organizations, with a particular focus on business banking. Many domains use the [keyword]-[bank].com format, slotting in keywords such as “secure,” “disable,” “protect,” and “cancel.”

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

A handful of servers spread across two shared hosting providers run the backend of Suspended infrastructure, which has also been tied to phishing campaigns targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and government services in the UK, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand. As a result, the researchers believe that either a single operator is behind the setup or that the server infrastructure is part of a wider phishing-as-a-service platform.

This phishing campaign stands out because of how the cybercriminals behind the scam are protecting it: by issuing takedown notices.

When you visit a website and see a message that it has been taken down or suspended, it’s usually because the domain has been associated with malicious or illegal activity, including phishing and scams. Law enforcement agencies, often with help from technology firms, find these websites, obtain the necessary court orders, and seize the infrastructure or accounts behind them to force a suspension through a registrar or hosting provider.

You see the notice, you move on — and this also goes for scanners and security teams.

However, in this case, the scam artists created a mechanism to show it themselves, to avoid being flagged and taken down. But it’s when they show it that matters.

The false suspension notice appears deceptively simple at first glance. A phishing kit embedded in the domain registers the IP address of each visitor, and on their second visit, they are shown a fake “account suspended” page. The kit is disguised as a challenge page similar to those legitimately used by Cloudflare.

Researchers also detected other decoys, including “Sorry, you’ve been blocked” notices, blank pages, and redirections to Google. Some pages also have reCAPTCHAs, and the researchers detected scripts that block browser developer tools, likely to slow analysis.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how

But why show fake suspension notices in the first place? To scanners and cybersecurity teams, it looks like someone else has already dealt with the malicious domain, and they can move on to the next suspicious website.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down,” KELA says. “A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team or a takedown provider checks a reported site and then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown.”

As shown in the image below, while scanners would detect a suspension notice, victims would still see the cloned website, complete with lures to entice them into entering their information, leading to financial fraud and potentially identity theft. After all, one visit is enough.

As of this writing, there are 248 live domains, plus those taken offline after the researchers disclosed their findings to law enforcement; over 300 scam domains have been hosted on the same infrastructure since May this year. Unfortunately, this phishing campaign remains active, with new domains appearing every day.

One lead could reveal the operator: a remote desktop connection to the malicious infrastructure through a standard UK home broadband connection, but it has not been verified.

Use a phishing link checker to verify whether a URL is trustworthy, and remember that any email or message claiming to be from your bank may be fraudulent.

Typical signs of a bank phishing email include:

When it comes to organizations, KELA has released a free Bank Phishing Check tool that compares official domains and organizations against the websites uncovered during the firm’s research.

#3156. Google Is Forcing Schools to Choose Between Its Search Engine and AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Experts weigh in on the promises and pitfalls of Google’s new policy, which leaves schools unable to use Search unless they opt into its AI tools.

Google will automatically turn off its AI products for K-12 student accounts, requiring school administrators to manually opt in before students can use the technology, the company announced in a blog post on Tuesday. But there’s a big catch: If schools choose not to enable AI, students won’t be able to access Google Search.

In August, the company’s AI products were automatically enabled in Google Classroom, Google’s free learning management system for students of all ages. Tuesday’s announcement reverses that decision.

In October, tech and child-safety organizations wrote an open letter to 150 US school districts and their leadership, requesting that districts disable Google Gemini AI on school devices, concluding that “children are at risk of being harmed.”

“After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search,” wrote Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education.

For student accounts with Google Search enabled, Gemini will feature a new Guided Learning study tool. The interactive feature helps students solve homework problems step by step rather than providing direct answers. Later this month, at select US schools, Guided Learning will launch as a pilot program to collect feedback before rolling out to more schools.

According to a 2024 Google blog post, over 150 million teachers and students worldwide use Google Classroom and Assignments, the company’s assignment distribution and grading app.

A 2025 New York Times survey sent to the 20 largest US school districts found that Google’s Chromebooks, which start at $179, are the most common device in classrooms, with about 80% of teachers reporting that their school district provided Chromebooks for students.

The default search engine on Chromebooks is Google Search.

New York City Public Schools, the largest US public school district, is a Google client. When asked for comment, a NYC Public Schools spokesperson pointed to NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s X post.

“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” Mamdani wrote in the Tuesday post. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.”

The second largest US district, the Los Angeles Unified School District, is also a Google client.

A Los Angeles Unified spokesperson told CNET in an email that the organization is reviewing Google’s announcement and its potential implications for schools, educators and students. The district believes emerging technologies, including AI, have the potential to enhance teaching and learning when introduced thoughtfully, responsibly and with clear safeguards, the spokesperson said.

Ying Xu, an assistant professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and founder and director of the Harvard Child-Centered AI Lab, told CNET in an email that Google’s Guided Learning tool could buffer some of the negative consequences of using general-purpose AI tools.

“But to me, the deeper question is: Do students still need to learn how to search for information using traditional search engines?” Xu said.

In her work, Xu found that seeking information using traditional search engines, as opposed to AI models, involves different processes, ranging from how students formulate queries to how they evaluate information to how they integrate it from multiple sources.

“I’m a bit concerned that, even with Guided Learning, students may be losing opportunities to practice these important information-seeking skills,” said Xu. “One concern I have with Google’s announcement is whether schools will still have the option to support traditional information seeking without AI features.”

Until recently, the conversation focused on whether AI should be allowed in schools at all. Now, Google’s announcement is forcing schools to decide which specific AI features to use and under what conditions, without the support needed to make these decisions.

“I do think there’s a risk of widening inequalities here, as schools with more resources and technical expertise may be better positioned to navigate these decisions, while others may have fewer options,” Xu said.

However, she doesn’t think that moving away from Google entirely is necessarily the solution, especially for districts that already rely on its systems.

Instead, Xu thinks the type of support available to schools as they navigate AI-related decisions will be crucial.

“With or without Google’s decision about search functionality, the responsibility falls on schools to protect students’ right to learn from human teachers and peers in human-led classrooms,” said Jennifer L. Steele, a professor at American University’s Baker School of Education. “Tools like Gemini Guided Learning, which uses AI to walk students through difficult questions, are not the answer.”

When schools and teachers rely on tech companies to teach students how to use their AI tools and understand their strengths and weaknesses, that’s when problems occur, she said.

“If schools take that responsibility seriously, then how Google configures its apps won’t really matter,” Steele said.

When asked for a response to the backlash surrounding the decision to turn off its search engine for schools that reject its AI, a Google spokesperson pointed to the company’s X post stating that schools can choose to turn on Gemini, Gemini Notebook or Search individually.

However, that post doesn’t address the fact that AI Mode and AI Overviews will still be enabled alongside Google Search. So if schools don’t want AI enabled for students at all, they will still lose the ability to use the search engine.

A Google spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for further comment.

Tracy Pizzo Frey, a former Google managing director, wrote on LinkedIn that Google could allow schools to turn off AI Overviews, but instead is choosing to take search away from students.

Search engine DuckDuckGo, for instance, has noai.duckduckgo.com, its AI-free search engine that automatically disables all AI features and filters out AI-generated images.

“AI overviews is a search module like maps, flights or weather,” a DuckDuckGo spokesperson said in an email. “Google can determine when it shows up and when it doesn’t.”

Experts caution that educators can’t count on tech platforms to police themselves. Because AI tools are now permanent fixtures, schools must shape their own path forward.

The primary hurdle is an uneven playing field, where wealthier districts have the resources to adapt, leaving underfunded systems struggling to keep up.

#3154. 2 ETFs I'm Buying and Holding for Decades -- No Matter What the Market Does

Instead of picking stocks, I buy all the stocks. These two ETFs seem like solid long-term choices for buy-and-hold investors.

Being a "buy-and-hold" investor sounds simple, but it can be harder to do in real life. When stocks are wobbly, when the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 goes into a sell-off, when economists question the economic value of artificial intelligence (AI), it's easy to get nervous and make fear-driven moves based on short-term news.

But for most people who are not professional investors or money managers or hedge fund executives, the best investment strategy is often just to buy and hold. Buy stocks in a diversified portfolio like the S&P 500 index. Keep buying stocks as often as you can.

And then: hold them. Don't sell. Hold them for years -- five years, 10 years, or more. Don't try to day trade, don't try to move in and out of the market, don't try to sell your stocks based on a hunch about what the market will do tomorrow. If you're really in it for the long run, buy-and-hold investing can generate significant wealth for everyday investors.

My two favorite stock exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are low-cost index funds. They're simple. They're "boring." But these two ETFs together let me own basically all the stocks in the world.

Let's look at why I'm going to keep buying and holding the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI +1.54%) and the Vanguard Total International Stock ETF (VXUS +1.98%) for years to come -- through good times and bad, booms and busts.

Buying an S&P 500 ETF is a great way to quickly own a diversified portfolio of the 500 largest publicly traded companies in America. But the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI) is even more diversified than that. VTI owns 3,519 U.S. stocks. This fund has delivered average annual returns of 10.95% for the past five years.

Why do I want to own VTI instead of an S&P 500 ETF? Because I want all the small-caps and mid-caps, not just large-caps. Vanguard research forecasts that in the next 30 years, U.S. small-cap stocks could outperform U.S. large-cap stocks, and U.S. value stocks could outperform U.S. growth stocks.

I don't believe that the same stocks that are winning today are always going to keep winning forever. The market might rotate away from tech stocks. The biggest gains of AI tools might go to healthcare companies and banks, not necessarily to today's major tech names. In the long run, I'd rather own thousands of U.S. companies of all kinds, not just a few stocks in one volatile industry.

In case the current AI boom turns into a bear market for high-flying growth stocks, the value stocks and small-cap stocks in the VTI portfolio might help deliver steadier gains in the long run. I don't want to bet too much on any one U.S. stock or sector. VTI lets me hedge those risks. I'm not trying to beat the market. Instead, I will happily take whatever return the entire U.S. stock market will give me, and I'm going to keep buying and holding VTI.

Not only do I not know which stock or sector will be the best for the long run, I also don't know for sure if America will have the best stock market for the long run. It might. America has a dynamic economy. We work hard, we innovate, we create must-have technologies and powerful brands that keep consumers spending.

But what if the rest of the world goes on a long winning streak? What if America wobbles, or falls behind? What if the dollar loses its buying power against international currencies? In case any of those things happen, I want to own some international stocks as part of my diversified portfolio. The Vanguard Total International Stock ETF (VXUS) offers an impressive mix of 8,901 global stocks representing Europe (35.4% of the fund), the Pacific (29.3%), emerging markets (26.6%), and other regions of the world.

VXUS has delivered average annual returns of about 8.1% for the past five years. But its future could be brighter than the S&P 500. Along with U.S. small-caps and value stocks, Vanguard is bullish on international stocks. Its long-term outlook expects international stocks to outperform U.S. stocks by a substantial margin of 1.3% to 3.3% per year for the next 30 years.

There's no guarantee that either of these ETFs, or any stock or ETF, will be "safer" in case of a tech stock sell-off. It's also possible that today's biggest names in tech will keep winning and outperforming the rest of the market for the foreseeable future.

But I want to own everything: global stocks, U.S. stocks, small-cap, value, large-cap, and more. I don't know of a better way to lock in long-term gains from stock market investing than just to "buy all the stocks" and hold on to them for years to come.

Ben Gran has positions in Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF and Vanguard Total International Stock ETF. The Motley Fool has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3153. Shooting Video With Honor’s New Magic 9 Pro Max Lets You Feel Like a Movie Director

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Phone-maker Honor partners with the iconic cinema camera maker ARRI to enhance the look and color of videos recorded on its Magic 9 Pro Max.

While standing on the roof of the Griffith Observatory in Los Angeles for the first time, I pulled out my phone to commemorate the moment by filming a video that pans toward the Hollywood sign. And then I did it again, using a special cinema mode created by the legendary movie camera company ARRI to give it some old Hollywood flair. The second video had a grainier look and could have been shot in the 1960s, with the sky appearing teal.

This might look like a filter, but it’s actually ARRI’s Nostalgia look — one of many color configurations available on the company’s cinema cameras, which start at $80,000. I’m using it on a smartphone from the Chinese company Honor.

This Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, announced Wednesday, looks a lot like an iPhone 18 Pro Max, with a similar unibody metal design and two-tone back glass. I used the phone in a comforting moss green, but it also comes in shadow black and glacier silver.

Honor’s focus on video production underscores the increasing trend of smartphone use in studio environments. And the company is banking on its partnership with ARRI to help its Magic 9 Pro Max stand out among a number of phones with their own Hollywood pedigree — including the iPhone.

Even if you aren’t familiar with ARRI, you’ll likely know movies filmed with the company’s cameras, such as 2022’s Everything Everywhere All at Once and 1947’s Dark Passage, starring Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall. ARRI’s cameras are designed for movie sets and priced accordingly, costing $65,000 to upward of $95,000 new. Instead of creating a cheaper camera, ARRI is bringing its color technology to the Magic 9 Pro Max’s camera app, which includes a dedicated ARRI Cinema mode.

This cinema mode uses the phone’s 200-megapixel wide and 200-megapixel telephoto cameras and lets you capture video with a wider 2.39:1 aspect ratio — similar to what’s used in theatrical releases. Cinema geeks may be particularly interested in the mode’s access to ARRI’s Look Library and its ability to install LUT files. Some are preloaded, while others can be downloaded from Honor’s and ARRI’s websites.

To put it as simply as I can, Looks and LUT files allow you to record video with a variety of cinema-like looks, including settings that can closely mimic an ARRI Alexa camera.

During a media demonstration at ARRI’s Los Angeles facility, two different film sets were recorded by both an Alexa camera and a Magic 9 Pro Max with similar looks and LUT settings. Both sets had ideal lighting, but the recorded footage showed similar color shading and detail. An ARRI rep pointed out that you have to look at the fine details, like the shadows of a bookshelf, to see the differences between the phone and cinema camera. Clearly, the Alexa camera was far better at capturing the scene, as it should.

Using the Magic 9 Pro Max, I filmed my own faux rainy-evening scene featuring dark green walls, a brown set and two actors speaking to each other. While I do like the set’s movie-like look, I was more impressed when I shuffled through the different ARRI Looks while watching the sunset at Griffith Observatory. Like the iPhone’s Photographic Styles for still images, ARRI Looks offer plenty of choices for video, including several black-and-white options. It’s fun to know that they’re the same options available to camera teams using ARRI’s full-fledged cinema cameras.

Honor hasn’t shared the Magic 9 Pro Max’s price or release date, but it won’t be coming to the US. However, it does have quite the spec list beyond its ARRI Cinema mode, including a 6.8-inch display, an 8,000-mAh battery with 100-watt wired charging and 80-watt wireless charging. The phone’s powered by the new Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor.

A 50-megapixel ultrawide camera joins the wide and telephoto cameras, but it doesn’t support the ARRI Cinema mode. The 55-megapixel front-facing camera uses a square sensor, like Center Stage on recent iPhones, allowing vertical selfies whether you’re holding the phone vertically or horizontally. Honor said this is a first for Android. I’m hopeful that more Android phone companies will bring this feature to their front-facing cameras in 2027.

The phone also ships with Android 17 and Honor’s MagicOS 11 overlay (it looks a lot like iOS 27), and joins other Android phones with support for Apple’s AirDrop via Quick Share.

As it stands, Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max is being used in some baseball broadcasts, and the 2025 film 28 Years Later was shot primarily using the iPhone 15 Pro Max. Honor’s partnership with ARRI might lead to more cinema-quality features on smartphones, especially if more productions decide the pocket-sized camera is the right way to tell more big-screen stories.

Editors’ note: Mike Sorrentino’s travel costs for the Honor event were covered by Honor. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

#3152. Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver – but you have alternatives

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

One of Roku's most popular screensavers is about to make its last splash. Here’s how to switch before Dec. 1.

A fan-favorite Roku screensaver is going away, and users aren’t happy.

Over the last several days, users with the Aquatic Life aquarium screensaver set as the default have noticed a message appearing when the screensaver opens. “Starting Dec. 1, 2026,” the message reads, “the Aquatic Life screensaver will no longer be available, and your screensaver will switch to Roku City.”

Also: The free Roku City screensaver game has me hooked

The screensaver, which displays a digital aquarium with tropical fish swimming back and forth, was available as a downloadable theme pack and was a popular pick for many years.

Users on Reddit quickly lamented the loss in many posts, with dozens noting that the aquarium was part of their daily routine. Roku responded to one post, saying, “That makes sense, and we hear you. Aquatic Life has a lot of loyal fans, and we’re passing your feedback along to the team.” The post noted that when “the fish swim off,” Roku devices with Aquatic Life will switch to Roku City.

You can browse to Settings > Theme > Screensaver to find another theme.

Several online reports indicate that the removal is a licensing issue and that the creator of the screensaver posted on Reddit that he removed the license after Roku’s sale to Fox. That thread has now been deleted, so the comment is unavailable. Roku hasn’t issued any statement of its own about why, but I have reached out to ask. I’ve also reached out directly to the screensaver’s creator.

If you’re looking for the exact screensaver, it’s still available as a 2-minute clip on Roku’s YouTube channel. It takes a few extra steps, but if you want to keep the screensaver running on your TV, you can create a YouTube playlist with just that video, set it to loop, and use the YouTube app on Roku whenever you want to see it.

Even though the announcement of the screensaver’s departure happened less than 24 hours ago, the comments section of that video is packed with users begging Roku to keep Aquatic Life.

Also: I started clearing my Roku cache, and it fixed my biggest TV complaint

Alternatively, you could open one of the many YouTube videos that have aquarium displays and let one of them run for as long as you want.

There are also several dozen aquarium apps for Roku. I checked out several of them, and while they don’t look exactly like the Roku one, they do fill the void. Note that if you opt for one of these, most of them do have ads that play before the aquarium starts.

Lastly, you can download the original app for your phone or computer from SereneScreen.

#3150. The Gel That Became a Business

The problem with a cancer that keeps coming back.

Some cancers announce themselves with drama. Low-grade bladder cancer does the opposite. It is usually slow-growing and rarely life-threatening, which is the good news.

The hard part is that it tends to return. A patient has a tumor removed in a short operation under anesthesia. Months later, a follow-up camera exam finds another one, and then another procedure follows. For many people, that cycle continues for years.

Anyone who has watched a relative go through it knows the weariness. The medical risk is modest, but the burden of surveillance and repeat procedures is not.

That cycle is the opening UroGen Pharma (NASDAQ:URGN) saw. The company, listed on Nasdaq under the ticker URGN, sells treatments for cancers of the urinary tract. Its core idea is a better way to deliver an old drug.

The drug is mitomycin, a decades-old chemotherapy that is cheap and well understood. The problem was never the medicine. It was keeping it in contact with the bladder wall long enough to work, since the body flushes liquids out within hours.

UroGen mixes mitomycin into a gel that is liquid when cold and thickens at body temperature. It coats the bladder lining and releases the drug slowly over hours. The product is called ZUSDURI, approved by the FDA (the U.S. Food and Drug Administration) in 2025.

The results are encouraging. In the pivotal trials, roughly 72% of patients were still free of disease at 24 months. For a condition defined by recurrence, that is meaningful.

For the business, there is a second benefit. The treatment can be given in a urologist's own office, where about 70% of eligible patients are seen, instead of in a hospital operating room.

Biotech launches usually disappoint. Hospitals are slow, billing is tangled, and doctors are creatures of habit.

This one has worked. In the quarter just reported, UroGen's total revenue was $89.0 million, up from $27.5 million a year earlier. ZUSDURI alone brought in $68.0 million, up 35% from the prior quarter. Just a year ago it earned $1.8 million.

The company's loss shrank to match. The net loss was $1.5 million, compared with $33.3 million a year earlier. Management says it expects to turn a profit in the fourth quarter.

The most telling data is about doctors. Unique prescribers rose from 452 to 662 in a quarter, and repeat prescribers rose from 204 to 331, about half of the total.

That repeat figure matters because a doctor who tries a drug once is curious. A doctor who orders it again has decided it works in their practice.

One more detail: The number of active sites of care rose only modestly, from 1,444 to 1,538. Most of the growth comes from existing offices using it more, not from new offices signing on. That tends to be the sturdier kind of growth.

There was one operational change that helped. A permanent billing code, called a J-code (a unique identifier that tells insurers exactly which drug was administered), took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. Before it, urologists faced reimbursement friction. Now claims flow more smoothly.

UroGen's earlier product, JELMYTO, treats a rarer cancer of the upper urinary tract. It was the company's bread and butter. Management had hoped the new launch would pull it along, a so-called halo effect, where success with one product lifts its sibling.

That has not happened. In August, executives said there was no broad halo, the sales force was prioritizing ZUSDURI, and clinical trials might be enrolling patients who would otherwise have received JELMYTO.

The numbers have now caught up. Management cut its full-year JELMYTO forecast to about $90 million, from a prior range of $97 million to $101 million. That is below the $94 million it earned in 2025. Last quarter, JELMYTO sales were $21.0 million versus $25.7 million a year earlier, including a one-time $1.5 million charge.

This is not a catastrophe. It does mean the company's second pillar is eroding just as the first one rises.

ZUSDURI grew 73% in the previous quarter and 35% in this one. Percentages naturally fall as the base gets bigger, so dollars are the fairer test.

The drug added roughly $15 million in sales, then $21 million, then $18 million in successive quarters. The latest increment was smaller than the one before. One data point is not a trend, but it is the number for investors to watch.

The market appears to have the same worry. The stock rose to nearly $51 after the prior report, then gave back the entire gain, closing at $34.04 just before this one.

Management also declines to give a full-year ZUSDURI forecast. They said they would let demand trends develop first. That is honest, and also a reminder that the future here is still unknown to the people closest to it.

Management says it has enough money to reach profitability without selling more stock. The reasoning deserves a closer look.

The company ended the quarter with $90.5 million in cash and marketable securities. A quarter earlier it had $108.0 million, against total liabilities of $385 million and a shareholders' deficit of $132 million. Cash fell about $17 million in a quarter when the company nearly broke even.

Management points to $117 million in accounts receivable, which is money customers owe the company for products already delivered. That is more than a full quarter of revenue. It is earned on paper, but it is not cash until collected.

Two questions follow. How quickly do these customers pay? And how much product sits unused in distributors' warehouses, known as channel inventory? Revenue recorded on shipment can run ahead of actual patient use, and later reverse.

The company also carries fixed claims on its future. Interest on its long-term debt was $4.8 million for the quarter, and a financing arrangement with the investment firm RTW added $4.5 million in non-cash expense. In plain terms, the company has partly borrowed against its own success.

Here is the reason to stay interested. Operating leverage means that when costs are mostly fixed, extra revenue falls largely to profit.

Quarterly spending was $26.0 million on research and $47.2 million on selling and administration. That is about $73 million against $89 million in revenue from a product with a very high gross margin (the share of each sale left after the direct cost of making it).

If ZUSDURI keeps adding even $10 million a quarter, most of it lands as profit. Management is spending hard anyway, having raised full-year expense guidance to $260 million to $270 million. That is the right call if demand is durable, and a risk if it is not.

UroGen's protections are real. A new patent is expected to cover ZUSDURI and its successor, UGN-103, through July 2044.

UGN-103 is a next-generation version. Management has filed a New Drug Application, or NDA, the formal request for FDA approval. The agency's review deadline, called a PDUFA date (named for the Prescription Drug User Fee Act), is June 14, 2027, according to the company. If approved, it would need its own J-code.

The patent protects the gel, not the market. Larger companies are developing competing treatments in neighboring parts of bladder cancer. Johnson & Johnson currently has a drug-releasing device in late-stage trials for intermediate-risk disease.

Investors should read the company's quarterly report to the SEC (the Securities and Exchange Commission, the U.S. securities regulator), called a 10-Q. Look for four things:

The medicine is real, the launch is real, and patients are plainly being helped. The open question is whether the balance sheet and the share price were built for a launch that is maturing.

#3149. Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.
