#3148. Want a Challenge? Try These 10 Wordle-Like Word and Puzzle Games Now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Many of these games are free, and you can play them as many times as you want.

The popular word game Wordle is five years old, and it’s still popular. Josh Wardle launched the game in 2021 before The New York Times bought the game the following year. Since then, millions of people are estimated to play the game each day. If you want help with the daily game, CNET’s Gael Cooper has loads of tips and tricks to help you tackle each NYT Wordle puzzle, as well as solutions to each one.

Once you finish your Wordle, you’ll have to be patient and wait until the next day for the next puzzle. Thankfully, there are plenty of other word and puzzle games to choose from if you’re still craving a challenge. And some of these games let you play as many times as you want in a day.

Here are 10 other puzzle games you can play now for a fun challenge.

Another New York Times-owned puzzle, Connections is a tricky word game. “Players must select four groups of four words without making more than four mistakes,” the New York Times explained on X. There are also four color-coded difficulty levels for each game; yellow is the easiest, then green, then blue and finally purple. The game is also similar to the BBC quiz show Only Connect, and the show’s host took to X to point out the connection. See what I did there?

You can play Connections on any web browser, but you need a New York Times subscription (which starts at $1 a week) to play.

Strands is another New York Times-owned puzzle but this game resembles a word search more so than Wordle and Connections. This game presents a theme every day to help you find words in a grid. In Strands words can appear forward, backward, top-to-bottom or any number of ways in a traditional word search, and words can also form in the shape of an “L” or have a zigzag in them. When you find a word, tap the first letter and drag your finger to the other letters. Every letter in the puzzle is used, so if you still have letters that aren’t connected to words, you aren’t finished yet.

You can play Strands on any web browser but you need a New York Times subscription (again, $1 a week) to play.

You can play Quartiles on an iPhone or iPad but you need an Apple News subscription (which starts at $13 a month) to play.

Quordle has you solve four word puzzles at once, which sounds daunting.

Are you up for a challenge? If you love Wordle and want puzzle games that take more brain power, you’ll want to check out either Dordle, Quordle, Octordle or Sedecordle. Each of these word games resembles Wordle, but they add more rows, columns and words to solve. Each game requires you to simultaneously solve a different number of words at once: Dordle has you solving two words, Quordle four at once, Octordle eight at once and Sedecordle a whopping 16. Good luck.

You can play Dordle, Quordle, Octordle or Sedecordle on any web browser.

“Lewdle is a game about rude words,” this game’s content advisory reads. “If you’re likely to be offended by the use of profanity, vulgarity or obscenity, it likely isn’t for you.” Translation: It’s Wordle but with bad words. The words range from mild — like poopy — to words that would make a sailor blush. Thankfully, despite this game’s content warning, slurs are not included. Like Wordle, gray, yellow and green blocks are used in the same way and there’s only one puzzle per day. So go forth and let the bad words flow!

You can play Lewdle on any web browser. You can also download this game from Apple’s App Store or the Google Play store.

Not off to a great start with this Antiwordle puzzle.

Tired of seeing those gray, yellow and green blocks plastered all over your social media feed? Give Antiwordle a try. While Wordle wants you to guess a word in as few tries as possible, Antiwordle wants you to avoid the word by guessing as many times as possible. When you guess, letters will turn gray, yellow or red. Gray means the letter isn’t in the word and can’t be used again, yellow means the letter is in the word and must be included in each subsequent guess and red means the letter is in the exact position within the word and is locked in place. If you can use every letter on the keyboard without getting the word correct, you win. Honestly, I’ve found this version of Wordle to be much harder than the original.

You can play Antiwordle on any web browser.

Absurdle bills itself as the “adversarial version” of Wordle. While Wordle nudges you in the right direction with each guess, Absurdle is trying to avoid giving you the correct answer. According to the game’s website, “With each guess, Absurdle reveals as little information as possible, changing the secret word if need be.” Absurdle doesn’t pick a word at the beginning of the game for the player to guess. Instead, it uses the player’s guesses to narrow its list of words down in an effort to make the game go as long as possible. The final word might not even include a yellow letter from one of your earlier guesses either. You can guess as many times as you want, which is helpful, and the best score you can get is four. Have fun!

You can play Absurdle on any web browser.

For more word game fun, check out CNET’s Wordle tips and everything you need to know about the word game. You can also check out what to know about the other New York Times-owned games, Connections and Strands.

To get this incredible deal, there is a catch you need to know about: you must port in your existing phone number and prepay for two months of Boost Mobile’s Unlimited Premium plan. That plan runs $120 for the two-month period, which brings your out-of-pocket checkout total to $149.99 plus tax. Once you meet those two requirements, you get the Motorola Razr (2025) for just $29.

As for the phone itself, it remains an excellent flip phone even with newer devices on the market. That comes down to the sheer utility it holds over traditional slabs, largely thanks to its 3.6-inch external display. Beyond running full apps, another major benefit is effortless one-handed use — you aren't stretching your fingers across a massive screen, making it ideal for subway commuters holding onto a handrail with the other hand.

It’s also a fantastic tool for content creators. Pairing the main rear cameras with the outer display lets you frame high-quality selfies and video on the fly, while the folding hinge lets you prop the phone up in various flex modes for completely hands-free recording.

The main drawback of the Motorola Razr (2025) is its MediaTek Dimensity 7300X processor. While perfectly capable of handling everyday tasks and social feeds, it lacks the graphical muscle to push smooth frame rates in demanding 3D games. Low-light photography can also be hit-or-miss compared to pricier flagships.

Even so, snagging the Razr for $29 through Boost Mobile is a steal. While you are locked into paying for two months of premium service upfront, you can always drop down to a cheaper plan after the initial 60 days. Just keep in mind that if you plan on taking the phone elsewhere, Boost Mobile requires 12 months of active service before it unlocks the device.

#3146. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3145. I tried Sonos’ latest app features – these 2 small upgrades fix big annoyances

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Home Entertainment > Speakers

New Sonos software and firmware updates are rolling out. Here's what you can expect.

Sonos’ promise to release its AI-upgraded voice assistant is nearing its “Fall 2026” deadline, and before fans can use the highly anticipated update, the company continues to make small improvements to its app and player features.

Also: Sonos Ace Ultra vs. Sonos Ace: Who should upgrade

This time, Sonos added System Health, a new in-app page to access a more comprehensive view of your system(s), though it’s only available on iOS for now. However, a new blog post states that iOS and Android users can expect volume presets, more interaction with the app miniplayer, and spoken voice prompts for the Ace Ultra headphones.

I poked around in the app and tried some of the latest features. Here’s what to expect.

If your system consists of multiple speakers, a mix of modern and legacy speakers, or multiple systems, you’re bound to experience a hiccup and be unsure which speaker is causing the issue.

It usually takes me some time to Google my issue and scroll through the Sonos Community forum, Reddit, or the official Sonos help documents to find suggestions and troubleshoot it. Sonos’ new System Health feature provides an overview of your systems, showing your network status and name, as well as the number of speakers and rooms in each system.

Also: I used Sonos’s new home theater feature – it’s a competition killer

According to Sonos’ blog post, System Health can detect a Double Network Address issue, which usually occurs when you introduce a new router to your home or plug a mesh system into your ISP-provided router. The result is two home networks, and your Sonos speakers will split their connection between them, flagging “System not found” errors, missing speakers, or connection dropouts.

System Health is in the Settings tab, under the Help Center menu.

Once you tap into your system, you can see all of its speakers, with unconnected speakers bearing a red “Not connected” badge, and wireless speakers showing a black “Powered off” badge when they’re off.

Then, you can see a speaker’s connection information, including status, Wi-Fi signal strength, signal/noise ratio, frequency, IP address, and more. You can also find its volume output, Trueplay setup status, line-in connection, voice control status, serial number, hardware model and version, and which Sonos platform it operates on.

System Health can also show you your account details, Sonos ID, Controller ID, and your current app build version. System Health comes after Sonos updated the System Updates tab, which now displays an overview of your app, system, and headphone update status. This page also links to the Sonos release notes.

Sonos’ blog post states that this feature is new and still open to change, especially if the Sonos community has a particularly overwhelming response to it. The blog post also disclaims that this feature is a first look, not a deep dive.

However, after a brief first use, I see it as a great way to quickly access all the details you need about your systems and speakers, especially if you’re doing some rewiring, moving a speaker to a new room, or general troubleshooting.

System Health is rolling out to iOS users first. I updated my Sonos app in the App Store and was able to access it, but Sonos’ blog post states that this update is a phased rollout.

Updates to the Sonos app and its player are a long time coming. After receiving several new ways to control your speakers’ volume (I think we’re up to three), Sonos is realizing that granular volume control is a high priority for many Sonos users, including me.

The in-app volume dial is cool, and the interactive volume scrubber is a nice touch, but there’s nothing more jarring than wanting to play some tunes on my kitchen counter speaker, only for it to blast at 80% from when my husband was watching football the night before.

Sonos’ latest big update to volume this time around is Presets, a way to start playback in a specific room at a set volume. I haven’t found this feature in my app’s update yet, but I think it’s because my hardware needs an update. Presets will be available on iOS and Android.

Fortunately, I did use another update to the Sonos miniplayer: swipe to skip. What a teeny, tiny but useful feature. It works just like the miniplayer in Apple Music and Spotify; when the app is open, you can swipe left to skip to the next song.

One major caveat: swiping right to replay a track doesn’t work — at least not yet. Swiping both ways seems like a given to me, so it feels odd that you can’t. Still, being able to swipe the miniplayer to the next track is better than always having the main player open to toggle tracks. This feature is also coming to iOS and Android.

Sonos’ miniplayer is getting so much better; you can swipe to the next track and easily control volume from it, even when you have the Ace or Ace Ultra connected (I tried). The in-app volume dial also works with Sonos headphones.

Also: Sonos Play vs. Sonos Move 2: Why I’d go with the $200 cheaper Bluetooth speaker

Speaking of the Ace Ultra, a firmware update is available. A new Vocal Guidance feature can announce the battery percentage when you power on the headphones, when the audio mode changes from ANC to Transparency, and which device your headphones are connected to via Bluetooth.

It feels like this update is the final stretch before Sonos 27voice arrives, as the release notes suggest. It appears Sonos is laying the groundwork for speakers to support the AI-powered voice assistant in Early Access. Once it’s here, I’ll test it as soon as I can.

#3144. Dine Brands (DIN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Dine rejected a buyout bid as dual-brand restaurant expansion continued.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Dine Brands Global, Inc. (DIN +3.34%) reported third-quarter results driven by the strategic expansion of its company-owned restaurant portfolio and the continued rollout of its dual-brand concept. Management indicated that performance remained consistent with consumer behavior patterns observed over the past three years, characterized by a persistent focus on value propositions and stable average check levels. The company is prioritizing investments in restaurant remodels and technological enhancements, particularly in the catering and off-premise channels, while maintaining its asset-light franchising model. During the quarter, the board of directors rejected an unsolicited acquisition proposal and implemented a stockholder rights plan to protect shareholder interests.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Dine Brands Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press *11 on your telephone. If your question has been answered and you would like to remove yourself from the queue, simply press *11 again. As a reminder, today's program is being recorded. And now I would like to introduce your host for today's program, Matthew Lee, senior vice president, finance and investor relations. Please go ahead, sir.

Matthew Lee: Good morning, and welcome to Dine Brands Global's Third Quarter Fiscal 26 Conference Call. This morning's call will include prepared remarks from John W. Peyton, CEO and President of Applebee's and Vance Yuwen Chang, CFO. Following those prepared remarks, Lawrence Y. Kim, Chief Commercial Officer and President of IHOP, will also be available along with John and Vance to address questions during the Q&A portion of the call. Please remember our Safe Harbor regarding forward-looking information. During the call, management will discuss information that is forward looking and involves known and unknown risks uncertainties, and other factors, which may cause the actual results to be different than those expressed or implied.

Please evaluate the forward-looking information in the context of these factors which are detailed in today's press release and 10-Q filing. The forward-looking statements are as of today, we assume no obligation to update or supplement these statements. We will refer to certain non GAAP financial measures which are described in our press release, and is available on Dine Brands' Investor Relations website. With that, it is my pleasure to turn the call over to Dine Brands' CEO, John W. Peyton.

John W. Peyton: Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining us. Today, I will begin with an overview of Dine's Q3 performance. And share updates on the brand initiatives across Applebee's, Fuzzy's, and IHOP that are driving our results. After that, I will turn it over to Vance who will walk through our financial results in more detail. Dine delivered Q3 results in line with our expectations, while continuing to make deliberate investments in the brands and the business. For the quarter, Applebee's reported a 0.9% increase domestic comp sales driven by a strong July during which the brand outperformed Black Box on both traffic and sales.

IHOP posted domestic comp sales of positive 0.8% and delivered its 7th consecutive quarter of traffic outperformance and the 4th consecutive quarter of sales outperformance versus Black Box. And our adjusted EBITDA was $49 million compared to $49 million in the same quarter last year. With those results as the backdrop, let me share some insights on what is driving them, starting first with the consumer. Over the last 3 years, consumer behavior has been remarkably consistent. In the context of persistent inflation on food away from home, and higher gas prices, consumer sentiment has remained low, and guests are driven by a strong value proposition where they know the full price of the meal.

Notably, though, consumers are less likely to cut back on occasional dining and that is a benefit to us. We expect this dynamic to continue into 2027. Looking at guest behavior at our brands, specifically, average check levels have held steady reflecting mild check management. And value incidents also remained relatively consistent at 25% of transactions for Applebee's and 22% of transactions at IHOP. Which is roughly in the middle to high end of our historical range. This is another indication that value is a big decision driver. Overall, casual dining has shown resilience this year and, ultimately, our performance comes down to our consistency in messaging and conviction in our strategy.

So if you recall, in Q3 of last year, we made a deliberate set of changes. First, we introduced everyday value platforms at IHOP, and amplified 2 for $25 at Applebee's. We dialed up menu innovation at both brands. We sharpened our operational focus within the restaurants, and we rolled out a new marketing strategy to better integrate our brands into the cultural conversation. 1 of our greatest competitive advantages is that we own 2 of the most iconic brands. We have managed through different economic cycles, and we have demonstrated our ability evolve with our guest needs without sacrificing the core of what makes each brand so special.

And as we look ahead, we are prioritizing investments that improve both comp sales and the overall footprint of our brands, which includes refreshing restaurant appearance, through our remodel programs, and expanding our dual brand concept, both to drive more value out of each location and accelerating that work through our company owned portfolio as well. Of course, these investments require upfront capital, yet they yield significant long term upside. Over the past 2 years, we have been able to aggressively lean into this strategy for 2 reasons. First, our asset light model generates strong, consistent free cash flow, which gives us the flexibility to invest in our brands without compromising our financial discipline.

And second, we continue to see real commitment from our franchisees, who are investing in our brands and the strategy alongside of us. With the progress we are making on these strategic initiatives, we are well positioned to deliver long term sustainable value for our franchisees and shareholders. And so with that, I will share some updates across our portfolio beginning with Applebee's. Comp sales at Applebee's returned to growth in Q3, up 0.9% with traffic also improving versus the prior quarter. The quarter started strong with the return of our iconic Dollarita and the introduction of the Bacon Cheeseburger Wonton Taco on the 2 for $25 platform.

Leveraging the strength of our value platform and our bar and beverage program, these promotions delivered positive sales and traffic, during the period and outperformed Black Box. In fact, the Bacon Cheeseburger Wonton Taco, our strongest new appetizer launch since the pandemic, outperforming our previous best loaded potato WAVES that we launched just last quarter. Now I want to take a moment to put a finer point on this. Since reinvigorating our menu innovation engine about a year ago, each new menu item has built on the popularity of the last. And looking ahead, we expect to have more new food items launching over the next 12 months than we have had in the last few years.

Regarding off premise, we extended our streak of positive comp sales to a 7th consecutive quarter with comp sales growing 1.8%, supported by delivery growth. This is particularly notable given that only 1 of our 3 campaigns this quarter was available off premise, which tells us that demand is broadening beyond specific promotions. Applebee's also saw strengthening social media performance this quarter, with third party data from UBS showing that interactions more than tripled year over year, ranking among the top performing restaurant brands. On remodels, we have completed 107 Applebee's Lookin' Good remodels year to date, already exceeding our target of 100 for the year.

As part of a broader refresh cycle that will bring us to roughly half the portfolio remodeled by the end of 27. On average, these restaurants continue to see at least a mid single digit lift to sales driven by increased traffic following a reimage. From an operation standpoint, our focus on driving excellence through simplicity, and accountability continue to produce measurable results. Order accuracy is improved. Manager visibility in the dining room increased. Google ratings are up. All contributing to improving guest satisfaction. And last, I want to mention that we recently hosted our Applebee's global franchisee conference bringing together franchisees from across the system to align on priorities for the year ahead.

Our conversations reinforced our strong sense of partnership and our franchisees were engaged on the initiatives driving the brand forward, from menu innovation to remodels. And now moving on to IHOP. In Q3, comp sales at IHOP grew 0.8%. The brand also outperformed Black Box on both sales and traffic for the 4th consecutive quarter. With traffic app performance now extending to 7 consecutive quarters. Clearly, this is not a 1-quarter story, and it coincides with the launch of the everyday value menu last year. it is a steady performance, and that consistency is exactly the validation we are looking for in our strategy.

The growth in comp sales was supported by a healthy growth in check, driven by strong in store activations including server incentives and in restaurant point of purchase materials that drew attention to higher priced items. The everyday value menu is a foundational element of IHOP's barbell strategy providing accessible value while creating space for premium innovation led offerings as well. This quarter, the premium end was fueled by products like the Dubai Chocolate Pancakes, and our signature breakfast. Together, these offerings leverage cultural trends and menu innovation to drive incremental engagement and trade-up opportunities. Off premise recorded 5.6% comp growth, with 10% growth at our first party online to go channels.

We are also seeing early strength in catering, a newer part of our business, where sales grew 44% compared to a year ago. That growth reflects new technology and packaging built specifically to handle larger catering orders, and we believe there is still meaningful upside in this channel. Our social and earned media efforts also showed meaningful growth, with third party data from ListenFirst indicating engagement across all channels climbed 54% quarter over quarter. And finally, operationally, we continue to make good progress. Table turn times improved, and reached a new all time low post COVID, and average Google ratings also increased year over year reflecting improved and consistent in restaurant experience. Turning to fuzzies.

Traffic improved sequentially every quarter this year, driven by technology enhancements, menu simplification, a better in restaurant experience. Off premise remains a meaningful and consistent contributor to the brand's quarter over quarter progress. We are encouraged by Fuzzy's performance and are focused on sustaining this momentum through the end of the year. On development, our Dual brand platform is 1 of our strongest long term growth levers. Dual brand sales continue to perform well, averaging roughly 1.5 to 2x the sales of the original stand alone restaurant. As of today, we have 60 domestic Dual brand restaurants open, including 9 company-owned with 14 more under construction. We remain on track to reach 80 domestic Dual brands by year end.

As the platform has scaled, we have also refined how we operate. We have invested in additional training to help IHOP franchisees run the bar program more effectively, we have adjusted Applebee's kitchen operations and equipment to handle the volume of IHOP's scratch made breakfast daypart. With each new opening, we learn more, And together with our franchisees, we are getting better at running these restaurants. And that matters just as much to long term returns as the pace of our openings. Before turning the call over to Vance, I will note that Q4 trends have been mixed across the brand so far.

Applebee started the quarter somewhat soft, while IHOP is continuing its momentum, supported by the return of stuffed French toast in mid September. We are tracking toward the lower end of our full year guidance. All in all, we are pleased with the progress we are seeing across the business this quarter and we remain confident in the strategy we have laid out. Building long term value through consistent execution today and disciplined investment in our future growth. And with that, I will turn it over to Vance.

Vance Yuwen Chang: Thanks, John. You know, on the top line, total revenues increased 15.1% to $248.9 million in Q3, versus $216.2 million in the prior year. And it is driven by $36.9 million increase in company owned restaurant revenues from restaurants acquired or open since the third quarter of 25. So if we take out advertising revenues, franchise revenues in Q3 decreased by 1.5%, due to a reduction in the number of franchise restaurants, lower franchise termination fees due to fewer closures, and lower proprietary product sales due to the removal of gluten friendly product offerings.

Rental segment revenues for the third quarter of 26 decreased to $25.5 million versus $27.3 million in the prior year period primarily driven by restaurant closures as well as our decision to work with our franchisees to exit sub leases as they expire in favor of stimulating future. G&A expenses were $51.6 million in Q3 of 26, up from $50.2 million in the same period of last year, from higher professional services fees and higher employee related costs associated with our investment in company owned and Dual brand restaurant. Adjusted EBITDA for Q3 of 26 was flat at $49 million from $49 million in Q3 of 25.

Adjusted diluted EPS for the third quarter of 26 was $0.82, compared to adjusted diluted EPS of $0.73 for the third quarter of 25. Now turning to the statement of cash flows. We had adjusted free cash flow of $12.8 million for the first 9 months of 2026, compared to $68.2 million for the same period of last year. This decrease was primarily driven by a decrease in cash provided by operating activities which includes the impact of remodel and development incentives. And the increase in CapEx related to company owned restaurant remodels and Dual brand conversions. CapEx through Q3 of 26 was $31 million compared to $21.3 million for the same period of 2025.

We finished the third quarter with total unrestricted cash of $91.1 million, compared to unrestricted cash of $97.5 million at the end of the second quarter. On buybacks and dividends, we returned $9 million of capital to shareholders in Q3, including $7 million of shares repurchases and $2 million of dividends. Year to date, we have repurchased $35.9 million of shares which was approximately 8% of our shares outstanding at the beginning of the year. We continue to believe our shares are undervalued and remain committed to share repurchases. Our $500 million series 23 notes become callable at par in December. We will continue to monitor the market for opportunities to refinance these notes when beneficial to us.

Next, let me discuss Applebee's performance. Q3 domestic same restaurant sales increased 0.9% year over year. Domestic average weekly franchise sales per restaurant were $53.7 thousand including approximately $12.4 thousand from off premise, or 23% of total sales, of which 11.2% is from to go and 11.9% is from delivery. Our premise saw a positive 1.8% lift in comp sales in 2026 compared to the same period of last year. IHOP's Q3 domestic same restaurant sales increased 0.8%. Domestic average weekly franchise sales per restaurant were $38.5 thousand including $8.1 thousand from off premise or 21% of total sales. Of which 7.6% is from to go and 13.4% is from delivery.

Our premise saw a positive 5.6% lift in comp sales in 2026, compared to the same period of last year. Now turning to commodities. Applebee's commodity cost in Q3 increased by 5.4% and IHOP commodity costs increased by 1.3% versus the same period last year. Our coop supply chain partner, CSCS, continues to expect commodity costs in 2026 at mid single digits for Applebee's and low single digits for IHOP. The primary driver for both brands' commodity costs is higher beef prices, including the lapping of favorable beef contracts at Applebee's last year.

To date, in 2026, we implemented projects resulting in over $22 million of annualized savings across both systems and we continue to partner with CSCS to leverage our scale. Lastly, our company owned portfolio remains a focus in strengthening this health of the brands and supporting long term value creation for the business. As a reminder, we opportunistically took over restaurants with good opportunity for turnaround and value creation as we accelerate our Dual brand and remodeling initiatives. As of Q3, we own 136 restaurants, including 7 dual branded restaurants, represents approximately 4% of our system.

We believe we have an appropriate balance between the number of company owned restaurants versus franchise restaurants, so there is no reason to add to our company owned portfolio at this point. Our goal is to ultimately refranchise the restaurants as operations improve and we have already started to engage with the various franchisees who are interested in acquiring some of our restaurants. it is important to remember that because we have taken back these portfolios over time, each restaurant and portfolio is at a different stage in its multiyear investment plan. Which is why the portfolios are currently performing differently.

While we have seen an impact from increased loss operating days due to more Dual brand conversions and remodels, we are encouraged by the portfolios that have had the longest time to benefit from our ownership. Based on what we have seen in those cohorts, we expect our more recent portfolios to follow a similar path of improvement as they move through the same investment life cycle. Before turning the call back over to John for Q&A, I would like to add that we are maintaining the low end of our full year financial guidance at this time. With that, I will hand it back over to John.

John W. Peyton: Thanks, Vance. And to wrap up before Q&A, as you may have seen earlier this week, we filed an 8-K confirming receipt of an unsolicited offer for the company. The board, with the assistance of its outside advisers, carefully evaluated the offer and determined that the proposal was inadequate and substantially undervalued the company. And the board has since rejected that offer. Last week, the company also put in place a stockholder rights plan that protects all our all our stockholders from opportunistic share accumulations. #3143. The Switch 2 Zelda: Ocarina of Time Is a Brilliant Remake

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

It’s back, completely refreshed, and an absolute joy to experience again.

It was way back in 1998 when I finished Ocarina of Time. I remember how incredible it all was, not only to play but also to look at. N64 games back then felt stunning — so impressive that I rushed out to make the N64 the first Nintendo home console I ever owned.

Those days are gone, and N64 games now look pretty rough to my eyes. But with the $60 Ocarina of Time remake, exclusive to the Switch 2, Nintendo brings some of that magic back again; I’ve never had more fun replaying a game in my life.

When I first tried the new version of Ocarina for about an hour a few weeks ago, it felt like it was replacing my old memories of playing the original game. More than a week into playing at home, I can confirm that the remake has completely replaced my memories of the original. I’ve revisited the N64 version a few times through the Switch Online N64 app, but it feels so minimal and awkward compared to the remake that I can’t go back now.

But it’s also brought me right back to the feeling I had in 1998. Like in the game itself, I’ve been whisked back in time to reexperience the past — and it’s better than it’s ever been. I’ve been down the Ocarina rerelease road before, when the 3DS version arrived in 2011, but the Switch 2 version is far more impressive. It’s not a new game, but at times it almost feels like one.

Everything in Ocarina of Time has been created fresh again. Like some sort of set builder making all the pieces of an old show from memory, it’s astonishing how Ocarina is an old game made with completely redone graphics. It outdoes Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom in visual splendor, with similarly gorgeous open vistas at every turn.

Just as Ocarina of Time inspired Breath of the Wild, it’s Breath of the Wild that’s now reshaped Ocarina — at least visually. The scope, story and challenges in Ocarina remain just about the same, creating a more intimate experience despite its sense of epic scale. If you’ve never played it before, think of it as a theme park version of the supersized Hyrule in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

But I appreciate its more contained scale even more now. I got lost in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, and not always in a good way. To be honest, at times, parts of those games began to feel repetitive. Ocarina of Time’s story is told more directly, with clearly laid-out goals and a faster pace. It feels like a true fusion of the sandbox-like open worlds of recent Zelda games and the intricate, puzzle-driven storylines of older ones.

I’d love this new Ocarina even if it only brought updated graphics, reworked sound and new voice acting, which grew on me. But its control scheme makes the game far more intuitive to play. The old Ocarina didn’t have a jump button: Link just auto-jumped! Here, you can jump anywhere. The old game never had a second analog stick to control your viewing angle; it relied on “Z-targeting” to look ahead or recenter your focus on objects and enemies. Now, you can look around and Z-target with a trigger button — something that modern Zelda players probably just take for granted.

Some areas are different now: Early on in Kokiri Forest, the way you find the first sword is different. The dialogue has also changed. That’s just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the many little shifts here, which become hard to notice. At some point, my experience of the new 2026 version simply took over and overwrote all my old, fuzzy memories of the 1998 version. It’s now, once again, the game as it felt to me back then.

Maybe it’s that I’m getting older, or I don’t replay games such as Ocarina of Time year after year as some do, but I realize I forgot a lot of what happens in this game. But I look forward to every night I get a chance to play it again. It’s that good.

I didn’t think that would happen, not with RPGs and Zelda games advancing so much over the years. It’s a testament to Ocarina of Time that its structure and mystery still feel perfectly paced. There are tons of side missions, but the main story arc is strong and continuous. I felt a sense of awe more than once, even when it came to things I knew would happen. The time travel — which I hope doesn’t spoil too much for anyone who’s never played before, though, hey, it is called Ocarina of Time — still feels wondrous.

I was skeptical about Nintendo spending all its resources updating classic games over the last year or so — a trend that started with Star Fox, continued with Switch Sports Resort and has returned here. I wanted new games for the Switch 2 — not retreads. But I have to admit that Nintendo has done these remakes with expert care. And in the case of Ocarina of Time, the effort truly feels like it transcends the original. As much as I ended up loving Star Fox again, it never felt as much like a new game as this Ocarina remake does.

Is it a truly new game? No. But it feels like the most singular Zelda game again, taking precedence even over Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. And with its graphic overhaul, it now feels like a cousin to those games in a new way, a sort of trilogy (but not exactly). I find myself, once again, appreciating how absurd and adorable all the characters are. Zelda games have such a goofy sense of humor, and I feel like Ocarina does more than Breath and Tears do. I’ve gotten a kick out of finding every side character in Hyrule just to see their new faces.

And the dungeons in Ocarina of Time are so good. I want Zelda games to return to the kind of intricate, puzzle-filled dungeons found here.

I’m so stunned by how much I love the new Ocarina that I’m wondering what magic Nintendo could work on other throwbacks. Do this for Mario 64, or Pilotwings.

The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask is the “other” Zelda game for N64, and it’s even more brilliantly conceived. Remaking it for the Switch 2 now seems like a when — not an if — considering Ocarina’s Hyrule has been completely rebuilt with new graphics. Nintendo brought Ocarina and Majora to 3DS, and the cycle could repeat again here. I’d be all for it.

Could this all be a massive test run for a future Zelda that doesn’t exist yet? It certainly feels like it — but when? The remastered version of Metroid Prime paved the way for Metroid Prime 4‘s release. Beyond the battle-focused Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment, this is the first Zelda game made exclusively with the Switch 2’s hardware in mind — and its lush visuals show it. It’s the best-looking game on the Switch 2 yet, and naturally, it makes me wonder what a new Zelda game could feel like. Or heck, a new Mario.

This reconstruction of Ocarina of Time feels like it’s strutting, dripping with luxury, full of glorious style, a symphony played with a full orchestra. And somehow, unleashing it all in service of a fantastic remake doesn’t feel excessive. I’m having a blast playing it, but I also want to see what this opens up for the next generation of Nintendo Switch 2 games.

But if you’ve never played a Zelda game before and have a Switch 2, I envy you: The new Ocarina of Time is an incredible place to start.

#3141. Nvidia RTX 50 GPUs hit with more price hikes – up to $500

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Some GPUs will see bigger increases than others, while Intel and AMD remain mum on their pricing plans

Graphics are handled by an Nvidia Quadro M4000 card.

As the AI-driven global memory shortage rages on, Nvidia is notifying users that its RTX 50 series of graphics cards will see yet another significant price hike this week.

Also: I switched from Intel to AMD – here’s why I’m never going back

In August, Nvidia gave gamers and content creators fair warning that the company’s entire line of RTX 50 Series GPUs would get price increases of up to a 15%. The flagship 5090 is getting the highest: a nearly $500 increase on an already eye-watering $6,000 price tag at Best Buy. The lower-end 5050 and 5060 will get much more modest, if still grumble-worthy, $50-60 bumps, which puts the squeeze on consumers already caught between market hype and failed expectations.

Earlier iterations of the brand’s graphics cards, like the RTX 40 and RTX 30 series, won’t be directly affected by this decision. However, don’t be surprised if you see some resellers take advantage of the situation by adding their own price increases or snapping up stock to sell at a markup on the second-hand market.

Intel and AMD have been quiet about the possibility of a price hike on their own graphics cards, and neither company plans any immediate changes in response to Nvidia’s decision. Not yet, anyway. As companies like Nvidia continue to snap up the raw resources needed to manufacture AI chips and pledge their GPUs and motherboards to future AI data centers rather than the consumer market, it’s likely both companies will eventually follow suit with their own hefty increases.

#3140. So You Bought an iPhone 18 Pro. Do You Still Need a Real Camera?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Apple's phone takes beautiful photos, but is it as good as using a Fujifilm X-M5?

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

The iPhone 18 Pro is among the most accomplished phone cameras around, packing an array of sensors and lenses that are all capable of taking stunning images in a variety of conditions. Throw in the new creative tweaks to Apple’s Photographic Styles and the iPhone 18 Pro becomes a formidable partner to serious photographers.

But how does it compare to an actual camera? To see why you’d pick one over the other, I took the iPhone 18 Pro on some photo walks alongside Fujifilm’s X-M5, a compact-sized mirrorless camera with interchangeable lenses and a host of filmic profiles to choose from.

This isn’t designed to be a direct comparison between each specific model — after all, a phone has other advantages beyond a camera, some of which I’ll come to later. I’m not going to pixel peep at ultrafine details nor estimate which has the technically best dynamic range. This is more about which allows you to be more creative and more engaged in your image-taking and what each one offers.

With the iPhone 16 Pro Apple brought its Photographic Styles with the grid-like tool for adjusting the color tones and shadow depth for each of the looks. It was a huge boon to iPhone photographers who want to shoot with a specific look without having to manually edit each image after the fact. Apple took that further on the 18 Pro by bringing in more advanced tools, including the ability to add image grain and bloom to your images and giving manual control over white balance. Finally.

Fujifilm, meanwhile, has won the hearts of millions of photographers the world over with the ability to create filmic styles that can be shared and installed as “recipes” on its cameras. Like Photographic Styles, these looks change everything from color tones to film grain and allow you to shoot with an almost infinite array of filmic styles with no editing required.

In practice, both operate in much the same way. On the iPhone, I erred toward warmer styles such as Amber and Gold, bringing the shadows down and adding some film grain. My Kodak Gold-inspired Fujifilm recipes aimed to achieve a similar effect and while they’re not identical, I can’t say I like either one of them over the other.

I don’t like all of the iPhone’s styles, but there are a lot of Fujifilm recipes I don’t like either, and arguably this just comes down to personal taste anyway. But I have noticed that there’s a lot that Apple can do to improve Styles for photographers.

For one, you can’t save a specific style as a preset to recall later. While you can tell the phone to remember your last-used settings each time you open it, if you change those settings, you’ll need to remember what they originally were if you want to go back. It also means it’s difficult to share those presets with others, whereas Fujifilm camera owners have created a vast community sharing recipes far and wide.

Overall, Fujifilm’s recipes give much finer control over the look of your image and make it easier to recall a certain preset when you want to start shooting away. Both the iPhone and X-M5 (and indeed almost all regular cameras) also allow you to shoot images in raw format too, allowing you to apply your own edits later on in apps like Adobe Lightroom, Snapseed or VSCO.

The iPhone’s size makes it the dream camera for street or travel photography where you may be walking for miles every day and don’t want to be weighed down by equipment. It just slips into your pocket and can be whipped out just as easily when inspiration strikes. While Fujifilm’s X-M5 is small for a camera, with a lens on you’ll struggle to get it into a pocket, meaning you’ll need a dedicated camera bag to carry it around — or have it around your neck on a strap, which could become uncomfortable after a full day out.

That’s doubly the case if you have extra lenses you’d want to take with you, which the iPhone has built in. Even Fujifilm’s endlessly popular fixed-lens X100VI is still big enough that you’ll only manage to get it into a large coat pocket at best.

On the other hand, cameras are built to be ergonomic when taking images. Their larger sizes give you something to grip onto and hold steady. By comparison, holding a skinny iPhone when taking a photo can often feel delicate, especially when you’re trying not to accidentally press on the screen. Personally, I don’t enjoy the feel of taking photos with a phone, and it’s one of the reasons why I’d always reach for a real camera over a phone for a day’s photography.

That’s especially true when it comes to adjusting shooting settings. Changing exposure compensation means multiple taps on the phone’s screen. Ditto if you want to change white balance or shutter speed. Most cameras like the X-M5 or X100VI offer physical controls to instantly change settings when out shooting in the field, often without even needing to look, saving you crucial seconds when capturing the decisive moment.

While Fujifilm’s popular X100VI has a fixed lens offering a constant 35mm focal length, the X-M5 — along with many others in the range — has interchangeable lenses, allowing it to swap between a plethora of lenses from both Fujifilm and a wealth of third parties. Whether you want an ultrawide fisheye lens, a super-long telephoto for wildlife shots or creative lenses like PolarPro’s LightLeaks lenses, there’s an option out there.

But that means spending more money on more gear and then having to carry an increasingly heavy kit bag out on location to use all that fancy new glass. The iPhone has its multiple lenses built right in. Its focal lengths include 13mm, 24mm, 28mm, 35mm, 48mm, 100mm and 200mm, all from one pocket-sized device.

Sure, most of those include some kind of digital cropping or upscaling and the quality isn’t what you’d find from a pro-standard telephoto zoom lens, but for most people who want to take snaps out and about in the street, the iPhone’s lens options essentially put a full kit-bag of gear into your pocket.

If you do want more lens options for your iPhone, there are a range of add-ons you can pick up. I love shooting with Moment’s clip-on lenses, especially the anamorphic lens for video and the macro lens for close-up work. Then there’s PolarPro’s various filters, like the Everyday filter, which is the same one I slapped onto the front of the X-M5.

As Apple’s phones are so popular, accessories for them are the easiest to come by compared to almost any other Android phone. But the same can be said for Fujifilm’s camera — and most other compact cameras around. Alongside the aforementioned armada of lens choices, you can also pick up thumb grips and half cases to customize the camera and things like flashes and tripods for taking your photography further.

The iPhone, of course, has the benefit of also being a smartphone. It’s not just a camera, meaning that when you’re done taking your photos you’ve got the option to instantly edit them in whatever apps you like and share them to Instagram or over WhatsApp without first having to transfer them to your computer.

But for me that’s also one of the biggest downsides of using a phone as a camera. I’ve written about this before, but the problem essentially boils down to wanting to focus on one task at a time. A camera has just one function: taking pictures. I pick it up to do one thing and that’s all I have to pay attention to.

When I’m shooting with my phone, I can be bombarded with incoming notifications, phone calls and other pop-ups, all of which are desperate to take my attention away from the act and craft of shooting photos. I love having a great phone camera with me for those occasions when I want a photo and I’m not carrying a camera, but when I want to be purposeful in my photography and plan to head out to shoot work I’m proud of, it will always be a dedicated camera that I’ll reach for.

Which is best for you depends on two factors: Your budget and how serious you are about your photography. The iPhone is a superb camera phone for out-and-about snaps and while it’s certainly possible to take pro-level photos with it, it’s not always as easy to use — or as inspirational — as using a proper smaller camera like a Fujifilm X-M5, X100VI or other models like a Ricoh GRIV, Leica Q3 43 or even a small mirrorless camera.

Plus, if you’re keen for a great all-round imaging experience and you don’t have the cash for two tech purchases right now, going all in on just an iPhone 18 Pro is a smart move. But if you want to take a more authentic and intentional approach to your photography and feel creatively inspired by holding a physical camera and twiddling real, analog dials will absolutely benefit from looking toward adding a camera like the Fujifilm X-M5 or X100VI to your photography arsenal.

CNET Editor at Large Katie Collins found that when she used a proper camera on a big trip to China instead of just her phone, it rekindled her passion for photography that had long sat dormant.

While smartphone photography has come on in leaps and bounds in the past few years, there’s still nothing that beats that feeling of lifting a real camera to your eye and firing that shutter button.

#3139. Apple Wins Big in CNET’s People’s Picks Awards for Its MacBooks

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Two popular non-Apple brands still won awards for their affordability.

Of all of the laptop brands to choose from, CNET readers say Apple’s signature MacBooks really live up to the hype.

We recently surveyed CNET readers as part of our People’s Picks awards to find out what they think about their laptop and the brand behind it to help you make a more sound choice on the laptop you may be considering over the holidays. We listed several well-known names, including Dell, Lenovo — and Apple. We asked about everything that matters most on a daily basis, like battery life, durability and even its performance for handling tasks like gaming and graphics. Out of 10 categories, Apple swept up eight of the awards and claimed the overall winner for CNET’s People’s Picks award.

Here’s what readers say Apple gets right when it comes to its laptops, what the experts think about Apple’s landslide win and other brands worth considering.

Apple wins the overall award in CNET’s People’s Picks, and also takes home the overall satisfaction rating, with 74.2% of Apple users saying they’re extremely satisfied with their laptop. In comparison, 22.5% say they’re satisfied — bringing Apple to a near-perfect overall satisfaction score of 96.7%.

Apple’s overall impression also speaks to other awards it wins from CNET readers, including high ratings for its impressive battery life, display quality and high-quality build. All of those categories and more sum up Apple’s brand loyalty nod, with 68% of MacBook owners saying they would buy the same laptop and model from Apple again.

How much are people paying for MacBooks? CNET found that 43.5% of Apple users paid at least $1,500. Until earlier in 2026, the MacBook Air was Apple’s entry-level laptop, priced at least $1,299. The introduction of the budget-friendly MacBook Neo brought that down to a more reasonable $699. However, despite Apple’s laptops being more expensive than those from other brands, they still ranked high for their value proposition. Part of the reason for that is that MacBooks received high marks for hardware reliability. “Apple’s MacBooks might cost more than the average laptop, but their premium build quality means they’re built for the long haul,” said Matt Elliott, CNET’s laptop editor.

If you plan to have your laptop for a while, you may be impressed by other features that make work easier and faster, like its M-series central processing unit for task management and AI capabilities, great battery life and a one-of-a-kind operating system — currently MacOS 27. All of the features and specifications bundled together make Apple’s perception as a high-end laptop worth the investment for long-term satisfaction.

Apple clinches a near-perfect score for its value perception. According to our survey results, 44% of Apple users said their MacBook has exceptional value. Others say their MacBook is worth what they paid for it (50.9%) — for a total positive score of 94.6%.

Digging deeper into Apple’s cost-to-value rating, 81.8% of Apple owners paid at least $1,000 for their laptops, which may seem costly, but Apple users seem OK with the price. That could be because, even though Apple has only three laptop models in a handful of sizes in its lineup, each one delivers solid performance and storage.

Take Apple’s proprietary processing chips, for example — each upgrade since the M1 release has improved the laptop’s speed, battery life and performance. Now the M6 can handle the MacBook’s AI capabilities, storage and high-resolution graphics. And for all of that power, most MacBooks are relatively thin and lightweight, making them easier for mobility — just a few of the reasons Apple users may be OK with paying more for what they’re getting.

Battery life is a big deal for many laptop buyers, and that’s another area where Apple delivers. Over a quarter of those surveyed (25.7%) said their MacBook’s battery life exceeds 10 hours — which is more than enough for a full day of work in most cases. And 18.7% say their MacBook’s battery lasts between 8 and 10 hours — totaling 44.4% of MacBook users saying their battery lasts 8 hours or more.

Comparatively, non-Apple laptop brands fall short in this category. Only 16.4% of Lenovo users say their laptop’s battery lasts at least 8 hours, and even fewer for Dell (12.7%) and HP (11.8%). If you’re leaning toward a MacBook for its battery life, CNET’s lab test shows that the MacBook Neo lasts 13 hours and 26 minutes for online streaming, whereas the Apple MacBook Air 13-inch M5 (2026 model) lasts 17 hours and 2 minutes.

Apple sweeps the brightness, color accuracy and clarity category with 99.2% of its users either satisfied or extremely satisfied with their laptop’s screen performance. No Apple users reported dissatisfaction.

“Apple has long been a favorite for creative professionals and content creators for good reason: Its MacBook displays are some of the best you’ll find on any laptop,” said Josh Goldman, CNET’s managing editor for computers. “While Apple may use marketing names like Retina and Liquid Retina to describe display features, they do translate into sharp and clear text and images, with excellent brightness, contrast, color gamut coverage and color accuracy.”

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR even goes beyond what MacBook users have come to expect. It’s Apple’s first OLED touchscreen laptop and features next-level brightness, color and contrast.

Apple receives high ratings: 80% of MacBook owners say it has premium build quality, 18.2% say it’s solid, and those results don’t surprise us.

And MacBooks seem durable and reliable, with 87% of Apple users reporting no hardware failures on their MacBooks, while 8% say minor software fixes resolved their issues. Only 3% needed minor hardware repairs, and 2.2% needed major repairs — which could be fixes such as a battery or screen replacement.

Our editors say the M5 MacBook Air is thin and lightweight, but still has a well-built aluminum design. And the M5 Pro MacBook Pro is sturdy, too. What sets Apple’s laptop hardware apart could be its aluminum chassis — the casing that holds all of the components together.

“Apple makes three lines of MacBooks — the Neo, Air and Pro — and focuses on making those the best they can possibly be. They are all built to deliver a premium experience using high-quality materials, and that even includes the entry-level MacBook Neo,” said Goldman.

Lastly, Apple uses durable materials, such as the 100% recycled aluminum alloy it says encloses the 14-inch MacBook Pro. And the tech giant has several testing facilities to test MacBook durability.

When it comes to getting your daily tasks done, most CNET readers with MacBooks (70.9%) say Apple’s laptops handle workloads flawlessly. It’s worth noting that 45% use their MacBook for work tasks, but no Apple users reported poor performance.

Here’s why that might be: Apple’s laptops are packed with top-notch performance specs and features, like their powerful processors, unified memory and fast storage. Better processor performance means enhanced graphics, on-device AI capabilities and faster task speeds, all of which add up to being able to finish work, play games or stream videos without issues or lags caused by your laptop’s hardware.

On the software side, MacOS 27 Golden Gate gives you built-in AI features, like Siri AI and Visual Intelligence. And you can organize your Safari tabs by topic and use the Notify Me tool to be notified of website changes, like price drops or breaking news. Plus, you can create shortcuts to automate tasks. Coupling all of these features and specifications explains why Apple users rate MacBooks so highly for getting the job done.

Apple leads the way on brand retention with 68% of Apple users planning to buy the same MacBook model again, while 29.1% would buy another model from Apple’s lineup. Only 3% would switch to another brand that’s not Apple.

Usually, when you buy one Apple product, you’re likely to stick to the brand’s ecosystem, especially since Apple has its own operating systems to access its unique features and work seamlessly with other Apple products with Apple’s Continuity feature. For example, you can start an email on your iPhone, but finish typing it on your MacBook. Or you can call or send a text from your laptop without reaching for your iPhone. Other features work across Apple devices, including iCloud, Universal Clipboard and AirDrop.

Asus wins as a midtier laptop choice with 67% of Asus owners paying between $500 and $1,499. There’s a sweet spot in this range with 38% spending between $500 and $999, and 28% paying between $1,000 and $1,499.

If you’re planning to spend that amount on a new laptop, you may also be pleased to know that Asus earns a higher satisfaction rating compared with other non-Apple laptop brands — 48% of Asus users say they’re extremely satisfied.

Asus laptops have a few features and specifications that may speak to that rating, regardless of budget. For example, the Zenbook A14 has a thin, lightweight design that’s rigid, with long battery life and an OLED display with strong contrast and color performance. This Copilot Plus PC sells for $1,600 (but retailers like Best Buy regularly have it on sale for less). Comparatively, these premium features from other brands could cost more or sacrifice important must-have features for the price.

Asus has other laptops worth exploring depending on your needs, like the budget-friendly Asus ZenBook S 14 or the premium Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 that could be good for gamers and creators.

Over one-third of Acer laptop owners (38%) paid less than $500 for their laptop — which is greater than other laptop brands in this price range. Yet, 44% of Acer users say their laptop has exceptional value, while 50% say the value is fair — bringing a total positive cost-to-value score of over 94%. Acer also has an overall satisfaction score of 92.6% — the highest of non-Apple laptop brands.

If you’re impressed by Acer’s value and satisfaction scores, there are a few budget-friendly Acer options to consider. The Acer Aspire 16 AI wins CNET’s Editors’ Choice award. It has a big 16-inch screen but is still lightweight (3.5 pounds). And it has good battery life (over 21 hours on CNET’s battery drain test). There are a few other pluses, like the 1440p web camera that may be good for video conferencing and a sizable touchpad. All of those features and more add up to $700, which could make it a good computer for work or casual browsing. If you’re looking to spend slightly less, its predecessor, the Aspire 14 AI, is originally $639, but you may be able to score deals on both models during holiday sales.

Even though Apple is highly recommended by CNET readers, there are plenty of other laptop models and brands worth considering depending on your needs. Here are a few non-Apple laptop brands that are runner-ups to CNET’s People’s Picks winners that you shouldn’t count out of your laptop search.

Lenovo is best known for packing a powerful laptop into a compact design with tablet functionality, like its Yoga line, and its durable ThinkPad business models. But CNET readers with Lenovo laptops say the brand’s battery life stands out most compared with other non-MacBook laptops.

Survey findings show that 16% of Lenovo owners say their laptops can run for 8 hours or more. And 10.5% say their laptop battery lasts between 8 and 10 hours, while 6% say their Lenovo laptops can withstand at least 10 hours before needing a charge. That’s more than what readers say about other non-Apple brands. The Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition lasts 25 hours and 45 minutes — making it one of the best laptop batteries CNET experts have tested.

Goldman said Lenovo has such a large and varied PC selection using the latest chips from Intel, AMD, Qualcomm and Nvidia that there is something for everyone and every budget. Even those who spend less on a Lenovo laptop can expect solid performance, including battery life.

If your laptop’s hardware fails or it breaks, you may be in the market for a new laptop sooner than expected. Think about cooling fan problems, overheating or your laptop not powering on at all. Over half (68%) of Lenovo laptop owners said they haven’t had any hardware issues with their laptops — the most compared to other non-MacBooks.

Beyond hardware durability, Lenovo also scores highly for its build and construction — overall making it a sturdy laptop choice. In our survey, 38% of Lenovo laptop owners say their laptop has a premium feel, while 51% say it’s solid — totaling a positive score of 89%.

If you’re looking for recommendations, the Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 has an all-metal design. And the Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 is a business laptop with Lenovo’s well-known X1 Carbon exterior and new Space Frame design, which Elliott says makes it easier to repair or replace parts if needed.

Many Lenovo laptop users are loyal to the brand, which speaks to the overall positive satisfaction rating of 83%. If Lenovo owners were in the market for a new laptop, nearly three in four (73.2%) say they would buy another Lenovo laptop. Breaking down the percentage, 33.6% say they would buy the same model again. Meanwhile, 39.6% would buy a different model but stick to Lenovo.

Here’s why that might be. Lenovo offers a plethora of options to choose from based on your needs — while still evolving its laptops. For instance, the Lenovo Legion 5i Gen 10 has an open M.2 slot for a second storage drive and an OLED screen for crisp, colorful images — making it perfect for gaming. Its Yoga two-in-ones let you seamlessly switch between a tablet and traditional laptop, while Lenovo’s ThinkPad and ThinkBook business laptops offer everything from ultralight 2-pound bodies to expanding rollable screens. And its new designs don’t sacrifice the must-have needs like long battery life, durability and chip efficiency that lend to strong performance.

Asus wins over nearly half of its laptop owners, with 47.5% giving it an exceptional value rating  — exceeding expectations for its price. Take our Editors’ Choice pick, the Asus Zenbook A14. It’s super thin and lightweight, but it’s still sturdy thanks to its Ceralumnium body. Plus, it has supreme 24-hour battery life, 1TB of storage and an OLED display — all for $1,200. While that’s more expensive than some laptops, it’s what’s included in that price that makes it worthwhile compared with other non-Apple laptop brands.

Asus is the top non-Apple laptop option to consider for tasks, with 47.7% of CNET readers giving it high ratings. That’s followed by 40.4% of Asus laptop owners who say it has very good task performance. When it comes to tasks, 37% primarily use their Asus laptops for work, while 5% use theirs for gaming.

Asus is well known for having lightweight laptops with all-day-and-night battery life and stunning display quality. Asus laptops like the Asus ROG Zephyrus G16 have a good port selection, which could be good for gaming, work or simply connecting different devices without the need for additional adapters. And the Asus Zenbook S 14 has a strong neural processing unit that contributes to its high-speed AI performance.

Asus scores highest for its screen brightness and clarity, with over half (51%) extremely satisfied with its screen quality and brightness, while 38.6% say they’re satisfied, giving Asus an overall satisfaction rate of 90%. One common thread we noticed in Asus laptops is their OLED screens, which deliver high-resolution video and graphics. Asus laptops also combine stunning display quality with excellent performance and at surprisingly low prices for all of their features.

For example, the Asus Zenbook 14 isn’t the highest-quality OLED we’ve seen, but it still produces clear text and graphics on a 14-inch screen, along with exceptional black levels, Elliott said. That’s still better than LCDs that many other non-MacBooks have, and could be the reason Asus owners rate it so highly in this category.

Dell wins our readers over as a top choice for high-end laptops. One-third (33.3%) of Dell owners spent over $1,500, and of that percentage, 15.2% spent over $2,000.

Dell’s premium laptops largely cater to business and gaming with their standout features and performance. The Alienware 16X Aurora is Dell’s midrange gaming laptop with user-replaceable RAM, a bright display and strong performance for $2,280. But if you want more gaming features, Dell has the Alienware 16 Area-51, which has even better gaming performance, upgradable RAM and three SSD slots for $2,530. And if you’re looking for a non-Mac alternative that comes close to MacBook quality and performance, the higher-end Dell XPS 14 is the one to choose. It has the Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, Intel Arc B390 graphics and 1TB of storage for $1,950.

CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,003 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken from Sept. 1 to Oct. 10, 2026.

#3138. HomeView with an arm? Apple reportedly plans $1,000 swiveling smart panel

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The HomeView Ultra is expected to feature a robotic arm and 9-inch display. Shades of Amazon's discontinued Echo Show 10?

The Apple HomeView is the company’s first dedicated smart home display, and new reports of how Apple plans to improve the product are already circulating. Apple is reportedly planning to announce a HomeView with a robotic arm as early as next year. The dynamic display is expected to cost up to $1,000.

Also: Apple’s HomeView may double as security camera

The HomeView isn’t even on the market yet — it will be available for purchase next week, starting at $299. This 7-inch smart panel features a speaker that doubles as a stand, and Apple will also sell a wall-mounted option.

As a smart home device, the HomeView is designed to serve as a platform for interacting with your Apple ecosystem, including Apple Home and Siri. It’s a smart dashboard that lets you view all your smart home devices and security cameras, as well as your calendar, messages, and other integrated apps.

The Information reported that Apple is rumored to be working on a higher-end smart display for 2027, with shipments starting in 2028. The new device, codenamed J595, may be branded HomeView Ultra and feature a robotic arm and a 9-inch display.

The new HomeView’s screen would be mounted on an articulated mechanical arm to swivel the display, tracking users during FaceTime calls to keep them on-screen. The device could feature proactive smart home automations, such as turning on devices or triggering a room scene when someone walks into the room.

Also: Google’s latest Home updates just fixed my biggest annoyances

The same report indicates that the hardware has been complete for a couple of years, but launch delays are attributed to software development issues. Integrating advanced AI features and proactive automation has, according to The Information, been a challenge for Apple.

A swiveling smart home display isn’t entirely new. Amazon used to sell an Echo Show 10 with a display that tracked users to keep them in the camera’s view during video calls, though this model has been discontinued.

However, one that works within the Apple ecosystem could change how users interact with their home interfaces, given the popularity of FaceTime calls and the prevalence of iPhone users.

Also: 4 big Amazon smart home announcements

A HomeView Ultra could even anticipate users’ needs by tracking people’s movements and automatically executing routines and scenes depending on where they are in the home.

While there’s reason to doubt whether most smart home users would welcome such technology in their homes or consider it too invasive, premium robotic smart displays indicate that companies are standardizing interactive central hubs for the home.

#3136. Colliers (CIGI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Guidance trimmed as rate swings and geopolitical tension slowed late-quarter deals.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Colliers International Group Inc. (CIGI -4.48%) reported growth across its three global platforms of commercial real estate, engineering, and investment management despite increasing market volatility. Management reported that consolidated revenue rose 12% in local currency, supported by a 37% increase in the engineering segment and solid performance in capital markets. The company revised its full-year 2026 outlook to low-teens growth across key financial metrics, citing geopolitical tensions and interest rate volatility that slowed transaction velocity late in the third quarter. Management stated that the company remains focused on its long-term strategy of compounding value through a mix of organic growth and strategic acquisitions, noting that 70% of earnings are now derived from resilient, recurring service lines.
