#3088. Greif (GEF) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management outlines a bigger savings target and higher capital spending for a tough industrial market.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Greif, Inc. (GEF -5.60%) reported fiscal 2026 results and issued guidance for 2027 focused on structural cost reductions and capital allocation in a weak industrial demand environment. Management reported the achievement of its multiyear cost-saving targets one year ahead of schedule and established a new cumulative goal for the upcoming fiscal year. The company stated that its strategy involves divesting noncore assets, such as the Sweetwater mill and previous containerboard operations, to concentrate on high-return segments like polymers and closures. Capital allocation priorities for fiscal 2027 include increased organic growth investment, maintaining leverage below 2x, and continuing shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Greif Fourth Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker, Bill D'Onofrio, Vice President of Investor Relations and Corporate Development. Please go ahead.

Bill D’Onofrio: Good morning, and thank you for joining Greif's Fiscal Fourth Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Today, our CEO, Ole Rosgaard, will provide a strategy and market update, followed by our CFO, Larry Hilsheimer, with a review of our financial results and fiscal 2027 guidance. Please turn to Slide 2. In accordance with Regulation Fair Disclosure, please ask questions regarding topics you consider important because we are prohibited from discussing material nonpublic information with you on an individual basis. During today's call, we will make forward-looking statements involving plans, expectations and beliefs related to future events. Actual results could differ materially from those discussed.

Additionally, we will be referencing certain non-GAAP financial measures and the reconciliation to the most directly comparable GAAP metrics that can be found in the appendix of today's presentation. I'll now turn the call over to Ole on Slide 3.

Ole Rosgaard: Thank you, Bill, and good morning, everyone. Before we discuss the fourth quarter, I want to start with the bigger picture, how Greif has changed over the past 2 years and what that means for our shareholders. Two years ago, we set out to build a simpler, stronger, more profitable Greif. We introduced our solutions-based operating model, brought our global commercial teams together and committed to taking $100 million of structural costs out of the business. Today, those actions are delivering. We have achieved $105 million in annual run rate cost savings and expanded adjusted EBITDA margins by approximately 160 basis points. We sharpened our portfolio through the containerboard and timberlands divestitures.

We reduced leverage from 3.5x to 1.2x at year-end, and we have returned capital to shareholders, raising the dividend by nearly 15% over 2 years and repurchasing approximately $225 million of shares in fiscal '26. This is meaningful progress in a short time. Greif has greater earnings power, a stronger balance sheet and more room to invest in growth. Our shareholders have participated in that progress with total shareholder returns of more than 35% over the past 2 years, and we are not finished. Our priorities are straightforward: win new customers, grow our share of business with existing customers, invest in high-return opportunities in polymers and closures and keep taking structural costs out of the business.

We will remain disciplined with capital, including targeted acquisitions and shareholder returns while keeping leverage below 2x. These results belong to our thousands of colleagues around the world. They have driven this change while continuing to serve our customers. I want to thank them for their commitment and execution. Please turn to Slide 4. Now look at what this means for our fiscal 2026. Adjusted EBITDA reached $625.7 million, up nearly 12% from last year despite another year of weak industrial demand. Adjusted earnings per Class A share rose to $4.04, an improvement of 75% from a year ago. Our year-end leverage ratio was 1.2x. We repurchased $225 million of shares during the year.

These are clear signs of stronger earnings and financial flexibility. We also announced our exit from coated recycled board through the closure of our Sweetwater mill. While it may be a difficult decision for those affected, it's the right one for the long-term health of our fiber business. It sharpens our portfolio and supports a more efficient network. The key point is this. We are producing better results through actions we control. We are not depending on an industrial recovery to improve Greif. Please turn to Slide 5. Cost improvement is one of the clearest examples of that approach. At the end of fiscal '25, we have delivered $50 million of annual run rate savings.

At the end of fiscal '26, that number reached $105 million. We met our original $100 million commitment a year early. We're now raising the target to $150 million by the end of fiscal '27. That is 50% above our original commitments and another $45 million of annual run rate savings beyond what we have already delivered. The work is practical, improve operating efficiency, simplify our network and reduce overhead. These savings are structural. They're designed to make Greif more competitive and support margin expansion through the cycle. We have earned confidence by delivering. Now we need to deliver the next $45 million. Please turn to Slide 6 for our fourth quarter results. Turning to demand.

The industrial backdrop remains difficult. We have not seen convincing signs of a broad recovery. In the fourth quarter, primary product volumes in polymers and metals each declined about 2.3% from a year ago. Closures declined 3.5%. Fiber was the exception with volumes up 1.3%. Within polymers, intermediate bulk containers grew at a high single-digit rate, while smaller containers faced customer destocking, higher resin costs and weaker agricultural demand. Metals continue to reflect soft industrial activity across regions. Fiber benefited from steady converting demand. And closures experienced lower volumes, but we remain confident in its long-term growth opportunities. We're being realistic about the markets. We do not control when demand recovers.

We do control how well we serve our customers, how quickly we win new business, how efficiently we run our operations and where we invest. That is where our teams are focused. We are strengthening our commercial execution, pursuing growth in attractive end markets and continuing to improve our cost base. With that, I will turn the call over to Larry to review the quarter, our financial performance and our outlook.

Lawrence Hilsheimer: Thank you, Ole. Adjusted EBITDA declined approximately $5 million or 3.1% year-over-year in Q4. However, the prior year quarter included $18.2 million of favorable incentive accrual reductions without regard to the sale of containerboard. Excluding this prior year item, adjusted EBITDA increased $13 million or 8.7% and margins expanded approximately 60 basis points year-over-year, reflecting disciplined price/cost management and structural cost optimization. Adjusted EPS increased 50% year-over-year in Q4, driven by lower interest expense from our strengthened balance sheet, lower tax expense and the impact of stock repurchases.

Adjusted free cash flow declined $89 million year-over-year in Q4, primarily due to the inclusion of containerboard cash flows in Q4 '25, higher cash taxes, partially offset by better working capital on a year-over-year basis. This brings full year adjusted free cash flow to $279.3 million. As we discussed in Q3, the Middle East conflict created significant disruption in raw material markets, particularly resin. At the time, we expected conditions would allow us to normalize inventory levels during the quarter. However, as supply disruptions intensified and raw material costs remained elevated, we made the decision to maintain higher inventory levels to ensure continuity of supply for our customers.

These elevated inventory balances, combined with higher resin costs, increased our investment in working capital and negatively impacted free cash flow relative to our prior guidance. While this created a near-term cash flow headwind, the decision ensured continuity of supply for our customers. Importantly, this is a working capital timing impact rather than a structural change in our cash generation capabilities. Please turn to Slide 8 for our segment results. In Polymer Solutions, sales increased due to favorable pricing, partially offset by lower volumes. Gross profit percent declined due to product mix and the flow-through of higher resin costs. In Metal Solutions, gross profit dollars and percent improved year-over-year due to favorable price/cost, partially offset by lower volumes.

In Fiber Solutions, net sales benefited from higher volumes and the flow-through of our previously announced April $60 per ton price increase. While gross profit dollars [ and percent, $11 million ] and 230 basis points, respectively, both remain below the prior year due in part to the delayed recognition of our June announced $60 per ton price increase. That increase was recognized by RISI in September, and we expect the full benefit to begin flowing through the P&L in the second quarter of fiscal '27. In Closures, favorable price mix and variable cost management drove approximately 40% year-over-year gross profit dollar growth and a 490 basis point gross margin expansion.

This segment continues to benefit from technologically advanced products, new logo growth and strategic investment. Please turn to Slide 9 for our capital allocation update. Our capital allocation framework remains unchanged as we enter fiscal '27 with a continued focus on maintaining a strong balance sheet, returning capital to shareholders and investing in high-return growth opportunities. Our top investment priority remains organic growth. Our fiscal '27 CapEx guidance is $185 million, up from $160 million in fiscal '26, reflecting increased investment in high-return growth opportunities, primarily in polymers and closures serving our target end markets as well as investments to drive operational efficiency gains in fiber and metals. Returning capital to shareholders remains an important priority.

In fiscal '26, we repurchased $225 million of our shares, representing approximately 6% of the shares outstanding. While our long-term objective remains approximately 2% annually, we took advantage of attractive opportunities to repurchase shares during the year. We will continue allocating capital with discipline while maintaining our commitment to leverage below 2x. Please turn to Slide 10 for our fiscal '27 guidance. Our fiscal '27 guidance reflects our consistent methodology of incorporating potential headwinds while recognizing tailwinds only when they are known and highly likely to occur. Our adjusted EBITDA guidance of $645 million assumes $60 million of favorable price/cost, including $33 million from improved URB pricing relative to OCC cost.

The remaining benefit reflects favorable price/cost in polymers and metals based on current raw material trends and continued pricing discipline. This is partially offset by $20 million of transportation and other non-raw material cost inflation. We also assume a $10 million tailwind from incremental Envaplast ownership and partial year benefits from the Sweetwater closure, partially offset by a $5 million currency headwind. Our volume assumptions represent an $11 million headwind driven by low single-digit declines in metals. We assume flat volumes in polymers, fiber and closures with new customer wins offsetting continued industrial demand softness.

Finally, SG&A represents an $11 million net headwind as approximately $15 million of structural cost savings are more than offset by $30 million of inflation and strategic investments. Turning to free cash flow. Our low-end guidance of $290 million begins with $645 million of adjusted EBITDA and assumes $185 million of CapEx, $50 million of cash interest, $80 million of cash taxes and $40 million largely related to restructuring and pension costs. We also assume flat working capital. While we expect inventory levels to normalize during fiscal '27, our low-end guidance assumes those benefits are offset by inflationary pressures on working capital.

As in prior years, our low-end guidance reflects a conservative view of performance without assuming a broader recovery in industrial demand. Due to our usual Q1 seasonality and the delayed impact of our most recent fiber price increase, which will not fully benefit the P&L until January of '27, our guidance assumes Q1 will be again our lowest EBITDA dollar and margin contributor of the year at approximately 20% of our total EBITDA guidance and flat EBITDA margins in Q1 of '26. I'll now hand it back to Ole on Slide 11.

Ole Rosgaard: Thanks, Larry. Before I close, I want to reinforce the financial progress we make. As this slide illustrates, we are delivering meaningful improvements in profitability, shareholder returns and balance sheet strength. These results reflect the actions we've taken to fundamentally strengthen Greif and provide a solid foundation for continuous value creation. I'm proud of what our team has accomplished and confident in the direction we are taking Greif. Please turn to Slide 12. The progress we've made over the past 2 years reinforces our confidence in Greif's long-term investment thesis. We have a strong foundation, clear priorities for organic growth and margin expansion and the financial flexibility to invest in our future while returning capital to shareholders.

Thank you for your continued trust and support. Operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question will come from the line of Mike Roxland of Truist Securities.

Michael Roxland: Larry, first question, just in terms of the $645 million of adjusted EBITDA guidance for '27, you mentioned $60 million of price/cost benefit includes $33 million from improved URB pricing versus OCC. Does that $33 million incorporate the $60 per ton September price increase that you mentioned goes into effect in your books in January?

Michael Roxland: So that fully bakes in the $60 for the flow-through. Okay. Got it. Perfect. Second question, just back in late 2024 at your Investor Day, you guided to about $1 billion of adjusted EBITDA by fiscal '27. Obviously, Ole highlighted the containerboard and timberland sales and you've also rationalized other assets. Can you help us think about what a normalized EBITDA number would mean today given all those moves?

Lawrence Hilsheimer: Yes. Essentially, obviously, with containerboard gone, I think the simplest thing to think about is if you just backed off the $220 million of containerboard plus the $5 million to $10 of Soterra and then added back in the M&A stuff we've done since then. So I would say, Michael, roughly $750 million kind of thing would be sort of normalized just using that kind of rough math. And that sort of reconciles if you think about how we talk about -- if we ever got back to normalized volumes, I mean, we would be above that number, but we have inflationary costs that have eaten the other way. So that's how I would think through it.

Ole Rosgaard: And Mike, just to add, we remain committed to the long-term earnings ambitions that we outlined at Investor Day that you're referring to. But we've also been clear that we are not managing the business to a headline number or a fixed time line. Our focus is building a much stronger Greif.

Michael Roxland: Very clear. One last question, I'll turn it over. How should we think about your portfolio and any further moves? Obviously, you recently announced the closure of Sweetwater by end of this calendar year as you focus on your resources and businesses and assets where you have leading market positions. So just realizing that you're always evaluating your assets and performance from a portfolio perspective, what do you think is left to be done?

Ole Rosgaard: We are very happy with the portfolio we have right now. We have leading positions in all our portfolio companies. And we also have long runways of growth opportunities, particularly in polymer and closures. When you're #1 or you're the leader of the world in particular, like in metals, it's difficult to grow. So as we've outlined, that's where we are focused on really optimizing the business. But we're very, very happy with the portfolio we have now. It's sharp, it's leading edge.

Operator: And our next question will come from the line of Ghansham Panjabi of Baird.

Joshua S. Vesely: This is Joshua Vesely on for Ghansham. Maybe if I could just start off with a broader volume question. Just looking at your guidance, obviously, flat to low single -- or down low single digits depending on the category. I'm just curious what you guys think the market is going to do this year or what your customers are saying about volumes just in context of what you guys have been talking about in terms of gaining share via your commercial actions.

Ole Rosgaard: Josh, Ole here. So overall, I mean, demand was consistent with our expectations, first of all. As we outlined, we don't have a crystal ball to give a comment on the whole year. We have assumed basically flat demand like we have experienced here now. But I would say in terms of our organic growth engine, in the year, we won more than 4,000 new logos. And we're seeing business from them starting to come through. So as we said, we're helping ourselves, and I'm confident that we will grow the business.

Just to give you an example of this new logo growth, we have a customer that we have dealt with for many years, but this is relating to the data center markets. Through the good work of our commercial organization, we won a very large chunk of this customer's business, and this is a global chemical producer serving the water treatment markets. And through the focus that we now have, we actually won a significant new contract, and this customer is now up 200% compared to the same period last year. And another example is another global customer in the high-end perfume market. We've served this customer for many years with a part of our portfolio.

But again, through the intensive work of our new commercial organization, we managed to secure this customer's other business. In fact, the Chief Procurement Officer named us an official strategic partner. And the result of all that is that our volume with this customer is up 40% compared to the same period.

Lawrence Hilsheimer: Josh, the thing I would supplement to what Ole said is I'd just remind this is low-end guidance. So we're taking the most sort of pessimistic view. We're seeing the trend lines continue where the industrial economy just continues to suffer. If you're not tied into that data center business, everything else is off. And a little even worse in Europe with what's going on there. So we're really excited about the commercial efforts. And obviously, our expectation is we exceed this low-end guidance.

Joshua S. Vesely: Great. And then maybe just for my second question, just curious if you could provide some more specifics on the destocking that you saw in the small plastic volumes. Just more color there on maybe the timing of that and whether or not that's contained in the fourth quarter or if you expect that to kind of linger into 2027?

Ole Rosgaard: Yes. It really, it's twofold. The increase in cost in resin caused customers to destock, hoping that resin will come down again. And that's a big element of that. The other one is the agricultural season, which was very weak so far due to weather events and diesel costs for that matter.

Joshua S. Vesely: And is that supposed to continue into 1Q? Or is it going to linger or is it kind of contained into 4Q?

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Matt Roberts of Raymond James.

Matthew Roberts: Question on fiber, volumes seem to be a bright area and recently took some actions on Sweetwater. You're assuming flat fiber volumes in '27. Are there any offsets within that from the exited tons from Sweetwater? If so, how much? And how do you think about the margin in that business? You spelled out the price/cost benefit in '27, but any other considerations from exiting lower-margin businesses or potential productivity gains from that Sweetwater announcement?

Ole Rosgaard: I mean on Sweetwater, the effect there is 120,000 tons that's been removed and 60% of that was CRB, the remaining was URB. We have moved that URB to the profitable part of that to other mills. I can't give you a percentage of how much that is, but certainly, it's a business we like, and we're still seeing very solid demand in that business. In fact, that's the business that's grown this year.

Lawrence Hilsheimer: Yes. The other part, Matt, is just you asked about other elements of the margin in that business. That one is particularly impacted by the diesel cost and transportation cost increases because you're shipping raw material into the plant and out of the plant at higher levels than maybe in some of our other businesses.

Matthew Roberts: Right, right. That makes sense. And then maybe relatedly on the cost side, but the $15 million in SG&A and the '27 bridge, I might have missed this on the call, but was that net of the incremental $30 million in savings? Or how much inflation is absorbed from the prior cost outs? And given the announcements, basically, is it fair to say that, that incremental $30 million is largely in fiber? Or how would you split that?

Lawrence Hilsheimer: It's pretty much spread across the businesses. So we've got incremental cost saves that are hitting SG&A, about $15 million. The remaining increases will be in our cost of operations. That's offset by $30 million of SG&A cost increases, labor inflation. Medical is just going crazy. So those are the inflationary costs that we are working hard to overcome with the cost-out actions.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of George Staphos of Bank of America.

George Staphos: I wanted to cover a bit the waterfall chart, Larry and Ole on Slide 10. And we're familiar, obviously, with your approach now to basically giving us the most pessimistic view that you can have in terms of your guidance. Of those waterfall bars, if you will, based on what you know in terms of initiatives you have underway, dialogue you have with customers, with employees within the supply chain, which of those bars would have the most potential upside? Would there be a way to dimensionalize that at this juncture, recognizing that you really want to give us more of the low-end guidance.

Second question, in terms of the capital spending this year, the $185 million, you might have mentioned it, and if you did, I missed it. What is embedded in that number for organic growth, high-return projects?

Lawrence Hilsheimer: Yes. So as to your first question, George, on those blocks, the one with the most upside is volume. To the extent our commercial activities drive success, that one has got the most upside in it. Most of the others, the transportation and if somebody can tell us when the Russia, Ukraine and Middle East conflicts end, we might see some upside there, but I don't think anybody's high bets on that. So that's the biggest one, clearly, the volume. On the CapEx, we basically got the -- we've got our safety investments. We've got our maintenance CapEx. Those are fairly consistent. What's the number on that?

Bill D’Onofrio: So on maintenance, it's around $85 million a year, and then we'll spend another $5 million to $10 million on safety.

Lawrence Hilsheimer: So then the balance of that is toward high organic growth projects, George. Now most of those aren't going to deliver any results in this year because we're spending the money now for future. But we're very excited about the number of projects the teams are bringing to us and our ability to execute because of our balance sheet.

George Staphos: That makes sense. I don't want to overdo the point, but I just want to come back to the volume trend in polymers. Were you surprised with the performance relative to what your expectation was going into the quarter? And on the destocking, look, recognizing it's behind you from what your remarks pointed to, normally wouldn't you see destocking when raw material prices are going down as opposed to going up? It sounded like your customers destock because resin prices were going up. So it's -- maybe it's the same -- two sides of the same quarter, but just wanted to probe that.

Ole Rosgaard: On expectations. So it's very difficult to have expectations to the weather and what's going on in the Middle East in terms of diesel costs and all that. But what happened here, George, is it's a seasonal business and customers are building up stock in sort of in advance of the season because once the season starts, you simply can't do it to order.

But what they did because resin costs were increasing, they delayed the stocking exercise, getting ready for the season because there was some speculation that the resin costs will go down and then the plants will kick in and then they will get it cheaper instead of sitting with high stocks with -- at a high cost. So it's kind of the reverse of what you alluded to.

George Staphos: Yes. Look, I get it, it all depends on the context over time, people stock up when costs are heading higher because they're worried about further price hike, but we got it. Was it related to any particular customer or not?

Ole Rosgaard: No. Generally, it generally all our customers.

Lawrence Hilsheimer: Yes. And George, this is one of the things as we got -- as we've gotten more into the jerrycan business, you can store a lot more of those. You don't store a bunch of big steel drum or plastic drums. But small jerrycans, you can speculate, buy them, get and then the weather impacted it as well. So then when they didn't need it, that also contributed to the destock.

Operator: And I would now like to turn the call back to Ole Rosgaard for closing remarks.

Ole Rosgaard: Thank you. And thank you for your questions today and your continued interest in Greif. We remain focused on disciplined execution and building a fundamentally stronger company, and we're confident in our ability to continue that progress in fiscal '27. Thank you for your time.

#3086. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3084. Don't Surrender Standards: Who Decides Whether AI Work Is Any Good?

Marcus Torres is the Chief Product Officer at Quickbase.

​One of the most overlooked aspects of AI’s impact on organizations is how it will affect standards of excellence. While there’s a lot of talk right now about how AI might replace skills or create efficiencies, the real danger for companies of all sizes is mistaking the approval of AI work for judgment of quality.

AI does more than just change who does what work. It changes who develops the judgment to know whether that work is good. ​

Here’s the pattern to look for: As AI takes on more work doing the building—whether that’s code, copy, analysis or the first draft of nearly everything—more people are quietly sliding from the role of creator to approver.

This can often feel like progress, freeing team members from menial tasks. But it’s a double-edged sword if you’re not careful—because those menial tasks mean something. They can create or deepen human judgment, which stops people from becoming irrelevant. Or, at the very least, those tasks are what allow people to build a sense of what’s good and what’s not. ​

In other words, many organizations are still asking, “Can AI do this work?” Yes, of course it can, and it can do that work increasingly well. But there’s a more important question that’s not getting asked as frequently: Who decides if the work is any good?

You might say that there are people who check the work that AI does, and they’re the ones who decide if it’s good. That’s true, but only to a point. Developer surveys are already showing just how far that goes. The reality is that trust in what AI has generated, like code accuracy, has fallen, even as AI usage has steadily climbed. People are approving AI, even as they either believe it less or, worse, question it less. That’s not oversight. ​

And the slippage matters everywhere, not just on the major items. It could be approving an AI-generated client note that misses the nuances of the client’s concerns, accepting an AI-generated piece of analysis that gets key underlying assumptions wrong or leveraging a bit of code that works but can’t properly scale. ​

It also makes people passive in an environment where the imperative should be for them to be active. Organizations need human ingenuity and creativity more than ever, even (or maybe especially) in roles where AI has taken over some of the work. That discernment is invaluable, but it’s become something organizations now have to deliberately look for—a reversal from when these capabilities were simply assumed.

Companies and organizations should rethink that now—and maybe even start assigning it directly as part of people’s jobs. Standards ownership could mean that every team is responsible not only for using AI efficiently but also for defining what “good” looks like in their own context, whether that’s accuracy, usefulness, scalability or customer impact. ​

IT has long been the default for this kind of assessment, asked to hold the line for standards in many companies. But it’s often beyond their scope to judge it. IT is built to judge safety, governance, reliability and risk. It is not always built to judge whether a message is persuasive, whether an analysis answers the right question or whether a product decision meets a customer need. ​

Instead of asking IT to do a job that was never theirs, companies should use governed environments that set clear guardrails from the start. That gives workers more room to create useful, specific solutions while keeping those quality standards closest to the people who understand the work and the problems that need solving. ​

Start by asking yourself a few questions: Does your AI wireframe or feature spec reflect your user research, competitive differentiation or tech constraints that your team understands? Does AI-generated content answer specific questions for your customers or audience, or does it just sound polished? Does an AI-assisted cost model account for real business constraints like supplier relationships or seasonal patterns?

We have reached yet another turning point with AI that goes beyond a single team or tool. Everyone has spent the last few years chasing the question of whether they could build. That’s now been answered: yes. The harder question now is whether what gets built actually changes how the business runs for the better and raises the standard—or if it simply becomes yet another thing to approve. ​

Every organization is at this juncture now. One path with AI—an endless stream of approvals until there’s nothing left to approve—is passive. The other empowers people at all levels to decide what good means and make the tools work for that standard rather than around it. That’s harder work. But it’s more meaningful, and it requires the kind of nuanced human understanding of quality that AI can’t yet replace.

AI can always build something. That’s not the hard part anymore. Now it’s on us to decide what’s worth building and what standards we refuse to surrender. ​​

#3083. AppLovin Turns 81% of New Sales Into Profit: Rapid Earnings Reaction

AppLovin's ad platform added hundreds of millions in revenue last quarter at very little extra cost. Here's what drove the profit gain, where cash fell behind, and what the outlook implies.

AppLovin (APP +10.69%) grew third-quarter revenue 55% to about $2.2 billion, and profit grew faster. Shares rose about 18% in after-hours trading. The ad platform is turning nearly all of its growth into profit: About 81% of the added revenue became operating income, even as research spending more than doubled.

AppLovin's costs barely move when revenue jumps. Total expenses rose only about $150 million, since running more ad spend through the same software costs little extra. That gives management room to spend heavily on research without squeezing margins.

Free cash flow grew about half as fast as net income, and higher tax bills are a big reason. Cash paid for income taxes in the first nine months was more than five times last year's level. Rising receivables, the money customers owe as sales grow, also tie up cash. A much bigger share of profit now leaves as cash taxes.

Guidance says the momentum holds. The midpoint implies roughly 9% growth over the third quarter, with adjusted EBITDA margin expected to stay near this quarter's level. The board also expanded the buyback authorization, and repurchases have already shrunk the share count this year.

Watch whether free cash flow growth catches up to earnings growth next quarter. Also watch whether AppLovin starts breaking out revenue by advertiser type, since the release gives no split showing how much growth comes from outside gaming.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

#3080. Trusted AI Governance Starts Where Intent Becomes Action

CTO at WSO2, Inc., humanizing tech and architecting transformation; author & keynote speaker; advocating distributed, agentic systems.

​Most enterprise AI governance conversations still start with the model. Accuracy, safety, bias, explainability and output reviews dominate the discussion. But now, those concerns are no longer enough.

In the agentic era, AI systems are not just generating answers. They are calling tools, invoking APIs, retrieving data, delegating work and taking action inside business processes.

Now, the enterprise also has to determine whether the agent was allowed to take a specific action, under the right authority, with the right context, through the right tool, at the right time and for the right purpose. Trusted AI governance starts where intent becomes action.

Traditional enterprise governance assumes software behavior can be specified before deployment. A service exposes an API contract. A workflow follows a defined sequence. A release can be reviewed, tested and approved before it goes live. Runtime governance usually confirms that the system continues to behave according to what was already specified.

Agentic systems do not fit that model cleanly. An agent can reason over context, call tools, retrieve data, invoke APIs, delegate tasks and decide when to continue, stop, escalate or retry. The output matters, but the path matters, too. The authority used, data accessed, tools called and decision to act all become part of the governed surface.

That creates an inversion. In deterministic systems, governance can start with the output specification. In agentic systems, the enterprise must govern the boundary where intent becomes action and retain evidence after the action. Pre-deployment review still has value, but there is no final output contract that can be verified once and trusted forever.

A model can be powerful, accurate and useful. That does not make it trusted in an enterprise. Trust comes from the architecture around the model, including controls that make agent behavior inspectable, attributable and bounded.

Inspectable means the enterprise can see what happened, including tool calls, data access, applied policies, human oversight and resulting action. Attributable means the enterprise knows who or what acted, and under whose authority. An agent should not act as an anonymous workload or shared service account. It needs identity, delegated authority and traceable actions.

Bounded means the agent operates within defined limits: access, tools, data, policy, cost, jurisdiction and human approval. Without these properties, trust collapses into hope.

Trusted AI governance requires two complementary enforcement models: inline governance and infrastructure-enforced governance.

Inline governance is implemented inside the agent or application flow. Teams add policy checks, validation logic, safety rules, approval steps and logging directly into the system. This matters because it has access to local workflow context, business intent and domain-specific rules.

But inline governance is not sufficient by itself. In a large enterprise, every team implementing its own governance logic creates uneven coverage. Controls get duplicated, drift over time and become hard to audit consistently.

Infrastructure-enforced governance applies controls outside the agent implementation through gateways, proxies, runtimes, service meshes, identity systems, model gateways, API gateways and other enforcement points. This gives the enterprise a common enforcement layer at shared boundaries for model calls, API calls, tool access, data access and agent-to-agent traffic.

The two models are not substitutes. Inline governance gives domain precision. Infrastructure-enforced governance gives enterprise consistency. One without the other becomes fragmented or too coarse.

Authorization is essential, but it is not the same as safety. An agent may be authorized to use an email tool, but that does not mean every email it writes should be sent. It may include confidential information, make an unapproved commitment or send a message to the wrong recipient.

The risk is rarely in the tool name alone. The risk is in the parameters of the action, such as which customer record, which amount, which recipient, which query, which file, which authority and which purpose. Authorization determines access to a capability. Safety determines whether a specific use is acceptable in context.

Agents also need identity. Many enterprise systems still depend on shared service accounts, user sessions and embedded credentials that are difficult to attribute cleanly. That model becomes dangerous when agents take multistep actions. The enterprise needs to know who the agent is and on whose authority it is acting.

For technology, AI and security leaders, the priority is to make governance executable, not to write another AI policy document.

Start with discovery. You cannot govern agents, tools, models, APIs, delegated authorities or agent-to-agent interactions you cannot see.

Then treat agents as first-class actors. Give them identities, make delegation explicit, and avoid hiding agentic behavior behind anonymous workloads or shared accounts. Define the boundaries where intent becomes action, such as the points where agents reach models, APIs, tools, data, workflows and other agents. Combine inline and infrastructure-enforced controls at those boundaries, and capture evidence after action.

The agentic era will not be governed by policy documents alone. Governance has to be designed before deployment, enforced while agents act and proven after action through evidence. Design-time governance defines policies, tools, evaluations and approval paths. Runtime governance enforces boundaries when agents access systems, use tools, invoke APIs, delegate work and coordinate with other agents.

Evidence closes the loop. Without evidence, governance becomes a claim. With evidence, it becomes something the enterprise can inspect, audit and improve. The enterprises that get this right will not simply “trust AI.” They will build systems where trust is inspectable, attributable and bounded by design.​
